questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with an acute exacerbation of COPD required mechanical ventilation and experienced a consistent drop in oxygen saturation. Auscultation revealed vesicular breath sounds on the right side. Based on the chest radiography findings, what would you expect to hear on auscultation of the left side?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absent breath sounds

Absent breath sounds on the left side are expected in this case of left pneumothorax.

A pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space, causing lung collapse and preventing normal lung expansion, which leads to absent or diminished breath sounds over the affected area. In patients with COPD, particularly during an acute exacerbation, the already weakened and hyperinflated lung tissue can rupture, leading to a pneumothorax. This is a serious complication, especially when mechanical ventilation is required, as the pressure from the ventilator can exacerbate the pneumothorax.

Other options:

Option B: Bronchial breath sounds: Typically heard in conditions like pneumonia, where there is lung consolidation, not in a pneumothorax.

Option C: Increased vesicular breath sounds: These indicate hyperinflation or normal lung function, which is not possible in a collapsed lung.

Option D: Increased vocal fremitus: Fremitus is usually decreased or absent in pneumothorax due to the insulating effect of air in the pleural space.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the recommended treatment for inguinal hernia in infants?
questions.explanation: In infants and children, nearly all inguinal hernias are of the indirect type and result from a patent processus vaginalis (a congenital developmental defect). Because the underlying abdominal wall muscles are typically strong and normal, the only surgical step required is the high ligation and excision of the patent hernia sac. This procedure is called a Herniotomy (Option A). Herniorrhaphy (Option B) involves suturing the abdominal wall to reinforce it, which is unnecessary in infants. Hernioplasty (Option D) involves using a synthetic mesh for reinforcement, which is standard in adults but strictly avoided in growing children. A Truss (Option C) is an outdated external belt that is ineffective and can lead to skin damage and incarceration. Inguinal hernias in infants never resolve spontaneously and carry a high risk of strangulation, so early surgical herniotomy is mandatory. Therefore, simple excision of the sac is the gold standard pediatric surgical intervention
questions.learning: In infants and children, nearly all inguinal hernias are of the indirect type and result from a patent processus vaginalis (a congenital developmental defect).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents with increased thirst and increased frequency and volume of urination. His random blood sugar was 205 mg/dl, what appropriate investigations should be done? i) HbA1c ii) Urine ACR iii) Echocardiography iv) Fundoscopy v) ECG vi) Serum protein electrophoresis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. i, ii, iv, v

In a patient with suspected or newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus, evaluation should include confirmation of glycemic status and screening for early diabetic complications.

Appropriate initial investigations include:

• HbA1c → assesses long-term glycemic control (average glucose over \~3 months).
• Urine albumin–creatinine ratio (ACR) → screens for diabetic nephropathy (microalbuminuria).
• Fundoscopy → detects diabetic retinopathy.
• ECG → evaluates cardiovascular disease, which is common in diabetics.

Tests like echocardiography and serum protein electrophoresis are not routine initial investigations for newly diagnosed diabetes unless specific clinical indications are present.
questions.learning: i, ii, iv, v In a patient with suspected or newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus, evaluation should include confirmation of glycemic status and screening for early diabetic complications.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During an investigation of a community outbreak of acute febrile illness (AFI), an epidemic curve is plotted with number of cases against time of onset of illness. Multiple successive peaks separated by approximately one incubation period are seen, indicating a propagated epidemic. Which disease is associated with this type of epidemic curve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Measles

A propagated epidemic results from person-to-person transmission, producing multiple successive peaks on the epidemic curve, with each peak occurring approximately one incubation period after the previous one. Measles is the classic example of a propagated epidemic because of its high infectivity and direct respiratory transmission.

• Measles spreads from one infected individual to another, leading to successive waves of new cases, which produce a propagated epidemic curve.

Why not the other options?

• B. Typhoid fever: Usually causes a common-source epidemic through contaminated food or water.
• C. Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning: Produces a point-source epidemic due to ingestion of preformed toxin.
• D. Salmonellosis: Commonly causes a common-source food-borne outbreak, not a propagated epidemic.
questions.learning: Measles — A propagated epidemic results from person-to-person transmission, producing multiple successive peaks on the epidemic curve, with each peak occurring approximately one incubation period after the previous one.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient given digoxin started having side effects like nausea and vomiting. The serum concentration of digoxin was 4 mg/dL. The plasma therapeutic range is 1 mg/dL. If the half-life of digoxin is 40 hours, how long one should wait before resuming the treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 80 hours

The treatment can be resumed after 80 hours.

The half-life (T1/2) is the time it takes for the plasma concentration of the drug to be reduced by 50%. In the given scenario, the half-life of digoxin is given as 40 hours. The serum concentration of digoxin is given as 4 mg/dL.

After 40 hours, the serum concentration of digoxin becomes 2 mg/dL (half of the initial concentration), and after 80 hours, it will be reduced to 1 mg/dL. So, to reach a serum concentration of 1 mg/dL (therapeutic range), it will take 80 hours.
questions.learning: 80 hours The treatment can be resumed after 80 hours. The half-life (T1/2) is the time it takes for the plasma concentration of the drug to be reduced by 50%.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drug dosages is not correct for the treatment of leprosy in adults?
questions.explanation: In the standard World Health Organization (WHO) Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for adult leprosy, the correct dose of Rifampicin is 600 mg administered once a month under supervision. A dose of 450 mg (Option D) is incorrect for adults; this lower dose is specifically designated for children aged 9–14 years. Regarding the correct dosages, Dapsone 100 mg (Option A) is the daily self-administered dose for both paucibacillary and multibacillary adult patients. For multibacillary cases, Clofazimine is administered as a 300 mg monthly supervised dose (Option C) combined with a 50 mg daily self-administered dose (Option B). Because the adult regimen relies on the higher 600 mg Rifampicin dose to ensure bactericidal activity against Mycobacterium leprae, 450 mg is inadequate and therefore the incorrect adult dosage in this list
questions.learning: In the standard World Health Organization (WHO) Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for adult leprosy, the correct dose of Rifampicin is 600 mg administered once a month under supervision.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the standard glucose load given for identifying diabetes in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 75 g

For IADPSG criteria, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is done in the fasting state using 75 g of glucose, and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if any one of the following cut-offs is met i.e.

* Fasting: >92 mg/dl

* 1 hour: >180 mg/dl

* 2 hour: >153 mg/dl

Earlier, a two-step approach was being used to diagnose GDM. In this, the first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT). The patients having a positive result of >140mg/dl, are candidates for the OGTT. A 100-gram, three-hour oral glucose tolerance test (GTT), is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus. GDM is diagnosed if two or more values are positive.

Diabetes in Pregnancy Societies of India(DIPSI) recommends a 1-step procedure with 75 g oral glucose without regard to the time of the last meal. A venous plasma glucose value at 2 hours >140 mg/dL is diagnosed as GDM.

Some complications of GDM include:

* Maternal

* Hypertension, preeclampsia

* Hydramnios

* Increased operative interventions

* Future development of diabetes mellitus

* Fetal and neonatal

* Fetal macrosomia

* Congenital anomalies

* Metabolic abnormalities such as hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

* Respiratory distress syndrome

* Subsequent childhood and adolescent obesity

Screening is usually done at 24-28 weeks of gestation. Early diagnosis and treatment are important to prevent complications.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female patient with hearing loss is examined and is found to be Rinne negative at 256 Hz and 512 Hz, while Rinne positive at 1024 Hz. What is the expected air conduction and bone conduction gap?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30-45 dB

The given clinical scenario of hearing loss with a negative Rinne at 256 Hz and 512 Hz and positive Rinne at 1024 Hz indicates air conduction and bone conduction gap of 30-45 dB.

Tuning fork tests are performed commonly with tuning forks of frequencies such as 128, 256, 512, and 1024. The tuning fork of 512 Hz is considered ideal as forks of lower frequencies produce a sense of bone vibration, while those of higher frequencies have a shorter decay time.

Rinne’s test is done by placing a vibrating tuning fork on the patient’s mastoid and when he stops hearing, it is brought beside the external auditory meatus (EAC). If he still hears the sound, air conduction (AC) is better than bone conduction (BC).

The inferences are as follows:

• Rinne's test is considered positive (normal) when the air conduction AC>BC is seen in normal people and people with sensorineural deafness.
• It is considered negative when the BC>AC, and is seen in patients with conductive deafness. It suggests a minimum hearing loss of 15-20 dB.

A prediction of the air-bone gap can be made using tuning forks of 256, 512, and 1024 Hz:

• A Rinne test negative for 256 Hz but positive for 512 Hz indicates an air-bone gap of 20-30 dB.
• A Rinne test negative for 256 and 512 Hz but positive for 1024 Hz indicates an air-bone gap of 30-45 dB.
• A Rinne negative for 256, 512, and 1024 Hz indicates an air-bone gap of 45-60 dB.
questions.learning: 30-45 dB The given clinical scenario of hearing loss with a negative Rinne at 256 Hz and 512 Hz and positive Rinne at 1024 Hz indicates air conduction and bone conduction gap of 30-45 dB.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant presents with severe pallor, failure to thrive, and hepatosplenomegaly. He has been receiving repeated blood transfusions since early infancy. Peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells. Which of the following hemoglobin patterns best supports the diagnosis in this child?
options: Predominant HbA with mildly increased HbA₂
Markedly increased HbF with absent HbA
Normal HbA with mildly reduced HbF
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Markedly increased HbF with absent HbA

A transfusion-dependent infant with severe microcytic hypochromic anemia, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, and target cells is most consistent with β-thalassemia major. It is caused due to defective β-globin chain synthesis causing ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis.

• Markedly increased HbF (fetal hemoglobin)
• Absent or very low HbA
• Variable increase in HbA₂

Clinical features:

• Severe anemia beginning in infancy (after 6 months when HbF declines)
• Transfusion dependence
• Hepatosplenomegaly
• Growth failure
• Bone marrow expansion → skeletal changes
questions.learning: Markedly increased HbF with absent HbA — A transfusion-dependent infant with severe microcytic hypochromic anemia, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, and target cells is most consistent with β-thalassemia major.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of flushing and diarrhea. Further evaluation reveals a mass in the distal small intestine, and laboratory testing shows elevated urinary levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA). Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of a small intestinal mass, cutaneous flushing, and secretory diarrhea is the classic clinical presentation of Carcinoid Syndrome. This syndrome occurs when a carcinoid tumor (a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor) metastasizes to the liver or arises outside the portal drainage, allowing bioactive amines like serotonin to enter the systemic circulation. The definitive diagnostic hallmark is the elevation of urinary 5-HIAA, which is the primary metabolite of serotonin. Neuroblastoma (Option B) is a common pediatric tumor that secretes catecholamines. Leiomyoma (Option C) is a benign smooth muscle tumor without endocrine activity. Chromaffinoma (Option D), or pheochromocytoma, secretes catecholamines and presents with hypertension and palpitations rather than intestinal masses and serotonin-related flushing. Therefore, the intestinal location and high 5-HIAA levels confirm that a carcinoid tumor is the underlying cause of the patient’s symptoms

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the helminth from the life cycle given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strongyloides stercoralis

The image shows the life cycle of Strongyloides stercoralis.

Strongyloides stercoralis is the smallest nematode known to cause human infection. It has both a free-living and a parasitic life cycle. Its natural host is man. The infective form to man is the filariform larva. Infection occurs through penetration of the skin by larvae in the soil. Then, the larvae migrate to the small intestine. They molt twice and become adult female worms in the small intestine. The eggs laid in the mucosa of the intestine hatch immediately releasing the rhabditiform larva (L1 stage). Thus, it is ovoviviparous. These rhabditiform larvae in the bowel can develop directly into filariform larvae that penetrate the colonic wall or perianal skin and enter the circulation to repeat the migration. This establishes ongoing internal reinfection.

The rhabditiform larva can also be passed in the stool. It may directly metamorphose to the infective filariform larva in the soil, or develop into adult worms. The free-living adult worms then pass eggs, which hatch and mature to form infective filariform larvae.

In Ancylostoma duodenale infestation, eggs containing segmented ova (not rhabditiform larvae) are passed in the stool. The rhabditiform larva hatches 2 days after the eggs are passed in the soil.

Note: Based on the method of reproduction, nematodes are classified as follows:

1. Oviparous - They lay eggs:

• Unsegmented eggs: Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichuria
• Segmented eggs:  Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus
• Eggs containing larva: Enterobius vermicularis

2. Viviparous - They produce larvae. e.g., Trichinella spiralis, Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi
3. Ovoviviparous – They lay eggs containing fully formed larvae that hatch immediately. e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis
questions.learning: Strongyloides stercoralis — The image shows the life cycle of Strongyloides stercoralis. Strongyloides stercoralis is the smallest nematode known to cause human infection.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented to OPD with complaints of ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. A diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome was confirmed after examination. Which nerves are compressed in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. III, IV, V(1), VI

In Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome, Cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (Trochlear nerve), VI (Abducens nerve), and V1 (Ophthalmic division of the Trigeminal nerve) get compressed causing ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and sensory loss in the V1 area.

The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows several critical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face. The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of the nose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity.

Superior orbital fissure syndrome is characterized by the following:

* Pain, typically labeled as retro–orbital ache

* Sensory loss/disturbances in the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the 5th cranial nerve

* Ipsilateral ophthalmoplegia due to the involvement of the 3rd, 4th, and 6th cranial nerves involvement

* Ptosis, due to 3rd nerve paralysis

Trauma affecting the orbital region is the most common cause of superior orbital fissure syndrome. Other causes include infections such as herpes zoster ophthalmicus, inflammatory disorders, and tumors. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by imaging modalities like CT or MRI to identify the underlying pathology. Management depends on the cause and may involve surgical decompression, corticosteroid therapy, or antiviral treatment.

Pearl PF0436: Superior orbital fissure

Structures passing through the Superior orbital fissure

Above the common tendinous ring: LFT (Superolateral compartment)

* Lacrimal nerve

* Frontal nerve

* Trochlear nerve

* Superior opthalmic vein

Within the common tendinous ring: BAN (Intermediate compartment)

* Both divisions of oculomotor nerve

* Abducens nerve

* Nasociliary nerve

Below the common tendinous ring (Inferomedial compartment)

* Inferior ophthalmic vein

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman was found dead at home. She was brought to the mortuary by the police and the following findings were noted on examination. Which of the following is the likely cause of her death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Throttling

In the given case scenario and autopsy images showing carotid intimal tear and muscle hematoma with nail marks on neck and absence of ligature mark point towards a diagnosis of throttling.

Other options

Option A- Strangulation by ligature - ligature mark with signs of a struggle would've made this diagnosis more likely.

Option B- Hanging - ligature mark with a suicide note would've made it more likely.

Option C- Drowning- Body recovered from a pond or other water body with other suggestive features like frothing etc  would've made this more likely.
questions.learning: Throttling — In the given case scenario and autopsy images showing carotid intimal tear and muscle hematoma with nail marks on neck and absence of ligature mark point towards a diagnosis of throttling.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a 30-year smoking history presents with an 8-month history of progressive dyspnea and a persistent dry cough. Examination reveals digital clubbing and bilateral fine inspiratory crackles. Pulmonary function tests show FVC at 78% of predicted and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 92%. Based on these findings and his smoking history, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with chronic dyspnea, digital clubbing, and "fine crackles" (Velcro-like rales), which are the hallmark clinical signs of Interstitial Lung Disease. The PFT results show a restrictive pattern: low FVC with a high/normal FEV1/FVC ratio (92%), which rules out obstructive diseases like Asthma (Option A) or COPD (Option D). The provided CT scan provides definitive confirmation, showing a "honeycombing" pattern and traction bronchiectasis. This is the pathognomonic radiological picture of Pulmonary Fibrosis (specifically Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis or UIP). Pulmonary tuberculosis (Option C) would typically show consolidations or cavities rather than diffuse basilar honeycombing. Therefore, the combination of clinical crackles, restrictive lung function, and the classic honeycombing CT appearance makes pulmonary fibrosis the definitive diagnosis. This condition is progressive and irreversible, requiring management of hypoxemia and consideration of antifibrotic therapy
questions.learning: The patient presents with chronic dyspnea, digital clubbing, and "fine crackles" (Velcro-like rales), which are the hallmark clinical signs of Interstitial Lung Disease.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A metal factory worker suffers from noise-induced hearing loss. Which of the following structures will be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Outer hair cells

Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) damages the outer hair cells, starting in the basal turn of the cochlea. Outer hair cells are affected before the inner hair cells.

NIHL occurs after chronic exposure to less intense sounds. The damage caused by noise trauma depends on the frequency of noise (frequency of 2000 to 3000 Hz causes more damage) intensity, duration of the noise, and preexisting ear disease.

The audiogram in noise-induced hearing loss shows a typical notch at 4000Hz both for air and bone conduction known as acoustic dip/boiler's notch. Patients at this stage complain of high-pitched tinnitus and difficulty hearing in noisy surroundings. Pre-employment and annual audiograms for persons working at places where noise is above 85 dB (A) help in the early detection of NIHL.

The human ear can hear frequencies from about 20 to 20,000 Hz. Below 20 Hz, the vibrations are infra-audible, and above 20,000 Hz, they are ultra-sonic. Pure tone audiometry can detect only up to 8000 Hz.

Extended high-frequency audiometry is recommended for early detection of hearing loss, as it can identify hearing impairments before the frequencies necessary for speech comprehension are affected. Distortion product otoacoustic emissions is a more sensitive tool than conventional audiometry, particularly in children under 5 years old for early detection of hearing loss.

A noise of 90 dB(A) SPL (acceptable noise levels, sound pressure level), 8 hours a day for 5 days per week is the maximum safe limit as recommended by the Ministry of Labour. As per WHO, 85 dB(A) is considered the highest safe exposure level up to a maximum of 8 hours.

The silence zone extends to a distance of 100 meters around the premises of hospitals, nursing homes, educational institutions, and courts.

Permissible limits of noise as per the noise pollution (Regulation and Control) rules:

Noise levels are measured in dB(A), which prioritizes middle-range frequencies for assessing noise-induced hearing loss while giving less weightage to low and high frequencies.

Other options:

Option A: Crista ampullaris is a thickened ridge of neuroepithelium in the ampullated end of semicircular ducts.

Option B: Macula is the sensory epithelium of the utricle

Option C: Cupula is a gelatinous mass extending from the surface of the crista (peripheral receptor located in the ampullated end of semicircular ducts) to the ceiling of the ampulla, into which project the cilia of sensory hair cells.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true about longevity dividend?
options: The intervention can delay the onset of the disease
Small amounts of damage is accumulated over time
The older you are the more prone you are to disease
Economic and health benefit for the society
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The intervention can delay the onset of the disease

The intervention can delay the onset of the disease (Statement 1) is true about longevity dividend.

The longevity dividend is a horizontal approach to public health which is based on a broader strategy which means to foster health for all generations. This can be done by developing a new model for health promotion and disease prevention. The longevity-dividend model aims to prevent or delay the root causes of disease and disability by decimating the one major risk factor which is biological aging.
questions.learning: The intervention can delay the onset of the disease — The intervention can delay the onset of the disease (Statement 1) is true about longevity dividend.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-kg toddler requires maintenance intravenous fluid therapy. Using the Holliday–Segar method, what is the total maintenance fluid requirement over 24 hours?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1100 mL

The Holliday–Segar method is used to calculate maintenance fluid requirements in children.

Maintenance fluid calculation:

• First 10 kg: 100 mL/kg/day
• Next 10 kg (11–20 kg): 50 mL/kg/day
• Each kg >20 kg: 20 mL/kg/day

For a 12-kg child:

• First 10 kg = 10 × 100 = 1000 mL
• Remaining 2 kg = 2 × 50 = 100 mL
• Total = 1100 mL/24 hours

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The following Lineweaver-Burk plots depict enzymatic action in the presence of enzyme inhibitors. The enzyme action without inhibitor is represented by a blue line. What type of inhibitors are depicted in images 1 and 2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1- Noncompetitive inhibition 2- Competitive inhibition

The Lineweaver-Burk plot in image 1 depicts non-competitive inhibition, and that in image 2 depicts competitive inhibition.

Important parameters in a reaction include:

• The affinity of the enzyme for its substrate, given by the Michaelis constant or Km. A low Km reflects a high affinity of the enzyme for substrate and vice versa. The value of Km is given by the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is equal to one-half Vmax. It does not change with changes in enzyme concentration.
• Vmax is the maximum velocity of a reaction.

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration by which maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the concentration of the substrate required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased in this condition.

In a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the addition of a competitive inhibitor causes plots with the same y-intercept (Vmax is unaffected) but different x-intercepts (due to increased Km).

Noncompetitive inhibition is by binding of inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

In a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the addition of a non-competitive inhibitor causes plots with the same x-intercept (Km is unaffected) but different slopes and y-intercepts (due to decreased Vmax).

In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors bind with the enzyme-substrate intermediate complex and inhibit it. This leads to a decrease in both Vmax and Km.
questions.learning: 1- Noncompetitive inhibition 2- Competitive inhibition The Lineweaver-Burk plot in image 1 depicts non-competitive inhibition, and that in image 2 depicts competitive inhibition.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
Given below is a USG taken at approximately 8 weeks of gestation. Which anomaly can be observed here?

USG - ultrasound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anencephaly

The given ultrasound image shows an open defect in the calvaria and skin. This is consistent with the diagnosis of anencephaly.

Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. It is one of the earliest detectable congenital defects that can be detected as early as 10 to 11 weeks of gestation.  Screening can also be done by serum estimation of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP). The following are the radiological signs seen in anencephaly.

• Frog eye sign - Absence of cranial calvaria, prominent orbits thereby resembling the face of a frog.
• Shower cap sign - The absence of the cranium could lead to the protrusion of a disorganized mass of brain tissue. This resembles a shower cap giving rise to a characteristic triangular facial appearance.

Neural-tube defects can be prevented with pre-conceptional supplementation of folic acid. A dose of 4 mg daily is recommended in subsequent pregnancies.

The frog eye and showercap signs are shown below:

Other options:

Option B: Hydranencephaly: This condition involves the absence of cerebral hemispheres, replaced by fluid-filled sacs.

Option C: Meningocele: It involves herniation of the meninges through a defect in the skull or spinal column, forming a sac filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

The image below shows meningocele:

Option D: Encephalocele is caused due to defects in the skull through which the meninges and/or neural tissue herniate. The squamous part of the occipital bone is the most frequently affected bone.

The image shows a newborn with encephalocele.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Perception of pain in an area that lacks sensation is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anesthesia dolorosa

Anesthesia dolorosa refers to pain perceived in an area that is otherwise numb or lacks normal sensation. It occurs due to damage to sensory pathways, especially after nerve injury or central nervous system lesions.

• Loss of normal sensory input (anesthesia)
• Simultaneous abnormal spontaneous pain signals from damaged nerves

Clinical examples:

• Trigeminal nerve injury after procedures for trigeminal neuralgia
• Thalamic lesions or other central sensory pathway injuries

Other terms:

B. Hyperalgesia: Increased response to a painful stimulus

C. Paresthesia: Abnormal sensations like tingling or “pins and needles”

D. Allodynia: Pain due to a normally non-painful stimulus

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents with antepartum hemorrhage. Previous ultrasound showed placenta previa, and Doppler demonstrates the placenta adherent to the uterus with invasion and extension into the urinary bladder. What is this pathology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placenta percreta

The clinical scenario of a patient with antepartum hemorrhage, known placenta previa on ultrasound, and a placenta adherent to the uterus with invasion and extension into the urinary bladder is most consistent with placenta percreta.

The placenta accreta spectrum is characterized by abnormally implanted, invasive, or adhered placenta. This occurs due to partial or complete absence of the decidua basalis and imperfect development of the Nitabuch layer. Risk factors include associated placenta previa and previous cesarean delivery as seen in this patient.

There are three variants of this condition based on the depth of trophoblastic growth.

* Placenta accreta, the villi are attached to the myometrium. (Option A)

* Placenta increta, the villi invades into the myometrium.( Option B)

* Placenta percreta, the villi penetrate the myometrium into the serosa. (Option C)

Ultrasound findings in placenta percreta:

* Loss of normal hypoechoic retroplacental zone between uterus and placenta

* Placental vascular lacunae

* Placental bulging into the posterior bladder wall

* Attenuation of retroplacental myometrium

Based on the adherence of placental lobules, all three types of morbidly adherent placenta can be:

* Total - involving all lobules of the placenta

* Focal - involving a single lobule or part of a lobule of the placenta

Morbidly adherent placenta can lead to torrential post-partum hemorrhage. It is managed via C-section and peripartum hysterectomy.

Other options:

Option D: Placental abruption is the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from its bed before delivery, which causes antepartum haemorrhage. It might present as external bleeding or maybe concealed. Risk factors include hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, trauma, Multifetal pregnancy, polyhydramnios, PROM, cigarette smoking, and thrombophilias.
questions.learning: Placenta percreta — The clinical scenario of a patient with antepartum hemorrhage, known placenta previa on ultrasound, and a placenta adherent to the uterus with invasion and extension into the urinary bladder is most consistent with placenta percreta.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a follow-up case of prostate cancer, what do we need to check?
questions.explanation: Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) is the most critical and sensitive marker for monitoring the progression and recurrence of prostate cancer. Serial PSA checks allow for the early detection of biochemical recurrence after surgery or radiotherapy and help evaluate the effectiveness of hormonal therapy. Alkaline phosphatase (Option A) is a marker for bone turnover and may be elevated in the presence of bone metastases, but it is not specific for prostate cancer follow-up. Testosterone (Option C) is monitored specifically in patients undergoing androgen deprivation therapy to ensure "castrate" levels are maintained. Acid phosphatase (Option D), once common, is an outdated marker that has been superseded by the superior sensitivity of PSA. A rising PSA level is often the first indicator of treatment failure, necessitating a change in management. Thus, PSA remains the definitive follow-up tool
questions.learning: Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) is the most critical and sensitive marker for monitoring the progression and recurrence of prostate cancer. Serial PSA checks allow for the early detection of biochemical recurrence after surgery or radiotherapy and help…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents with sudden onset of loud, abnormal breathing sounds. Based on the symptoms, a specific type of stridor is suspected. Stridor is a high-pitched sound caused by turbulent airflow in the upper airway, reflecting the phase of breathing most affected by obstruction. Which type of stridor is most likely in this child?
questions.explanation: In a 2-year-old child, acute onset of loud breathing sounds (stridor) is most commonly caused by obstructions in the extra-thoracic upper airway, such as Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) or a foreign body at the level of the glottis. This typically results in an inspiratory stridor, which is audible only during the inhalation phase. This occurs because the negative pressure within the upper airway during inspiration causes the flexible tissue above the thoracic inlet to collapse inward, narrowing the lumen further. Expiratory stridor (Option B) is associated with obstructions below the thoracic inlet, such as a foreign body in the bronchus or asthma. Biphasic stridor (Option C) indicates a fixed, severe obstruction at the level of the glottis or subglottis that affects both phases of the respiratory cycle. Given the common pediatric presentations of acute airway narrowing, inspiratory stridor is the most frequent clinical finding
questions.learning: In a 2-year-old child, acute onset of loud breathing sounds (stridor) is most commonly caused by obstructions in the extra-thoracic upper airway, such as Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) or a foreign body at the level of the glottis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following contrast agents is safe to use in renal failure patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ultrasound contrast agent

Ultrasound contrast agents are gas-filled microbubbles that are administered intravenously to the systemic circulation. Hence, considered as low risk in patients with renal impairment.

Ultrasound contrast agents are used to enhance the visibility of blood vessels, organs, and tissues during ultrasound imaging. These agents typically consist of tiny gas-filled microbubbles encapsulated within a shell. When injected intravenously, they flow through the bloodstream and resonate in response to ultrasound waves, producing strong echoes that enhance the ultrasound image.

Perflutren/Optison is an ultrasound contrast agent. Levovist (consisting of galactose microparticles, air bubbles, and palmitic acid) is another example of an ultrasound contrast agent. Sulfur hexafluoride with a phospholipid shell is also used as an ultrasound contrast agent.

Other options:

Option A: Gadolinium contrast used in MRI is predominantly excreted through the kidney. In renal failure, it gets accumulated in the body and releases gadolinium ions. Since the ion is toxic, the body tries to contain it by fibrosis resulting in multisystem painful fibrosis called nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

Option B: Iodinated ionic contrast agents increase the risk of Contrast-induced nephropathy(CIN). Hence alternative imaging methods, without iodinated contrast media, should be chosen in patients with considerably impaired renal function (CKD 4 or 5).

Option C: Non-ionic contrast agents have a lower risk of causing adverse reactions compared to ionic contrast agents. They are generally better tolerated by patients, with fewer incidences of allergic reactions and nephrotoxicity. However, USG contrast agents are among the safest in renal failure patients.
questions.learning: Ultrasound contrast agent Ultrasound contrast agents are gas-filled microbubbles that are administered intravenously to the systemic circulation. Hence, considered as low risk in patients with renal impairment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a 13-year-old with acute flaccid paralysis, the pediatrics resident orders an RT-PCR on a CSF sample to identify the causative virus. Which of the following describes the enzyme correctly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. RNA-dependent DNA polymerase

Reverse transcriptase has RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity and it uses RNA as a template and then synthesizes a single-stranded DNA by reverse transcription of RNA, and finally leads to the formation of double-stranded DNA.

The given case scenario is suggestive of paralytic poliomyelitis caused by the poliovirus. Viral RNA is demonstrable in CSF by reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR).

Note: In RT-PCR, reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from RNA which is used as a template for PCR. It is used in detection of viruses from nasopharyngeal swabs (SARS-CoV2, H1N1). In real-time PCR, fluorescent dyes or DNA probes are used to quantify the pathogen DNA load in the specimen. It's used to quantify viral loads in HIV, hepatitis B, etc., and is also called quantitative PCR (qPCR).
questions.learning: RNA-dependent DNA polymerase Reverse transcriptase has RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity and it uses RNA as a template and then synthesizes a single-stranded DNA by reverse transcription of RNA, and finally leads to the formation of double-stranded DNA.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes with complaints of fever and increasing fatigue for the past week. On examination, he is febrile, hypotensive and tachycardic. The findings of his peripheral blood smear are given below. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium falciparum

The given clinical history and the blood smear showing multiple ring forms in RBCs are suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum.

Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria. This means that the fever has a periodicity of 48 hours corresponding to one cycle of erythrocytic schizogony. Malignant because it is a more severe and fatal type of malaria.

Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include unarousable coma/ cerebral malaria (failure to localize or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 min after generalized convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Other manifestations include hemoglobinuria, hyperparasitemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness.

Falciparum malaria shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infection than in infection by other plasmodia. After the ring form in the peripheral blood, the rest of the erythrocytic cycle occurs in the capillaries of the brain and internal organs. So, only ring forms can be seen in the peripheral blood and not the late trophozoites and schizonts. The gametocytes of P. falciparum are crescent-shaped or “banana-shaped” (as shown below), whereas those of the other plasmodia are spherical.

The treatment of choice is artesunate given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary.

In Plasmodium falciparum, recrudescence can be seen which is defined as the recurrence of asexual parasitemia. It usually occurs within 8 weeks of treatment and is due to incomplete treatment or drug resistance.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: If the diameter of an artery was found to be reduced to one-third. By what value does the resistance of the artery increase?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 81 times

The resistance increases by 81 times.

The relationship between the flow in a long narrow tube, the viscosity of the fluid, and the radius of the tube is expressed by the Poiseuille-Hagen formula.

Airflow can be derived from Poiseuille- Hagen formula:

Q =π ΔPr4/8ηL

Where

* Q is the flow rate

* π is pie symbol

* ΔP is the pressure difference

* r is radius

* η is viscosity

* L is length

Also,

Flow rate (Q) = pressure difference (ΔP)/ resistance (R).

Therefore, substituting this in Poiseuille- Hagen formula,

ΔP/ R = π ΔPr4/8ηl

1/R = π r4/8ηl

R = 8ηl/ π r4

Therefore it can be derived that airway resistance is inversely proportional to the radius by the power of four.

In the given question, the diameter is reduced to one-third. So, the radius is also reduced to one-third. Hence, vessel resistance will increase by 34 or 81 times.

With Poiseuille- Hagen formula we might feel that the smallest airways are the major site of resistance. However, the contribution by the smallest airways is very little to the overall total resistance. This is because, the airway branches in each generation exist in parallel rather than in series. As the parallel branching increases, the resistance decreases. (Total cross-sectional diameter of small airways put together is high). Thus the overall resistance of the small airways is very small. Also, airflow velocity decreases substantially as the effective cross-sectional area increases (i.e., the flow becomes laminar).

Other factors affecting airway resistance :

* Lung volume, as lung volume increases the resistance decreases and vice versa. Lung volume increases the transairway pressure thus increasing the caliber of the airway.

* Airway mucus, edema, and contraction of bronchial smooth muscle increase the airway resistance. Its clinical application is seen in asthma, bronchitis, and emphysema

* The density and viscosity of inspired gas also contribute to airway resistance. A gas with more density imparts more resistance.
questions.learning: 81 times The resistance increases by 81 times. The relationship between the flow in a long narrow tube, the viscosity of the fluid, and the radius of the tube is expressed by the Poiseuille-Hagen formula.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man came with complaints of dark-colored stools to the OPD. After undergoing endoscopy, the patient was diagnosed with an upper GI bleed. Which of the following structures is used as a demarcation point to differentiate it from a lower GI bleed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ligament of Treitz

The ligament of Treitz is used as the demarcation point to differentiate between upper gastrointestinal bleeding and lower gastrointestinal bleeding. It is a part of the duodenojejunal junction.

Upper GI bleeding refers to bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, and lower GI bleeding refers to bleeding distal to the ligament of Treitz.
questions.learning: Ligament of Treitz — The ligament of Treitz is used as the demarcation point to differentiate between upper gastrointestinal bleeding and lower gastrointestinal bleeding.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a markedly swollen foot associated with multiple discharging sinuses, as shown in the provided image. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the classic clinical triad for Mycetoma (Madura foot): localized swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and the discharge of purulent fluid containing granules. Mycetoma is a chronic granulomatous infection typically contracted by farmers who work barefoot and sustain minor trauma from thorns or soil. It can be caused by fungi (eumycetoma) or bacteria (actinomycetoma). Squamous cell carcinoma (Option B) presents as a non-healing ulcer but not with multiple sinuses and granules. Nocardia (Option C) is a cause of actinomycetoma but the overall "condition" is termed Mycetoma. Sporotrichosis (Option D) usually follows a "lymphocutaneous" pattern with nodules along the lymphatic channels rather than a massive localized foot swelling. Therefore, the characteristic physical appearance of the sinuses and swelling in a rural worker confirms Mycetoma as the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The image depicts the classic clinical triad for Mycetoma (Madura foot): localized swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and the discharge of purulent fluid containing granules.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: To perform MTP for a mentally challenged female, consent is obtained from?
questions.explanation: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act of India, the general rule is that only the consent of the pregnant woman herself is required for the procedure. However, there are specific legal exceptions for minors (under 18 years) and mentally challenged females. In these cases, the law mandates that the written consent of the legal guardian must be obtained before the MTP can be performed. Consent from the husband or partner (Option A) is never a legal requirement for an adult woman of sound mind. The Doctor (Option C) provides the medical opinion but cannot provide the legal consent. A Magistrate (Option D) might be involved in cases of sexual assault or missing guardians, but the primary legal provision is for the guardian. This requirement ensures that the rights of vulnerable individuals are protected while allowing them access to necessary medical services through their designated legal representative
questions.learning: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act of India, the general rule is that only the consent of the pregnant woman herself is required for the procedure.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA)?
options: It can be used for screening for hearing loss
It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss
questions.explanation: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) is an objective, non-invasive electrophysiological test that measures electrical activity generated in the cochlea and auditory brainstem pathways in response to click stimuli. It is widely used as a screening tool for hearing loss, particularly in neonates, infants, and uncooperative patients who cannot participate in conventional audiometry. Why other options are wrong: (B) It is an invasive procedure is incorrect because BERA is completely non-invasive. It involves only placing surface electrodes on the scalp and earlobes — no surgical intervention or penetration of any body structure is required. (C) It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss is incorrect as a standalone best answer because while BERA can detect sensorineural hearing loss, its primary and most characteristic use is screening — making option A more specific and complete as the correct answer. (D) It is a subjective investigation is incorrect because BERA is a purely objective test — it does not require any behavioral response from the patient. Results are based entirely on recorded electrical waveforms, making it ideal for testing infants and unconscious patients
questions.learning: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) is an objective, non-invasive electrophysiological test that measures electrical activity generated in the cochlea and auditory brainstem pathways in response to click stimuli.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Two blood-stained handkerchiefs are recovered from a crime scene. What is the most appropriate method for handling and preserving these items?
options: Place them in same plastic bag and seal it for preservation
Rinse the bloodstains with water to prevent contamination
Place them in different plastic bags and seal it for preservation
questions.explanation: Biological evidence, particularly wet or blood-stained clothing and items, must be handled with specific protocols to prevent the degradation of DNA. The gold standard for preserving blood-stained items is to air-dry them and then place them individually in an envelope or a breathable paper bag. Paper allows for air circulation, which prevents the buildup of moisture and the subsequent growth of mold and bacteria that would destroy the biological evidence. Plastic bags (Options A and D) trap moisture and accelerate the putrefaction of blood, making DNA analysis impossible. Placing multiple items in the same container (Option A) leads to cross-contamination. Rinsing the stain with water (Option B) is a critical error that washes away the evidence. Proper evidence collection is vital for maintaining the chain of custody and ensuring that forensic results are admissible and reliable in a court of law
questions.learning: Biological evidence, particularly wet or blood-stained clothing and items, must be handled with specific protocols to prevent the degradation of DNA. The gold standard for preserving blood-stained items is to air-dry them and then place them individually…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
In which of the following statements will you suspect primary amenorrhea

1. Failure to attain menarche by 15 years of age
2. Failure to attain menarche even after 3 years of thelarche
3. High levels of TSH and short stature
4. Failure of development of breasts by 13 years of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 4

Primary amenorrhea is suspected in patients who have not menstruated by age 15 or within 3 years of thelarche or has not menstruated by age 14 and shows signs of hirsutism, excessive exercise, or eating disorder. The conventional definition of primary amenorrhea is a failure of the onset of menstruation beyond 16 years of age or failure to attain seconday sexual characteristics by 13 years of age.

Secondary amenorrhea is absence of menstruation for 3 months in a female who was previously menstruating normally.

Causes of primary amenorrhea:

• Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

• Hypothalamic and pituitary dysfunction
• Kallmann's syndrome
• CNS tumors - craniopharyngioma
• Delayed puberty

• Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism

• Primary ovarian failure
• Resistant ovarian failure
• 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency

• Chromosomal abnormalities

• Turner's syndrome (45 X)
• Pure gonadal dysgenesis (46 XX or 46 XY)
• Androgen insensitivity syndrome (testicular feminization syndrome) (46 XY)

• Developmental defect of the genital tract

• Imperforate hymen
• Transverse vaginal septum
• Vaginal atresia/cervical atresia
• Absent uterus in Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome)

• Others:

• Uterine synechiae (congenital)
• Adrenogenital syndrome
• Cretinism
• Juvenile diabetes
• Malnutrition
• Anemia
• Weight loss
• Tuberculosis
questions.learning: 1, 2, 4 Primary amenorrhea is suspected in patients who have not menstruated by age 15 or within 3 years of thelarche or has not menstruated by age 14 and shows signs of hirsutism, excessive exercise, or eating disorder.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the marked region in the given spirometry.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Functional residual capacity

The marked area in the spirometry shows the total amount of air present in the lung after normal expiration. This is called functional residual capacity.

questions.learning: Functional residual capacity — The marked area in the spirometry shows the total amount of air present in the lung after normal expiration. This is called functional residual capacity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Four patients were brought to the casualty after sustaining trauma. Which of the following is the correct match of injuries and signs among the following?
options: Extra dural hemorrhage (EDH)- Pin point pupil
Penetrating injury to eustachian tube- CSF otorrhea
Penetrating injury to eye- Battle sign
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gaze paresis- Mid brain lesion

Gaze paresis- Mid-brain lesion, is the correctly matched pair among the given options.

Traumatic injury to the brain affecting the mid-brain or brainstem dysfunction produces:

* Gaze paresis - Inability of the eye to look across beyond the midline.

* Dysconjugate gaze - Inability of the eyes to work together.

* Roving eye movements.

Battle sign and CSF rhinorrhea are features of a middle cranial fossa fracture.

Middle cranial fossa fracture is associated with:

* CSF otorrhea or rhinorrhea

* Hemotympanum

* Ossicular disruption

* Battle sign: Bruising behind the ear

* 7th and 8th cranial nerve palsies

A double target sign is seen in patients with CSF rhinorrhea. The nasal discharge in a patient with CSF rhinorrhea after head trauma is mixed with blood. When this discharge is collected on a filter paper, it shows a double target sign with a central red spot and a peripheral lighter halo as seen in the image below.

The image below shows the 'battle' sign.

Anterior cranial fossa fracture is associated with:

* Subconjunctival hematoma

* CSF rhinorrhea

* Periorbital hematoma or “Raccoon eyes”

Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes): Pooling of blood surrounding the eyes, associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa (given below).

The pinpoint pupil is seen in patients with pontine hemorrhage and opioid overdose.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient is found on a railway track with hot dry skin, raised temperature, dilated pupils, slurred speech, and a staggering gait. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dhatura poisoning

Dhatura (Datura stramonium)

A plant packed with anticholinergic alkaloids:

• Atropine
• Scopolamine
• Hyoscyamine

Hot dry skin, hyperthermia, mydriasis, slurred speech, and ataxia indicate an anticholinergic toxidrome. Dhatura contains atropine-like alkaloids causing central and peripheral antimuscarinic effects. Classic features are “hot as a hare, dry as a bone, blind as a bat.”

Opioids cause miosis and respiratory depression, not dryness or hyperthermia.

| Feature | Anticholinergic | Opioid | Cocaine

| ------- | --------------- | ------ | -------

| Skin | Dry | Normal | Sweaty

| Pupils | Dilated | Pinpoint | Dilated

| Temp | ↑ | ↓/normal | ↑

| CNS | Delirium | Depressed | Agitated
questions.learning: Dhatura poisoning Dhatura (Datura stramonium) — A plant packed with anticholinergic alkaloids: • Atropine • Scopolamine • Hyoscyamine Hot dry skin, hyperthermia, mydriasis, slurred speech, and ataxia indicate an anticholinergic toxidrome.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with a sac-like protrusion on the lower back, covered by a thin membrane containing spinal cord tissue and nerves, along with lower limb weakness and sensory deficits. The mother reports inadequate folic acid intake during pregnancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The description of a sac-like protrusion on the back containing neural tissue (specifically a myelomeningocele) is the hallmark of Spina Bifida (Option D) . This is an open neural tube defect resulting from the failure of the caudal neuropore to close during the fourth week of embryological development. The associated neurological deficits (weakness and sensory loss) result from the exposed spinal cord. The mother's history of insufficient folic acid intake is a well-documented primary risk factor for this condition. Cleft lip (Option A), Down syndrome (Option B), and gastroschisis (Option C, a ventral wall defect) are different congenital anomalies with distinct presentations unrelated to spinal cord herniation. Therefore, given the specific structural defect and its established link to folic acid deficiency, spina bifida is the definitive diagnosis. Early surgical closure and multidisciplinary management are essential to prevent infection and manage long-term neurological and orthopedic complications
questions.learning: The description of a sac-like protrusion on the back containing neural tissue (specifically a myelomeningocele) is the hallmark of Spina Bifida (Option D) .

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the cycles listed below is absent in muscle tissue?
questions.explanation: Ketogenesis, the metabolic process of producing ketone bodies from acetyl-CoA, occurs exclusively in the mitochondria of liver cells. While muscle tissue can utilize ketone bodies for energy during starvation, it lacks the necessary enzymatic machinery to synthesize them. Glycogenolysis (Option A) and glycogenesis (Option C) are both highly active in muscle tissue, where glycogen serves as a critical local energy reserve for contraction. Lipolysis (Option D), the breakdown of triacylglycerols, also occurs in muscle cells to provide fatty acids for beta-oxidation during aerobic exercise. Because the liver is the sole organ capable of significant ketone body production to be exported to other tissues like the brain and muscles, ketogenesis is definitively absent from muscle tissue. This metabolic compartmentalization ensures that the liver remains the primary provider of alternative fuels during periods of low glucose availability
questions.learning: Ketogenesis, the metabolic process of producing ketone bodies from acetyl-CoA, occurs exclusively in the mitochondria of liver cells. While muscle tissue can utilize ketone bodies for energy during starvation, it lacks the necessary enzymatic machinery to…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with peripheral edema has the following findings on clinical examination: • A soft systolic murmur at the lower left sternal border with raised JVP showing prominent C-V wave. • The murmur increases in intensity on deep inspiration. The most likely valvular abnormality is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tricuspid regurgitation

Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) presents with a pansystolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border, prominent C-V waves in the JVP, and a murmur that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign) due to increased venous return to the right heart. Peripheral edema and raised JVP are features of right-sided heart failure.

Why not the other options?

• A. Ventricular septal defect: Harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border but no prominent C-V waves or inspiratory accentuation.
• B. Mitral regurgitation: Pansystolic murmur best heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla; does not increase with inspiration.
• D. Mitral valve prolapse: Characterized by a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur, best heard at the apex.
questions.learning: Tricuspid regurgitation Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) presents with a pansystolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border, prominent C-V waves in the JVP, and a murmur that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign) due to increased venous return…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A male presents to the ENT department with complaints of unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent episodes of epistaxis. On anterior rhinoscopy, a mass in the superior nasal cavity is visualized. Bone erosion is seen on CT. What is the least likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Antrochoanal polyp

Unilateral nasal obstruction with recurrent epistaxis and a nasal mass should raise suspicion for a sinonasal neoplasm until proven otherwise. Bone remodeling or bony erosion on CT is characteristic of locally aggressive tumors, whereas an antrochoanal polyp is a benign inflammatory lesion that usually arises from the maxillary sinus, extends into the choana, and does not typically present with recurrent epistaxis or bone remodeling.

• Antrochoanal polyp typically presents with:

• Unilateral nasal obstruction
• Mouth breathing
• Nasal discharge

• Epistaxis is uncommon, and bone remodeling is not a typical feature.

Why not the other options?

• B. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma: Highly vascular tumor presenting with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and bone remodeling/remodeling of adjacent structures on imaging.
• C. Olfactory esthesioneuroblastoma: Malignant tumor arising from the olfactory neuroepithelium in the superior nasal cavity; commonly presents with unilateral obstruction, epistaxis, and bony destruction/remodeling.
• D. Inverted papilloma with malignant transformation: Locally aggressive sinonasal tumor causing unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and bone remodeling or erosion; associated with an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.learning: Antrochoanal polyp Unilateral nasal obstruction with recurrent epistaxis and a nasal mass should raise suspicion for a sinonasal neoplasm until proven otherwise.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old Rh-negative woman had one full-term pregnancy 3 years ago. Her husband is Rh-positive. She is unsure whether she received anti-D immunoglobulin after delivery. The child was later found to be Rh-negative. She is now planning another pregnancy. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Administer anti-D immunoglobulin immediately before conception
Perform an Indirect Coombs Test (Indirect Antiglobulin Test) to assess maternal sensitization
Administer anti-D immunoglobulin only after the next delivery regardless of the baby’s Rh status
No further evaluation or prophylaxis is required
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Perform an Indirect Coombs Test (Indirect Antiglobulin Test) to assess maternal sensitization

A previously pregnant Rh-negative woman with an uncertain history of anti-D prophylaxis should undergo an Indirect Coombs Test (ICT) before or early in the next pregnancy to determine whether she has already become alloimmunized (sensitized).

In this case, the previous baby was Rh-negative, so anti-D prophylaxis was actually not indicated after that delivery because there was no Rh incompatibility. However, since the maternal sensitization status is unknown, the appropriate next step is to screen for anti-D antibodies using ICT.

High-Yield Points

• Indirect Coombs Test (ICT): Detects maternal anti-D antibodies (screening for Rh sensitization).
• Direct Coombs Test (DCT): Detects antibodies attached to fetal/neonatal RBCs.
• Anti-D immunoglobulin is prophylactic, not therapeutic—it is not given before conception.
• Anti-D is administered only if the mother is unsensitized and after a sensitizing event or delivery of an Rh-positive infant.
questions.learning: Perform an Indirect Coombs Test (Indirect Antiglobulin Test) to assess maternal sensitization A previously pregnant Rh-negative woman with an uncertain history of anti-D prophylaxis should undergo an Indirect Coombs Test (ICT) before or early in the next…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Despite substantial improvements in immunization coverage, institutional deliveries, and healthcare accessibility under the rural health program, these indicators continued to lag considerably behind those observed in urban populations. Which of the following pillars of primary health care is most likely to be exploited?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Equitable distribution

Equitable distribution is a core principle of Primary Health Care (PHC), ensuring that essential health services are available and accessible to all segments of the population, irrespective of geographic location or socioeconomic status. Persistent disparities between rural and urban health indicators, despite overall improvements, reflect a failure to achieve equitable distribution of healthcare.

Why not the other options?

• A. Appropriate technology: Refers to the use of scientifically sound, affordable, and locally acceptable technologies; it does not address rural–urban disparities in access.
• B. Community participation: Involves active involvement of the community in planning and implementing health programs but does not primarily explain unequal service distribution.
• C. Intersectoral coordination: Refers to collaboration between sectors such as health, education, sanitation, and nutrition to improve health outcomes; it is not the main issue highlighted in the question.
questions.learning: Equitable distribution Equitable distribution is a core principle of Primary Health Care (PHC), ensuring that essential health services are available and accessible to all segments of the population, irrespective of geographic location or socioeconomic status.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presented with easy fatigability, irritability and inability to concentrate. Labs revealed the following findings a and b (light and oil immersion respectively) on the bone marrow aspiration. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glucocerebrosidase

The given clinical scenario of a child with easy fatiguability, irritability, and inability to concentrate with the images showing a crumpled tissue paper appearance(Gaucher's cell) is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase). I

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype.

Gaucher's cells - These are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.

Option A: Deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A is seen in Tay-Sachs disease. The deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A and B causes Sandhoff's disease. Clinical features are seizures, macrocephaly, and hyperacusis.

Option C: Deficiency of sphingomyelinase leads to Niemann-Pick disease. It is characterized by the presence of foam cells in the bone marrow. There may be pulmonary infiltrates leading to lung failure.

Option D: Deficiency of N-acetylglucosaminidase leads to Sanfillipo's disease. It is a type of mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS - III). There is an accumulation of heparan sulfate leading to severe cognitive degeneration.
questions.learning: Glucocerebrosidase — The given clinical scenario of a child with easy fatiguability, irritability, and inability to concentrate with the images showing a crumpled tissue paper appearance(Gaucher's cell) is suggestive of Gaucher's disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a case of shoulder dystocia, if the McRoberts maneuver fails, what is the next appropriate step in management?
questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency where the fetal head is delivered but the anterior shoulder remains stuck behind the maternal symphysis pubis. The first-line management is the McRoberts maneuver (hyperflexing the mother's hips). If this fails, the next immediate step is applying Suprapubic pressure (Rubin I maneuver) to help dislodge the shoulder. Woods maneuver (Option A, internal rotation) and Gaskin maneuver (Option B, all-fours position) are subsequent internal or positional maneuvers performed if suprapubic pressure is unsuccessful. The Zavanelli maneuver (Option D) is an extreme "last resort" involving pushing the head back into the uterus for an emergency C-section. A useful mnemonic for the sequence is ALARMER: Ask for help, Legs (McRoberts), Anterior shoulder pressure (Suprapubic), Rubun/Woods, Manual delivery of posterior arm, Episiotomy, Roll (Gaskin). Rapid and sequential application of these maneuvers is critical to prevent neonatal brachial plexus injury or hypoxic brain damage
questions.learning: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency where the fetal head is delivered but the anterior shoulder remains stuck behind the maternal symphysis pubis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman presents with breathlessness and fatigue and has a past history of breast cancer treated with chemoradiation. Examination reveals a jugular venous pulse with prominent rapid x and y descents. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of chest radiation for breast cancer is a major risk factor for developing radiation-induced constrictive pericarditis. The key diagnostic physical sign is the jugular venous pulse (JVP) showing "rapid x and y descents". This "W" or "M" shaped JVP occurs because the rigid pericardium allows rapid early diastolic filling (steep y descent) but then abruptly halts it (the dip-and-plateau sign). Cardiac tamponade (Option B) typically shows a prominent x-descent but an absent or blunted y-descent. Dilated (Option C) and Restrictive (Option D) cardiomyopathies lack this specific rapid y-descent pattern. The provided X-ray (Option R) likely displays pericardial calcification, which is pathognomonic for constriction. Other classic findings include Kussmaul's sign and a pericardial knock. Management usually involves surgical pericardiectomy. Therefore, the clinical history and JVP morphology definitively point to constrictive pericarditis
questions.learning: The patient’s history of chest radiation for breast cancer is a major risk factor for developing radiation-induced constrictive pericarditis. The key diagnostic physical sign is the jugular venous pulse (JVP) showing "rapid x and y descents".

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following layers is responsible for maintaining the hydration and transparency of the cornea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endothelial cells

The hydration level and transparency of the cornea is maintained mainly by the endothelial cells of the cornea.

The endothelium possesses Na+/K+ ATPase, which keeps the corneal stroma in a relatively dehydrated state. This helps maintain corneal transparency. Endothelial cells decrease in number with age. If the cornea becomes overhydrated, it begins to scatter light and gradually begins to lose its transparency

Other factors contributing to the transparency of the cornea are as follows:

• Regular arrangement of corneal lamellae (Maurice theory)
• The peculiar refractive index of corneal lamellae (Goldmann theory)
• Avascularity of the cornea
• A balance between the intraocular pressure (IOP) and swelling pressure

The different layers of the cornea are as follows:

• Epithelium
• Bowman’s membrane
• Stroma (substantia propria)
• Dua’s layer (pre-Descemet’s layer)
• Descemet’s membrane
• Endothelium
questions.learning: Endothelial cells — The hydration level and transparency of the cornea is maintained mainly by the endothelial cells of the cornea. The endothelium possesses Na+/K+ ATPase, which keeps the corneal stroma in a relatively dehydrated state.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with anemia and hemoglobinuria. Investigations reveal increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). The peripheral smear image is given below. Which of the following physical examination findings can support the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mechanical second heart sound

The above scenario with anemia, increased LDH, and hemoglobinuria along with peripheral smear showing schistocytes are suggestive of macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). The presence of a mechanical second heart sound can support the diagnosis.

Macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia is a type of hemolytic anemia that results from trauma to red cells by artificial mechanical cardiac valves that produce turbulent blood flow and pressure gradients that cause hemolysis from shear forces. This traumatic damage leads to intravascular hemolysis and the appearance of red cell fragments (schistocytes), burr cells, helmet cells, and triangle cells in blood smears.

The given below peripheral smear shows schistocytes and helmet cells.

Laboratory findings in hemolytic anemia resulting from trauma to red cells:

• Hemoglobin- decreased
• Reticulocytes- increased
• Platelets- normal
• Unconjugated bilirubin- increased
• Lactate dehydrogenase- increased
• Haptoglobin- decreased
• Hemoglobinuria due to intravascular hemolysis

Treatment is conservative. But, if more than mild anemia develops, reintervention to correct regurgitation may be required.

Option A: Splenomegaly is seen in various disorders of white and red cells. But splenomegaly in intravascular hemolysis is less likely.

Option B: Frontal bossing is seen in thalassemia due to expansion of hematopoietically active marrow. An X-ray of the skull shows a 'crewcut' appearance. Peripheral smear in thalassemia shows microcytic hypochromic cells with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, and target cells.

Option D: Goiter is usually associated with iron deficiency anemia. A peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic cells.
questions.learning: Mechanical second heart sound — The above scenario with anemia, increased LDH, and hemoglobinuria along with peripheral smear showing schistocytes are suggestive of macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the drug of choice for scrub typhus during pregnancy and otherwise respectively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Azithromycin, doxycycline

The drug of choice for a case of scrub typhus during pregnancy is azithromycin. For other patients the drug of choice is doxycycline.

An alternative treatment option in pregnant women and patients allergic to doxycycline is chloramphenicol.
questions.learning: Azithromycin, doxycycline — The drug of choice for a case of scrub typhus during pregnancy is azithromycin. For other patients the drug of choice is doxycycline.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25 year old male with history of fever and enlarged lymph nodes and sore throat was suspected to have infectious mono-nucleosis and was ordered a Paul Bunnel test. Which of the following is the principle of the test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Heterophile antibody test

Paul Bunnell test is a heterophile antibody reaction test and is used in glandular fever like Infectious Mononucleosis.

Heterophile antibodies have the ability to agglutinate RBCs of different animal species.

Paul Bunnell test uses sheep erythrocytes for agglutination and Monospot test uses horse erythrocytes for agglutination.

In Infectious Mononucleosis, IgM heterophile antibodies are detectable for the first 3 months of infection and they can agglutinate sheep erythrocytes.
