questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which among the following is the key feature of depression?
options: Loss of interest in pleasurable activties
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loss of interest in pleasurable activties

The key feature of depression among the given is loss of interest in pleasurable activities.

The Diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder are as follows:

A. Five or more of the following symptoms have been present during the same 2-week period. At least one of the symptoms is either depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure.

* Depressed mood most of the day

* Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia)

* Significant weight loss when not dieting or weight gain, decrease or increase in appetite

* Insomnia or hypersomnia

* Psychomotor agitation or retardation

* Fatigue or loss of energy

* Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt

* Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness

* Recurrent thoughts of death, recurrent suicidal ideation

B. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

C. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or to another medical condition.

D. The occurrence of the major depressive episode is not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, or other specified and unspecified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders.

E. There has never been a manic episode or a hypomanic episode.
questions.learning: Loss of interest in pleasurable activties — The key feature of depression among the given is loss of interest in pleasurable activities. The Diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder are as follows: A.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: An 18-year-old girl was brought by her mother with complaints of primary amenorrhea and acute retention of urine. She had cyclical abdominal pain and on examination, a supra pubic mass and a tense bluish bulge were seen in her vagina. What is the most appropriate cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Imperforate hymen

The features of primary amenorrhea, cyclical abdominal pain, acute retention of urine along with a tense bluish bulge make the diagnosis of imperforate hymen more likely.

Imperforate hymen is a type of Mullerian defect, of urogenital origin. Failure of canalization leads to the formation of mucocolpos; this may be recognized in early infancy. However, the anomaly often continues unrecognized until puberty. It presents with amenorrhoea in the presence of secondary sexual characters, cyclic abdominal discomfort, retention of urine and a suprapubic bulge caused by hematocolpos. Examination of the external genitalia reveals the presence of a telltale bluish bulging membrane in the region of the hymen.

A simple cruciate incision followed by an excision of the hymenal tags allows the drainage of the retained menstrual blood. The operation should be performed under aseptic conditions and under an adequate antibiotic cover to avoid any ascending infection.

Other options :

Option B - Transverse vaginal septum is a much rarer condition that occurs due to faulty fusion or canalization of the urogenital sinus and the Müllerian ducts. The majority of the cases involve the upper portion of the vagina. It can be differentiated from imperforate hymen by the presence of a short vagina and the absence of a bulging membrane.

Option C - Vertical vaginal septum occurs when the distal parts of the Müllerian ducts fail to fuse. On examination, there is a longitudinal anteroposterior septum which may be partial or complete, extending right down to the vaginal outlet. It may be associated with a double uterus and double cervix.

Option D - Mullerian agenesis is characterized by congenital absence of the uterus and vagina (small rudimentary uterine bulbs are usually present). The female presents with primary amenorrhea and preservation of female secondary sexual characteristics.
questions.learning: Imperforate hymen — The features of primary amenorrhea, cyclical abdominal pain, acute retention of urine along with a tense bluish bulge make the diagnosis of imperforate hymen more likely.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 17-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea accompanied by cyclical lower abdominal pain, suggesting concealed menstruation. She has normal secondary sexual characteristics. On examination, an abdominal mass is palpable, and a bluish bulge is seen at the vaginal introitus on separating the labia, indicating an obstructive genital tract anomaly. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
options: The cruciate incision on the hymen
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic triad of "imperforate hymen": primary amenorrhea, cyclical pelvic pain (cryptomenorrhea), and a "bluish bulge" at the introitus. The bulge is caused by the accumulation of menstrual blood behind the intact hymen (hematocolpos). The "abdominal lump" represents a hematometra (blood in the uterus) or a hugely distended vagina reaching the abdomen. The standard surgical treatment is a "cruciate (cross-shaped) incision" on the hymen to allow the trapped old blood to drain. Excision of a septum (Option A) is used for a transverse vaginal septum, which would not typically present with a bulge at the introitus. Extensive vaginoplasty (Option B) is for vaginal agenesis. Hysterectomy (Option D) is entirely inappropriate as the uterus is normal and reproductive potential is preserved. After the incision, the redundant flaps of the hymen are often excised to prevent re-closure. Immediate pain relief follows the drainage of the chocolate-colored blood
questions.learning: The patient presents with the classic triad of "imperforate hymen": primary amenorrhea, cyclical pelvic pain (cryptomenorrhea), and a "bluish bulge" at the introitus.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the hospital with complaints of pain and limping. The symptoms started 6 months back and gradually worsened. The child appears to be healthy with normal height and weight. On examination, there is mild wasting on the right side. Abduction (especially in flexion) and internal rotation are limited due to pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perthes disease

A young male patient with normal height and weight and complaints of pain and limping gradually progressing over 6 months and examination findings of limited abduction and internal rotation is likely to have Perthes's disease. The image shows a mushroom-shaped femoral head that is laterally displaced in a dysplastic acetabular socket.

Between 4 and 7 years of age, the femoral head may depend on the lateral epiphyseal vessels for its blood supply and venous drainage almost entirely. These vessels situated in the retinacula make them susceptible to stretching and to pressure from an effusion.

The disease is characterized by the disruption of blood flow to the head of the femur. Due to which the bone goes for osteonecrosis and stops growing. Over time, healing occurs by new blood vessels infiltrating the dead bone and removing the necrotic bone which leads to a loss of bone mass and a weakening of the femoral head. Clinical features include a boy of 4-8 years complaining of pain and limping. Symptoms continue for weeks on end or recur intermittently. The hip looks deceptively normal. Although initially, all movements are painful; with time, abduction with internal rotation is always limited.

Xray findings depend on the stages

* Necrotic phase: Radiographically dense areas which indicate new bone formation is soon followed by bone necrosis.

* Fragmentation phase: Alternating patches of density and lucency. Sometimes a crescentic subarticular fracture is often seen in lateral view

* Re-ossification phase: Epiphyseal density increases in this phase

* Healing phase: Normal femoral head or mushroom-shaped femoral head which is laterally displaced in a dysplastic acetabular socket.

There are different 'head at risk signs' described by Catrell which include:

* lateral subluxation of the femoral head

* speckled calcification in the lateral epiphysis

* Epiphysis being horizontal

* Gage's sign: V-shaped osteoporotic segment in the lateral epiphysis and adjacent metaphysis.

Guidelines to treatment are derived from the review by Herring,

* Children under 6 years - symptomatic treatment including activity modification is appropriate

* Children aged 6-8 years - Bonge age and Catterall Staging determines the modality of treatment. Options include abduction brace or osteotomy.

* For children aged 9 and above - operative containment is the choice.

Note:Salter's extrusion angle helps to assess the femoral head extrusion. Normal is 50 degrees or more.
questions.learning: Perthes disease — A young male patient with normal height and weight and complaints of pain and limping gradually progressing over 6 months and examination findings of limited abduction and internal rotation is likely to have Perthes's disease.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures passes through the foramen marked by the arrow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thoracic duct

The marked arrow indicates the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm. Out of the given options, the thoracic duct passes through it.

The diaphragm has several openings through which structures can pass between the thorax and abdomen. There are three large openings and several smaller openings. The large openings are the aortic hiatus, the esophageal hiatus, and the caval hiatus.

The aortic opening is the most posteroinferior large diaphragmatic opening. It is found at the level of the lower border of the twelfth thoracic vertebra and the corresponding intervertebral disc. It is bounded by the diaphragmatic crura laterally, vertebral column posteriorly, and the median arcuate ligament anteriorly.

Structures passing through the aortic opening are:

* Aorta

* Thoracic duct

* Azygous vein

* Hemiazygous vein

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ketone bodies are not utilized by the liver because it lacks:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiophorase

Ketone bodies are not utilized in the liver because it lacks the enzyme thiophorase.

Ketone bodies are synthesized in the liver mitochondria (by ketogenesis) and transported in the blood to the peripheral tissues. Here they are utilized by the following steps:

1. β-hydroxybutyrate (the most predominant ketone body) is oxidized to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase producing NADH.
2. Acetoacetate is then activated to acetoacetyl CoA by transferring a CoA molecule from succinyl CoA by succinyl CoA-acetoacetyl CoA transferase (thiophorase).
3. Acetoacetyl CoA is cleaved into two acetyl CoA molecules by thiolase and oxidized into CO2 by the TCA cycle.

Thiokinase or Acyl CoA synthetase catalyzes the only energy-requiring step in fatty acid oxidation. In the presence of ATP and coenzyme A, thiokinase catalyzes the conversion of a fatty acid to acyl-CoA. Acyl-CoA is the active form of fatty acid. This step uses one high-energy phosphate and forms AMP and PPi.

When higher than normal ketone bodies are present in the blood or urine, it is called ketonemia or ketonuria, respectively. The overall condition is called ketosis. The metabolism of free fatty acids to produce ketone bodies is exaggerated in pathologic states such as starvation and diabetes mellitus, thus causing ketosis. The continued buffering and excretion of ketone bodies deplete the alkali reserve, causing ketoacidosis.
questions.learning: Thiophorase Ketone bodies are not utilized in the liver because it lacks the enzyme thiophorase. Ketone bodies are synthesized in the liver mitochondria (by ketogenesis) and transported in the blood to the peripheral tissues.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: All the following are properties of ventricular muscle fibers: 1. All or none law 2. Length-tension relation 3. Tetanus 4. Long refractory period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, and 4

All-or-None Law

• Cardiac muscle behaves as a functional syncytium
• Once threshold reached → entire ventricle contracts maximally
• No graded contraction like skeletal motor units

Length–Tension Relationship

• Preload ↑ → sarcomere length ↑ → force ↑
• Mechanism:

• Optimal actin-myosin overlap
• ↑ Ca²⁺ sensitivity of myofilaments

This is the Frank-Starling law: “The heart pumps what it receives”

Ventricular muscle behaves like a syncytium with unique electrical discipline.

It contracts as a unit, obeys Frank–Starling law, and absolutely refuses tetanus.

Cardiac action potential (with plateau)

↓

Prolonged Ca²⁺ influx (L-type channels)

↓

Long absolute refractory period

↓

No re-excitation possible

↓

No summation → No tetanus

• Cardiac AP duration: \~200–300 ms
• Contraction duration: overlaps with refractory period

So:

• Second stimulus cannot trigger contraction
• Prevents sustained contraction (which would be fatal)

| Option | Property | Present in Ventricular Muscle? | Explanation

| ------ | -------- | ------------------------------ | -----------

| 1 | All-or-none law | ✅ YES | Entire myocardium contracts as a syncytium via gap junctions

| 2 | Length-tension relation | ✅ YES | Basis of Frank-Starling mechanism (↑ filling → ↑ force)

| 3 | Tetanus | ❌ NO | Prevented due to long refractory period

| 4 | Long refractory period | ✅ YES | Due to plateau phase (Ca²⁺ influx)
questions.learning: 1, 2, and 4 All-or-None Law • Cardiac muscle behaves as a functional syncytium • Once threshold reached → entire ventricle contracts maximally • No graded contraction like skeletal motor units Length–Tension Relationship • Preload ↑ → sarcomere length ↑ →…

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In the case of rape of a young child, the hymen is usually:
options: Ruptured since it is superficially situated
Ruptured since it is very thin
Unruptured since it is deeply situated
Unruptured since it is highly elastic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Unruptured since it is deeply situated

In the case of a young child, the hymen is deeply situated and usually intact after intercourse. As the vagina is very small, it is impossible for the penetration of the adult organ to take place.

In children, there are few or no signs of general violence, as the child is unaware of the assault and incapable of resisting. A few indicators for inquiry are:

• Pain on urination and/or defecation
• Abdominal pain
• Inability to sleep
• Sudden withdrawal from peers/adults
• Feelings of anxiety
• Nervousness
• Helplessness
• A feeling of ending one’s life
questions.learning: Unruptured since it is deeply situated — In the case of a young child, the hymen is deeply situated and usually intact after intercourse. As the vagina is very small, it is impossible for the penetration of the adult organ to take place.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: How is an electrical synapse different from a chemical synapse?
options: No cytoplasmic continuity between presynaptic and postsynaptic membrane
Connexons are involved in electrical synapse
Electrical synapse has more latent period than chemical synapse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Connexons are involved in electrical synapse

In electrical synapses, the cytoplasm of adjacent cells is directly connected by gap junctions (connexons) that allow free movement of ions from the interior of one cell to the interior of the next cell.

The transmission in electrical synapses is bidirectional and there is no synaptic delay. Unlike chemical synapses, electrical synapse has cytoplasmic continuity.

Note:

Most of the synapses used for signal transmission in the central nervous system are chemical synapses.
questions.learning: Connexons are involved in electrical synapse — In electrical synapses, the cytoplasm of adjacent cells is directly connected by gap junctions (connexons) that allow free movement of ions from the interior of one cell to the interior of the next cell.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the most favourable prognostic parameter in Bell’s palsy?
options: Incomplete paralysis in the first week
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Incomplete paralysis in the first week

Bell’s palsy is an acute idiopathic lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, thought to result from reactivation of Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) causing inflammation and edema of the facial nerve within the facial canal.

The most important prognostic factor is the severity of facial weakness at presentation. Patients with incomplete facial paralysis have an excellent prognosis, with the majority achieving complete recovery.

Why not the other options?

• B. Mild CSF lymphocytosis: CSF examination is not routinely performed in Bell’s palsy and has no prognostic significance.
• C. Denervation on EMG after 10 days: Indicates significant axonal degeneration and is associated with a poor prognosis.
• D. Pain behind the ear: Common early symptom but does not predict recovery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are true about superior mesenteric artery syndrome except?
options: Third part of duodenum is compressed
Angle between SMA and aorta is more than 70 degrees
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Angle between SMA and aorta is more than 70 degrees

Option B is the false statement. In superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome, the aortomesenteric angle is reduced to less than 25 degrees. The normal aortomesenteric angle is approximately between 38-65 degrees.

SMA syndrome, also called Wilkie's syndrome (option D), is characterized by an obstruction of the third part of the duodenum by the SMA (option A) due to compression against fixed retroperitoneal structures.

Symptoms include episodic epigastric pain associated with vomiting. Risk factors include rapid childhood growth without compensatory weight gain, profound weight loss, abdominal surgery, inflammatory diseases of the abdomen, and immobilization in a cast that increases lordosis and accentuates the angle of the SMA with the aorta.

Abdominal CT angiography is the investigation of choice. The CT image below shows narrowed aortomesenteric angle in SMA syndrome:

Lifestyle therapy includes frequent small feedings and patients may benefit from lying prone or on their left side postprandially.

In some cases, weight gain or removal of a body cast improves symptoms. Laparoscopic lysis of the ligament of Treitz is beneficial in few cases. The preferred surgical treatment is Strong's procedure involving duodenojejunostomy (option C).
questions.learning: Angle between SMA and aorta is more than 70 degrees Option B is the false statement. In superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome, the aortomesenteric angle is reduced to less than 25 degrees.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following vitamins is breast milk deficient in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin K

Breast milk is deficient in vitamin K.

Therefore infants have to be supplemented with vitamin K to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

The composition of breast milk varies at different time points of lactation to suit the needs of the baby.

* Colostrum is secreted in small quantities during the first 3 to 4 days. It is thick, and yellow and contains many antibodies, immune-competent cells, and vitamins A, D, E, and K.

* Transitional milk is the one that is seen after 3-4 days until 2 weeks and has an increased fat and sugar content while the protein and immunoglobulin content reduces.

* Mature milk is secreted after transitional milk. It is essential for the baby's optimum growth as it contains all the nutrients. It is thinner and more watery.

Foremilk is the one that is secreted during the initial feed. It is watery and quenches the thirst of the baby. It is rich in proteins, sugar, vitamins, minerals, and water. Hindmilk is rich in fat and provides energy. It gives a sense of satiety to the baby. Hindmilk comes towards the end of the feed.

Components of breast milk and diseases they protect against:

Components of breast milk
Protection against

Lysozyme

• Escherichia coli, Salmonella
• Entamoeba histolytica

Lactoferrin

• E. coli, Shigella, Salmonella
• E. histolytica, Giardia lamblia
• Plasmodium falciparum
• Rotavirus

Bifidus factor
E. coli, Shigella, Salmonella

Low levels of para-aminobenzoic acid
Plasmodium

Breastmilk is also deficient in vitamin D and exclusively breastfed infants can develop vitamin D deficiency unless adequately supplemented.

Human milk is a rich source of vitamin C and contains around 5-15mg/100cal. Vitamin C is found in higher levels in breast milk than in cow milk.
questions.learning: Vitamin K Breast milk is deficient in vitamin K. Therefore infants have to be supplemented with vitamin K to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A chronic smoker with a 20-year occupational history of working in a cement factory develops mesothelioma. This association is most likely attributable to which exposure?
questions.explanation: Mesothelioma is a malignant tumor of the pleura that is almost exclusively associated with chronic exposure to asbestos fibers. Asbestos is commonly used in construction and cement manufacturing. The inhalation of these fibers leads to chronic pleural inflammation and mutations. Bagassosis (Option A) is caused by exposure to sugar cane dust. Silicosis (Option B) results from inhaling silica dust in industries like sand mining. Coal worker pneumoconiosis (Option D) is caused by long-term coal dust inhalation. While smoking significantly increases the risk of general lung carcinoma in asbestos workers, it is the asbestos exposure itself that is the specific primary cause of mesothelioma. Therefore, given the patient’s occupational history in a cement factory, asbestosis is the underlying causative condition
questions.learning: Mesothelioma is a malignant tumor of the pleura that is almost exclusively associated with chronic exposure to asbestos fibers. Asbestos is commonly used in construction and cement manufacturing.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are considered aetiological factors for Adenocarcinoma oesophagus? I. Barrett’s oesophagus II. Gastro-oesophageal reflux III. Obesity IV. Alcohol intake Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Esophageal adenocarcinoma most commonly arises in the distal esophagus and develops through the sequence: Chronic GERD → Barrett’s esophagus → Dysplasia → Adenocarcinoma.

The incidence has increased significantly with the rising prevalence of obesity and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

The following are established risk factors for esophageal adenocarcinoma:

• I. Barrett’s esophagus: The most important premalignant lesion for esophageal adenocarcinoma. It involves intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophageal squamous epithelium due to chronic acid reflux.
• II. Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD): Chronic acid reflux leads to Barrett’s esophagus and markedly increases the risk of adenocarcinoma.
• III. Obesity: Particularly central obesity, which increases intra-abdominal pressure, promotes GERD, and independently increases the risk of adenocarcinoma.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Alcohol intake: Alcohol is a major risk factor for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.
questions.learning: I, II and III Esophageal adenocarcinoma most commonly arises in the distal esophagus and develops through the sequence: Chronic GERD → Barrett’s esophagus → Dysplasia → Adenocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents to the outpatient department with multiple, recurrent episodes of syncope. His ECG shows P waves at a rate of 75 bpm and QRS complexes at a rate of 35 bpm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This question is a duplicate of Question 155. The patient presents with syncope (fainting) and an ECG showing atrioventricular dissociation (P-rate 75, QRS-rate 35). This is diagnostic for complete (3rd-degree) heart block. Syncope resulting from this sudden cardiac output drop is termed Stokes-Adams syndrome. Mobitz Type II (Option A) is a 2nd-degree block where the PR interval is constant but some P-waves are not followed by QRS complexes; it often progresses to complete block. First-degree block (Option C) involves simple PR prolongation and is usually asymptomatic. WPW syndrome (Option D) involves an accessory pathway causing pre-excitation and a delta wave on ECG, not heart block. Complete heart block in an elderly patient is a high-risk condition and is the most common indication for permanent pacemaker implantation. The term "Stokes-Adams" remains a classic clinical eponym for this life-threatening interaction between arrhythmia and cerebral perfusion
questions.learning: This question is a duplicate of Question 155. The patient presents with syncope (fainting) and an ECG showing atrioventricular dissociation (P-rate 75, QRS-rate 35).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female from tribal area presented with fever for the last 3 days. On examination of the peripheral smear, a diagnosis of malaria was made. Which of the following is most likely to be the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. P. falciparum

The image shows ring forms/ early trophozoites in erythrocyte, which are binucleate (double chromatin) resembling stereo headphones in appearance, characteristic of P. falciparum.

There may be several rings present within a single erythrocyte. The rings are often attached to the margins of the red cells and are described as form applique or accole.
questions.learning: P. falciparum The image shows ring forms/ early trophozoites in erythrocyte, which are binucleate (double chromatin) resembling stereo headphones in appearance, characteristic of P. falciparum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A surveyor visits a household consisting of a 35-year-old man, his wife who is 6 weeks pregnant and a 3-year-old child. The man's brother along with his wife is currently visiting them for a month owing to winter vacation. What type of family would the surveyor classify the household?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nuclear family

A surveyor would label this house as a nuclear family.

The nuclear or elementary family consists of the married couple and their children while they are still regarded as dependents. This nuclear family has visitors who neither live permanantly in the same household or hold a common property which are characters of a joint or extended family.

The joint or extended family consists of a number of married couples and their children who live together in the same household and hold the property in common. The senior male member of the family is considered as the head.

Third generation family consists of three generations that are direct descents, living in the same house. It occurs usually when young couples continue to live with their parents and have their own children.

Pearl PF1702: The Family as a Social Organization

* A family is a group of biologically related individuals living together under the same roof and eating from a common kitchen.

* It is the most primary and basic unit of all societies.

* The basic and arbitrary model of a family cycle has six phases:

Phase

Beginning

End

1

Formation

Marriage

Birth of 1st child

2

Extension

Birth of 1st child

Birth of last child

3

Complete extension

Birth of last child

1st child leaves home

4

Contraction

1st child leaves home

Last child leaves parental home

5

Completed contraction

Last child leaves parental home

Death of 1st spouse

6

Dissolution

Death of 1st spouse

Death of survivor

* Types of families:

* A nuclear family or elementary family consists of only the married couple and their offspring while they are dependants.

* The term new family is applied when nuclear families are younger than 10 years and consist of parents and children.

* A joint family or extended family consists of a number of married couples and their children who live together in the same household with usually the men being related by blood. All property in joint families is held in common with the family income going into a common pocket. A senior male member is usually the head of the family who makes decisions.

* A three generation family is one where there are representatives from three different generations in one house.

* A communal family is one in which all the members play a part in its management.

* Functions of the family:

* Residence (patrilocal and matrilocal)

* Division of labour

* Reproduction and raising children

* Socialization and social care

* Economic functions

* Problems families are those that lag behind the rest of the community in terms of standard and quality of life of its members.

* Broken families are those in which the parental or family system has been disrupted by separation, divorce or death.
questions.learning: Nuclear family — A surveyor would label this house as a nuclear family. The nuclear or elementary family consists of the married couple and their children while they are still regarded as dependents.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: For which of the following conditions, surgery is indicated in a case of Fibroid Uterus? I. Symptomatic and failed medical management II. Size >12 weeks III. Pedunculated fibroid Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are the most common benign tumors of the uterus, arising from the smooth muscle cells of the myometrium. Surgery is indicated when fibroids cause significant symptoms, complications, or suspicion of malignancy, or when conservative treatment has failed.

All the listed conditions are indications for surgery:

• I. Symptomatic and failed medical management: Surgery is indicated in women with persistent heavy menstrual bleeding, pain, pressure symptoms, infertility, or recurrent pregnancy loss despite adequate medical therapy.
• II. Size >12 weeks: A uterus enlarged to more than 12 weeks’ gestational size is generally considered an indication for surgery, particularly if associated with rapid growth, pressure symptoms, or diagnostic uncertainty.
• III. Pedunculated fibroid: Pedunculated submucosal or subserosal fibroids are prone to torsion, degeneration, or prolapse, making surgical removal appropriate.
questions.learning: I, II and III Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are the most common benign tumors of the uterus, arising from the smooth muscle cells of the myometrium. Surgery is indicated when fibroids cause significant symptoms, complications, or suspicion of malignancy,…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Data arranged into two qualitative categories like 'Urban' and 'Rural' is best defined as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nominal data

Categorical scales are divided into nominal (names only) and ordinal (order/ranking). Urban and Rural fall under nominal scale as they are qualitative classifications with no inherent order, measurement capability, or comparative relationship.

Data is divided into four levels of measurement:

| Type | Definition | Example

| ---- | ---------- | -------

| Nominal | Categories with no natural order — names/labels only | Urban/Rural, Male/Female, Blood groups, Religion

| Ordinal | Categories with natural order/ranking but unequal intervals | Mild/Moderate/Severe, Socioeconomic class I–V

| Interval | Ordered, equal intervals, no true zero | Temperature (°C), IQ score

| Ratio | Ordered, equal intervals, true zero exists | Height, Weight, Blood pressure, Age
questions.learning: Nominal data Categorical scales are divided into nominal (names only) and ordinal (order/ranking). Urban and Rural fall under nominal scale as they are qualitative classifications with no inherent order, measurement capability, or comparative relationship.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What are the rays used in linear accelerator (LINAC) therapy for curing cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. X-ray

X-rays are the most common form of radiation used in radiotherapy. They are produced from a LINAC (linear accelerator).

It is used in radiation therapy to deliver high-energy X-rays or electrons to target specific areas of the body, typically to treat cancerous tissues. It uses microwave technology to accelerate charged particles (such as electrons) at a high speed and then directs them into a target (usually a heavy metal) to produce X-rays. These X-rays are then carefully directed at the patient's body to deliver therapeutic radiation doses to the tumor while minimising damage to surrounding healthy tissues. For precise therapy, this LINAC is referred to as a CyberKnife when it is mounted on an electronic robotic arm. It is used in inoperable cranial lesions as stereotactic radiotherapy.

Other options:

Option A: Proton beams offer a therapeutic advantage of having a steep dose falloff at the end of their path. Advantages are mostly physical, not biological; however, new data suggest different genes may be induced after proton versus X-ray treatment

Option B: Neutron beams are used in visualizing soft tissue and can even provide better contrast than X-rays in some cases, but are rarely used clinically due to complex setup and limited availability.

Option D: Cobalt 60 undergoes beta-decay and emits 1.25 MeV (average) gamma rays, which penetrate deeper tissues while sparing skin, used in the Gamma Knife. The gamma knife is mainly used to treat inoperable intracranial lesions.
questions.learning: X-ray X-rays are the most common form of radiation used in radiotherapy. They are produced from a LINAC (linear accelerator).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following children are considered at-risk babies? 1. Baby with a birth weight of 2.5 kg 2. Baby on artificial feeds 3. Baby of working mother/single parent 4. Baby with weight <85% of expected weight 5. Birth order of 3 or more
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 3

At-risk babies” are infants who have higher chances of morbidity and mortality due to biological or social risk factors, requiring closer monitoring.

• Social and feeding-related risks are important.
• Artificial feeding increases risk of infections and malnutrition
• Baby of a working mother or single parent may have inadequate care or feeding issues

Why other options are not included:

• Birth weight of 2.5 kg is normal (low birth weight is <2.5 kg)
• Weight <85% expected suggests malnutrition but applies to older infants/children, not specifically “at-risk baby” category
• Birth order alone is not a direct criterion unless associated with poor care
questions.learning: 2, 3 At-risk babies” are infants who have higher chances of morbidity and mortality due to biological or social risk factors, requiring closer monitoring. • Social and feeding-related risks are important. • Artificial feeding increases risk of infections…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A medical student is studying Meigs syndrome for a class presentation. Which of the following is not a classic feature of Meigs syndrome?
questions.explanation: Meigs syndrome is characterized by a specific clinical triad: a benign ovarian tumor, ascites (Option A), and a hydrothorax (pleural effusion), which is classically right-sided (Option B). The most common benign ovarian tumor associated with this syndrome is an ovarian fibroma (Option C). Dysgerminoma (Option D), while a common germ cell tumor in young women, is NOT a component of the classic Meigs triad . In some cases, other benign tumors like thecomas or cystadenofibromas can also cause the syndrome (sometimes called Pseudo-Meigs). A key feature of Meigs syndrome is that the fluid collections (ascites and hydrothorax) resolve spontaneously once the benign ovarian tumor is surgically removed. Because the syndrome is specifically defined by the association with benign fibromas, the malignant dysgerminoma is the correct "except" choice. Recognizing this syndrome is important to avoid misdiagnosing a treatable benign condition as advanced metastatic cancer
questions.learning: Meigs syndrome is characterized by a specific clinical triad: a benign ovarian tumor, ascites (Option A), and a hydrothorax (pleural effusion), which is classically right-sided (Option B).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is used to estimate relative risk (RR)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cohort study

Relative risk is best estimated in cohort studies.

Relative Risk:

* The ratio of incidence of disease or death among exposed to that among the non-exposed is called relative risk (RR).

* It is also called the risk ratio.

* It is the direct measure of the strength of association between suspected cause and effect in cohort studies.

* RR = 1 indicates no association.

* RR >1 indicates a positive association.

* RR of 2 or higher indicates a >/=100% increase in risk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the preferred treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria?
questions.explanation: Due to widespread resistance, chloroquine (Option A) is no longer effective for most cases of P. falciparum. The current global and WHO standard for treating uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria is Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT). This involves pairing a rapid-acting artemisinin derivative (like artemether) with a longer-acting partner drug (like lumefantrine). This dual approach ensures rapid clearance of parasites and prevents the development of further resistance. Primaquine (Option C) is primarily used to clear the dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) of P. vivax and P. ovale and should be avoided in P. falciparum unless as a single dose to reduce gametocyte transmission. Doxycycline (Option D) is used for malaria prophylaxis or as an adjunct in severe cases, but not as the primary treatment for uncomplicated falciparum malaria. Prompt diagnosis with a rapid test or microscopy and immediate initiation of ACT are life-saving, as falciparum malaria can rapidly progress to severe, fatal complications if left untreated
questions.learning: Due to widespread resistance, chloroquine (Option A) is no longer effective for most cases of P. falciparum. The current global and WHO standard for treating uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria is Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl and a 25-year-old man report that they had consensual sexual intercourse. The girl’s parents filed a police complaint, although there is no evidence of force or injury. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The girl's consent is valid because the relationship is consensual and both parties claim to love each other.
The girl's consent is not legally valid because she is only 16 years old.
The parents must first prove that the sexual act was forcible before any legal action can proceed.
The man cannot be prosecuted unless the girl herself files the complaint.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The girl's consent is not legally valid because she is only 16 years old.

Under Indian law, any sexual activity with a person below 18 years of age is considered statutory rape, irrespective of consent.

• Age of consent in India = 18 years
• A person <18 years cannot give legally valid consent for sexual intercourse
• Such cases are governed by the POCSO Act (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences)

Legal implications:

• Even if the minor states the act was consensual, it is legally invalid
• The adult partner is liable for prosecution
• Complaint can be initiated by parents or authorities; victim’s complaint is not mandatory

Why not other options:

• A: Consent is invalid if <18 years
• C: Force is not required in minors (statutory offence)
• D: Case can proceed without victim filing complaint
questions.learning: The girl's consent is not legally valid because she is only 16 years old. Under Indian law, any sexual activity with a person below 18 years of age is considered statutory rape, irrespective of consent. • Age of consent in India = 18 years • A person <18…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with severe hyperglycemia is started on insulin therapy. Which of the following effect is expected?
options: Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT2
Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT4
Increased glucose uptake by liver via GLUT4
Increased glucose uptake by liver via GLUT2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT4

Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting GLUT4 translocation from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, thereby increasing glucose uptake. In contrast, GLUT2 in the liver and pancreatic β-cells is insulin-independent.

Why is B correct?

• Skeletal muscle expresses GLUT4, which is activated by insulin, leading to increased glucose uptake.

Why not the other options?

• A. Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT2: Skeletal muscle does not express GLUT2.
• C. Increased glucose uptake by liver via GLUT4: The liver expresses GLUT2, not GLUT4.
• D. Increased glucose uptake by liver via GLUT2: Although the liver uses GLUT2, its glucose uptake is not increased by insulin through GLUT2 translocation; insulin instead promotes glycogen synthesis and glycolysis after glucose enters hepatocytes.
questions.learning: Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT4 Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting GLUT4 translocation from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, thereby increasing glucose uptake.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a chronic inflammatory disorder is found to have microcytic, hypochromic anemia. This condition is associated with reduced iron availability due to inhibition of ferroportin. Which cytokine is most likely responsible for inhibiting ferroportin in this patient?
questions.explanation: In patients with chronic inflammatory states, the body develops "Anemia of Chronic Disease" (ACD), which can appear microcytic and hypochromic. The central mediator of this process is Hepcidin, a small peptide hormone produced by the liver. During inflammation, the cytokine IL-6 (Interleukin-6) acts as the primary inducer of hepcidin synthesis. Elevated hepcidin then binds to and triggers the internalization and degradation of ferroportin, the only known cellular iron exporter. This action traps iron inside macrophages and enterocytes, preventing its release into the bloodstream and limiting its availability for erythropoiesis. While IL-1 (Option A), IFN-gamma (Option C), and TNF-Alpha (Option D) also play roles in the inflammatory response, IL-6 is the specific cytokine directly linked to the hepcidin-mediated inhibition of ferroportin. This mechanism evolved to sequester iron away from invading pathogens but results in significant anemia in chronic conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or malignancy. Management involves treating the underlying inflammatory disease to lower IL-6 and hepcidin levels
questions.learning: In patients with chronic inflammatory states, the body develops "Anemia of Chronic Disease" (ACD), which can appear microcytic and hypochromic. The central mediator of this process is Hepcidin, a small peptide hormone produced by the liver.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The characteristic triad of bruise, abrasion, and laceration is most commonly associated with which type of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bomb blast injury

The combination of bruise, abrasion, and laceration --> Characteristic Marshall triad of blast (bomb) injuries.

• Primary blast injury: Pressure wave → internal organ damage
• Secondary blast injury: Flying debris/shrapnel → lacerations and abrasions
• Tertiary blast injury: Body thrown → blunt trauma causing bruises

Why this triad occurs:

• Simultaneous exposure to blunt force + penetrating fragments + pressure effects
• Leads to mixed injury pattern (bruise + abrasion + laceration)

Why not other options:

• RTA: Mainly blunt trauma, not typical triad
• Strangulation: Neck findings (ligature marks, petechiae)
• Firearm injury: Entry/exit wounds, not mixed triad
questions.learning: Bomb blast injury — The combination of bruise, abrasion, and laceration --> Characteristic Marshall triad of blast (bomb) injuries. • Primary blast injury: Pressure wave → internal organ damage • Secondary blast injury: Flying debris/shrapnel → lacerations…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with gout develops hypertension. The uric acid level was found to be elevated. Which of the following is not administered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydrochlorothiazide

Hydrochlorothiazides are not given to this patient.

Gout is a metabolic disease associated with hyperuricemia.Thiazides increase direct urate reabsorption in the proximal renal tubules and are associated with elevated serum uric acid levels and may precipitate gout. Hence, hydrochlorothiazides are not used to treat hypertension in gout patients.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: At what level does the spinal cord end in infants?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. L3

In infants, the spinal cord ends at the L3 level.

As the child grows, the spinal cord moves up with age. Thus in adults, the distal termination of the spinal cord is at the lower border of L1.

The nerve roots from the lower end of the spinal cord form the cauda equina which exit through the intervertebral foramina. These fibers float in the dural sac and tend to be pushed away when a needle is advanced as in spinal anesthesia.

Thus spinal anesthesia is administered in adults below the lower border of L1 and in children below the lower border of L3, to minimize the chances of injury to the spinal cord

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Komal, a 2-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with a high fever, cough, red eyes, and rash. Parents say that the rash started on the forehead and behind the ears, then subsequently spread to the neck and body. On examination, a confluent maculopapular rash is noted as shown below. Which of the following is false regarding this child's condition?
options: The period of infectivity is 3 days before and 5 days after the appearance of rash
The most common cause of death is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The most common cause of death is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of measles. The most common cause of death is pneumonia (Hecht's giant cell pneumonia).

Measles (rubeola) is caused by RNA paramyxovirus. The infection is spread via droplets, with a secondary attack rate ≥of 90%. The patients are infectious from 3 days before to 5 days after the appearance of the rash. The rash appears on the 4th day of the fever. It starts from the retro auricular region. Koplik spots and Warthin–Finkeldey giant cells are pathognomonic.

Measles can lead to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) as a late complication.

Measles can be prevented by administering live attenuated, Edmonston–Zagreb strain or combined MMR given at 9 months of age.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: You see a child with delayed speech development as part of a health visit at a local school. The otoscopic appearance of the ear is shown below. Hearing loss of 20 dB is detected in audiometric tests. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serous otitis media

The given clinical scenario and image suggest a diagnosis of serous otitis media.

The golden yellow discoloration of the tympanic membrane is caused by the clear watery straw-colored effusion filling the middle ear. Since the fluid is clear, one can see the structures of the middle ear quite clearly on otoscopy.

Patients having serous otitis media will have hearing loss that rarely exceeds 40 dB. This deafness can pass unnoticed, and maybe accidentally discovered during audiometric screening tests. Because of hearing loss, the development of speech is delayed or defective.

Otoscopic findings in serous otitis media:

* Fluid level and air bubbles are seen when fluid is thin and the tympanic membrane transparent.

* In chronic cases, the fluid becomes very sticky. Hence, the name glue ear.

* The tympanic membrane is often dull and opaque with a loss of light reflex.

* The mobility of the tympanic membrane is restricted.
questions.learning: Serous otitis media — The given clinical scenario and image suggest a diagnosis of serous otitis media. The golden yellow discoloration of the tympanic membrane is caused by the clear watery straw-colored effusion filling the middle ear.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: TIGAR-O is an etiological classification used for:

TIGAR-O classification system

• TIGAR-O helps clinicians identify the cause of chronic pancreatitis and choose cause-specific treatment, improving outcomes and preventing disease progression.

TIGAR-O stands for

T – Toxic-Metabolic

I – Idiopathic

G – Genetic: Mutations affecting pancreatic enzymes

Examples:

• PRSS1
• SPINK1

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids primarily acts as a buffer in blood due to its ability to accept and donate protons at physiological pH?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histidine

At physiological pH, buffering action in blood is caused by histidine.

The imidazole group of histidine has a pKa value of 6.5-7.4, which is close to physiological pH.

Histidine is a positively charged amino acid that can exist in both its protonated (positively charged) and deprotonated (neutral) forms. It acts as a buffer by accepting or donating protons (H+ ions) in response to changes in pH, helping to maintain the blood's pH within a narrow physiological range.

Hence, histidine has the maximum buffering capacity at physiological pH.

Other options:

Option B: Arginine is a semi-essential amino acid involved in protein synthesis, wound healing, and immune function. It also serves as a precursor for nitric oxide, which regulates blood flow and vascular health.

Option C: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that serves as a precursor for serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood regulation. It is also a precursor for melatonin, which plays a key role in regulating sleep-wake cycles.

Option D: Tyrosine is a non-essential amino acid that plays a crucial role in the synthesis of neurotransmitters such as dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. It also contributes to the production of thyroid hormones and melanin.
questions.learning: Histidine At physiological pH, buffering action in blood is caused by histidine. The imidazole group of histidine has a pKa value of 6.5-7.4, which is close to physiological pH.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which ganglion is located in the area indicated in the image?
questions.explanation: The image indicates the infratemporal fossa, specifically the region just below the foramen ovale. The otic ganglion is a small parasympathetic ganglion located in this area, immediately below the foramen ovale and medial to the mandibular nerve. It serves as a relay station for secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland. The ciliary ganglion (Option B) is located within the orbit, posterior to the eyeball. The pterygopalatine ganglion (Option C) resides in the pterygopalatine fossa, accessible through the sphenopalatine foramen. The submandibular ganglion (Option D) is located on the hyoglossus muscle, suspended from the lingual nerve. The otic ganglion receives preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the lesser petrosal nerve (a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve). Postganglionic fibers then travel via the auriculotemporal nerve to stimulate the parotid gland. Precise knowledge of these cranial nerve ganglia and their locations is fundamental for diagnosing various autonomic dysfunctions in the head and neck region
questions.learning: The image indicates the infratemporal fossa, specifically the region just below the foramen ovale. The otic ganglion is a small parasympathetic ganglion located in this area, immediately below the foramen ovale and medial to the mandibular nerve.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency with epistaxis. There was no relief on pinching the nostrils. Nasal packing was done but the patient still continues to bleed. What would be the next appropriate step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ligation of sphenopalatine artery

The next appropriate step for the management of epistaxis which was not controlled by pinching of nostrils and nasal packing would be ligation of the sphenopalatine artery, as it is the main artery contributing to Kiesselbach’s plexus.

Little's area is the most common site of epistaxis. It is present in the anteroinferior part of the septum. Four arteries anastomose here to form Kiesselbach’s plexus.

The image below shows the blood supply of the nasal septum and areas of epistaxis.

The first step in treating epistaxis is to pinch the nose with the thumb and index finger for about 5 minutes. The patient should sit leaning slightly forward over a basin to spit out blood and breathe through the mouth (Hippocratic or Trotter’s method).

If the bleeding point is localized, cauterization can be done with electrocautery. In cases of uncontrolled bleeding or when the bleeding is posterior into the throat, anterior or posterior nasal packing may be required, respectively. If bleeding continues despite these measures, endoscopic procedures or vessel ligation close to the bleeding point can be considered.

The recommended hierarchy of ligation of vessels in a patient of epistaxis is the sphenopalatine artery first, the internal maxillary artery followed by the external carotid artery, and finally the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries.

The sphenopalatine artery is ligated first through a trans-nasal endoscope (transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation) at the sphenopalatine foramen which is situated at the posterior end of the middle turbinate.

However, if the bleeding persists, internal maxillary artery ligation is done at the pterygopalatine fossa via the Caldwell-Luc approach. If bleeding is still not controlled, external carotid artery ligation is done just above the origin of the superior thyroid artery.

If the bleeding site is located superior to the level of the middle turbinate, the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries should be ligated via Lynch incision in the medial wall of the orbit.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The image shows a femur bone. Which muscles are attached at point “A”?
questions.explanation: The anatomical landmark labeled "A" on the proximal femur is the lesser trochanter. This bony prominence serves as the primary insertion site for the iliopsoas muscle. The iliopsoas is the strongest flexor of the hip and is formed by the fusion of the psoas major and iliacus muscles. The gluteus maximus (Option A) inserts into the gluteal tuberosity and the iliotibial tract. The quadriceps femoris (Option C) consists of four muscles that primarily insert into the patella and tibial tuberosity. The adductor magnus (Option D) inserts along the linea aspera and the adductor tubercle. Clinically, avulsion fractures of the lesser trochanter are rare and often seen in adolescent athletes or as a sign of metastatic disease in older adults. Understanding these specific insertion points is fundamental for diagnosing musculoskeletal injuries and planning surgical interventions involving the hip and thigh
questions.learning: The anatomical landmark labeled "A" on the proximal femur is the lesser trochanter. This bony prominence serves as the primary insertion site for the iliopsoas muscle.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A CT scan of a patient with a hydatid cyst is shown below. What is the type of hydatid cyst as per the Gharbi classification?

CT - Computed Tomography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type 2

The given CT scan showing the hydatid cyst with detached membranes(Water Lily sign) is classified as CE-3 according to the WHO classification and Type 2 according to the Gharbi classification.

Hydatid Cyst is a zoonotic infection caused by the Echinococcus species(dog tapeworm ). Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus. Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human-to-human transmission.

The clinical presentation of a hydatid cyst is largely asymptomatic until complications occur. The most common presenting symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and vomiting. The most frequent sign is hepatomegaly.

Approximately 75% of hydatid cysts are located in the right lobe of the liver and are solitary.

CT scan is the best imaging modality for hydatid cysts. It shows the presence of a space-occupying lesion with a smooth outline with septa. Diagnosis is suggested by the finding of a multiloculated cyst on ultrasound and is further supported by the finding of a floating membrane within the cysts on a CT scan. Active cysts contain a large number of smaller daughter cysts (multi-vesicular rosette-like cystic lesions with daughter cysts) which is characteristic of hydatid cysts of the liver.

If there is a disruption of the inner layers of the cyst, the following signs may be noted:

• Water lily sign/ camalote sign - air-fluid level with a floating membrane (as shown below)
• Rising sun sign/ serpent sign - a double-wall, dry cyst with crumpled membranes lying at its bottom
• Empty cyst sign - when all the contents are removed

The ultrasound of an active hydatid cyst shows multiple septations and a rosette or honeycomb appearance (as shown below)

The serpent sign is seen as wavy membranes within the cyst, on CT imaging.

A ball of wool sign is seen on ultrasound when the contents settle in the dependent portion of the cyst, as seen below.

The water-lily sign is seen in hydatid infections when there is detachment of the endocyst membrane which results in floating membranes within the pericyst that mimic the appearance of a water lily, on USG.
questions.learning: Type 2 — The given CT scan showing the hydatid cyst with detached membranes(Water Lily sign) is classified as CE-3 according to the WHO classification and Type 2 according to the Gharbi classification.

questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for the negative charge in fibrinopeptide A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspartate and glutamate

Aspartate and glutamate are responsible for the negative charge in fibrinopeptide A and B of fibrinogen.

The negative charges contribute to the solubility of fibrinogen in plasma and importantly also serve to prevent aggregation by causing electrostatic repulsion between fibrinogen molecules.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 6-week-old male infant presents with post- feeding vomiting and failure to thrive. On abdominal examination, a firm, olive-shaped mass is palpable in the upper abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The palpation of a firm, "olive-shaped" mass in the upper abdomen of a 6-week-old infant is pathognomonic for Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis. This condition involves hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to progressive gastric outlet obstruction. Classic symptoms include non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeding and failure to thrive. Subacute Intestinal Obstruction (Option A) typically presents with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. GERD (Option C) causes spitting up or "wet burps" but does not feature a palpable abdominal mass or projectile vomiting. Esophageal Atresia (Option D) presents much earlier—immediately after birth—with drooling and choking during the first feed. The metabolic hallmark of pyloric stenosis is hypochloridemic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to loss of gastric acid. Ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality to confirm pyloric thickening, and treatment is surgical (Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy)
questions.learning: The palpation of a firm, "olive-shaped" mass in the upper abdomen of a 6-week-old infant is pathognomonic for Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis.

questions.text: SPIKES protocol is for:

Correct answer: D. Breaking bad news

SPIKES protocol is for breaking bad news.

Each letter represents a phase in the six-step sequence.

• S - setting
• P - perception
• I - invitation or information
• K - knowledge
• E - empathy
• S - summarizing or strategizing

Key components of the SPIKES strategy include:

• Demonstrating empathy
• Acknowledging and validating the patient's feelings
• Exploring the patient's understanding and acceptance of the bad news
• Providing information about possible interventions

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Please analyze the image provided and determine the specific abnormality or injury present.
questions.explanation: The provided image displays a classic dendritic ulcer, characterized by its linear, branching, tree-like appearance with terminal bulbs. This finding is pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) keratitis, a form of viral keratitis. These ulcers are highlighted when stained with fluorescein or rose bengal. Fungal keratitis (Option B) typically presents with feathery margins and satellite lesions. Bacterial keratitis (Option C) usually shows a well-defined, round, or oval suppurative infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect. Interstitial keratitis (Option D) involves inflammation within the stroma without primary epithelial ulceration. Patients with HSV dendritic ulcers often report pain, photophobia, and blurred vision, along with decreased corneal sensation. Management includes topical antiviral agents like acyclovir. Therefore, based on the unique branching pattern visible in the image, viral keratitis is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young man came to the medical OPD with complaints of early morning backache and stiffness, which improves on exercise, and persistent red eyes. On examination, lung expansion was less than 3 cm. X-ray is shown in the image given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ankylosing spondylitis

The given clinical vignette points towards the diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis.

Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting the spine and sacroiliac joint. It is more common in young males and has a strong association with HLAB27.

Clinically, patients present with recurring backache which worsens in the early morning or with inactivity and improves with exercise. Later, they develop fatigue, pain, joint swellings, and heel pain. Extra-articular manifestations include anterior uveitis, aortic incompetence, carditis, and apical lobe fibrosis. Examination findings include loss of lumbar lordosis, increased thoracic kyphosis, diminished spinal movements, and decreased chest expansion.

X-ray findings:

• Erosion of sacroiliac joints - earliest sign
• Periarticular sclerosis in later stages
• Squaring of vertebrae due to the flattening of normal anterior concavity of the vertebral body is the earliest vertebral change
• Bamboo spine appearance due to bridging of adjacent vertebrae
• Wedging of the vertebra, leading to hyperkyphosis

Complications of ankylosing spondylitis include

• Spinal fractures, the most common site is C5–7
• Hyperkyphosis
• Spinal cord compression
• Lumbosacral nerve root compression

Treatment consists of maintaining posture and preserving mobility. Pain and stiffness can be controlled with anti-inflammatory drugs. In severe cases, TNF inhibitors are used. Surgery can be considered to correct the deformity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following radioisotopes have a half-life of less than 1 day, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iodine 125

Most commonly used diagnostic radioisotopes have short half-lives (<24 hours) to minimize radiation exposure while allowing effective imaging.

• Technetium-99m: \~6 hours
• Iodine-132: \~2–3 hours
• 18F-FDG: \~110 minutes
• Iodine-125: \~60 days (long half-life)

Iodine-125 has a prolonged half-life and is mainly used in brachytherapy (e.g., prostate implants) rather than routine diagnostic imaging.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 32-year-old man who had travelled to Assam recently presents with fever,chills,seizures and altered sensorium. On examination, his blood pressure was 70/50 mm of Hg and labored breathing was present. A blood smear was sent which revealed Plasmodium falciparum. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intravenous artesunate

This scenario depicts a case of severe complicated falciparum malaria, and the drug of choice in this condition is intravenous artesunate.

Severe complicated malaria is caused by P. falciparum and is characterized by hyperparasitemia, hyperpyrexia, acidosis, respiratory distress, bleeding manifestation, cardiovascular collapse, renal failure and cerebral malaria.

As per WHO guidelines, all patients with severe malaria should be treated with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours. Once the patient recovers and can tolerate oral medications, oral ACT for 3 days is recommended. If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is given.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following classical disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs is/are considered safe for use during pregnancy? 1. Methotrexate 2. Sulfasalazine 3. Hydroxychloroquine 4. Leflunomide Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3

1. Methotrexate: Incorrect

• Contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic and can cause fetal loss and congenital abnormalities.

2. Sulfasalazine: Correct

• Considered safe during pregnancy.
• Folic acid supplementation is recommended because sulfasalazine can interfere with folate metabolism.

3. Hydroxychloroquine: Correct

• Considered safe and is commonly continued during pregnancy, particularly in rheumatoid arthritis and SLE.

4. Leflunomide: Incorrect

• Contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenic potential.
• It has a long half-life; cholestyramine washout is used when pregnancy is planned or occurs.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the histological image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lymph node

The image is that of a lymph node.

Each lymph node is bean-shaped. The concave part consists of the hilum, through which the blood vessels enter and leave the node. Each lymph node is surrounded by a thin capsule. Below the capsule is the clear space, which is called the subcapsular sinus. The lymph node contains the outer cortex and an inner medulla.

Cortex

* The outermost region of the lymph node, located beneath the capsule.

* Primary follicles: Composed primarily of small, resting B lymphocytes (naive B cells). These follicles are unactivated and appear as small, round clusters.

* Secondary follicles: These form when B cells within the primary follicle are activated by antigenic stimulation. They are characterized by a germinal centre (where B cells proliferate and differentiate) and a mantle zone (where small, resting B cells surround the germinal centre).

* Mantle zone: A ring of small, naive B lymphocytes surrounding the germinal centre.

Paracortex (T-cell Zone)

* Situated between the cortex and the medulla, this area is rich in T lymphocytes, which are involved in T-cell mediated immunity.

* The paracortex also contains dendritic cells that present antigens to T cells and is crucial for T-cell dependent immune responses.

* This zone lacks follicles and is more densely populated with T cells.

Medulla

* The innermost part of the lymph node, containing medullary cords and medullary sinuses.

* Medullary cords: These are dense clusters of plasma cells, B cells, T cells, and macrophages that are responsible for producing antibodies and providing immune surveillance.

* Medullary sinuses: Spaces that allow the passage of lymph and contain macrophages that filter out foreign particles and pathogens.

Option A: The thymus is a lymphoid tissue that is arranged in the form of lobules. The lobules are separated from each other by connective tissue.

Each lobule is made up of an outer darker staining cortex and an inner pale-staining medulla. The medulla contains pink rounded masses called Hassell's corpuscles.

Option B: The main features that can be used to identify the spleen are:

* Capsule and trabeculae extending from it.

* Arterioles arising from the network of vessels that have branched from the splenic artery in the trabecular spaces.

* White pulp - composed of aggregation of lymphocytes arranged around an arteriole.

* Red pulp - areas between the white pulp and trabecular spaces regions where blood cells flow into.

* Sinusoids -blood from spaces of the red pulp is collected by wide sinusoids that drain into veins in the trabeculae.

Option C: The tonsil consists of lymphoid nodules, which are surrounded by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its oropharyngeal surface. The epithelium dips into the substance of the gland and forms tonsillar crypts.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following methods of measuring intraocular pressure is based on the Imbert–Fick principle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Applanation tonometry

Applanation tonometry, particularly Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT), is based on the Imbert–Fick law.

According to this principle:

P = F/A

where:

• P = Pressure
• F = Force required to flatten the surface
• A = Area flattened

The Imbert–Fick principle states that the pressure inside an ideal, thin-walled sphere is equal to the force required to flatten a portion of its surface divided by the area flattened.

In Goldmann applanation tonometry, a known area of the cornea is flattened (applanated), and the force required to achieve this is used to determine the intraocular pressure (IOP).

Fluorescein is instilled into the tear film and the mires are viewed under cobalt-blue illumination. The endpoint is reached when the inner margins of the two fluorescein semicircles just touch.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 20-year-old patient presents with pain and swelling involving the proximal phalanx of the middle finger. Considering the patient’s age and the location of the lesion, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An enchondroma is a benign cartilaginous tumor that develops in the medullary cavity of bones. It is the most common tumor of the small bones of the hand (phalanges and metacarpals). On X-ray, it appears as a well-defined, radiolucent area often containing "stippled" or "popcorn-like" calcifications. While often asymptomatic, they can cause swelling or a pathological fracture. Osteosarcoma (Option A) and Ewing’s sarcoma (Option B) are highly aggressive, malignant tumors that rarely primary involve the small phalanges and would show significant bone destruction and periosteal reaction. Osteoclastoma (Option C), or Giant Cell Tumor, is typically found in the epiphysis of large long bones and would appear as an expansile "soap-bubble" lesion. Given the specific location in a finger phalanx and the well-defined lucency, enchondroma is the most statistically and radiographically probable diagnosis
questions.learning: An enchondroma is a benign cartilaginous tumor that develops in the medullary cavity of bones. It is the most common tumor of the small bones of the hand (phalanges and metacarpals).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Calculate the total percentage of burns depicted in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 30-40%

The percentage of burns calculated in this child is 36.5%, which falls within the range of 30-40%.

According to the latest ATLS guidelines, the Rule of Nines is applied to estimate the percentage of burns in this child as follows:

* Front of the right arm = 4.5%

* Whole of the right thigh + lower leg = 14%

* Front of abdomen and thorax = 18%

Total burn percentage = 4.5% + 14% + 18% = 36.5% Total Body Surface Area (TBSA)

The distribution of body surface area (BSA) differs significantly in children, as a child’s head accounts for a larger proportion of total surface area, while the lower limbs make up a smaller proportion compared to adults.

Note:

The goal of resuscitation is to maintain the fine balance of adequate perfusion as indicated by urine output. questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man presents with lower back pain, a mobile mass in the lumbar region that becomes more prominent on inspiration, and generalized weakness. Urine examination reveals the presence of red blood cells without pus cells. Based on these clinical and laboratory findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The triad of flank pain, hematuria (RBCs in urine without pus), and a palpable mass is the "classic triad" of renal cell carcinoma (RCC), although it is only seen in about 10% of patients. The fact that the mass moves with respiration indicates it is likely arising from the kidney, which is a retroperitoneal organ. Polycystic kidney disease (Option A) usually presents with bilateral masses and a strong family history. Hydronephrosis (Option B) is a secondary finding of obstruction and rarely presents as a large, primary palpable mass unless severe and chronic. Chronic pyelonephritis (Option D) would typically show pus cells (pyuria) and evidence of chronic infection rather than a solitary movable mass and hematuria. RCC is the most common primary renal malignancy in adults, frequently presenting as an incidental finding on imaging. The general weakness noted may be part of a paraneoplastic syndrome or anemia of chronic disease associated with malignancy
questions.learning: The triad of flank pain, hematuria (RBCs in urine without pus), and a palpable mass is the "classic triad" of renal cell carcinoma (RCC), although it is only seen in about 10% of patients.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most radiosensitive tissue in our body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bone marrow

The most radiosensitive tissue in our body is bone marrow.

The most radiosensitive:

* Tissue - bone marrow

* Blood Cell - Lymphocyte

* Stage of cell - G2-M interphase

* Cell type - Rapidly dividing cells

* Ocular structure - Lens

* Retinal structure - Rods>Cones

Least Radiosensitive:

* Tissue - nervous tissue

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding oculocutaneous albinism: I. The disease results from genetic abnormalities leading to destruction of melanocytes. II. Type 1 albinism is due to a defect in the tyrosinase gene. III. Patients may present with poor vision, rotatory nystagmus and alternating strabismus. IV. Patients are at an increased risk of sunburn or developing skin cancer. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. II, III and IV

Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a group of autosomal recessive disorders characterized by reduced or absent melanin synthesis in the skin, hair, and eyes due to defects in enzymes involved in melanin production. Melanocytes are present in normal numbers, but they are unable to produce adequate melanin.

• I. The disease results from genetic abnormalities leading to destruction of melanocytes. ❌

• Incorrect. Melanocytes are normal in number; the defect is in melanin synthesis, not melanocyte destruction.
• Destruction of melanocytes occurs in vitiligo, not albinism.

• II. Type 1 albinism is due to a defect in the tyrosinase gene. ✅

• OCA Type 1 results from mutations in the TYR (tyrosinase) gene, leading to absent or markedly reduced tyrosinase activity. This is the most commonly tested subtype.

• III. Patients may present with poor vision, rotatory nystagmus and alternating strabismus. ✅

• Ocular features include:

• Reduced visual acuity
• Nystagmus
• Strabismus
• Photophobia
• Foveal hypoplasia
• Iris transillumination defects

• IV. Patients are at an increased risk of sunburn or developing skin cancer. ✅

• Reduced melanin predisposes patients to:

• Sunburn
• Actinic damage
• Squamous cell carcinoma
• Basal cell carcinoma
• Increased lifetime risk of skin malignancies
questions.learning: II, III and IV Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a group of autosomal recessive disorders characterized by reduced or absent melanin synthesis in the skin, hair, and eyes due to defects in enzymes involved in melanin production.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An 8-year-old girl presents with abrupt onset of fever, oliguria, nausea, smoky urine, and puffy eyes. The parents say that she had lesions on her face similar to the ones shown in the image below, 2 weeks ago which are now resolving. Which of the following findings will be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. RBCs in urine

This patient's clinical features with h/o honey-crusted lesions on the face (impetigo) are suggestive of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Patients will present with haematuria and urine microscopy will reveal red blood cells.

The PSGN patient presents with hematuria, red cell casts in the urine, azotemia, oliguria, hypertension, mild to moderate proteinuria, and edema (features of the nephritic syndrome). It usually appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection of the pharynx or skin (impetigo). It occurs most frequently in children 6 to 10 years of age. In adults, it is less benign. Poststreptococcal GN is caused by immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens and specific antibodies, which are formed in situ.

The histologic picture shows enlarged hypercellular glomeruli. The hypercellularity is caused by infiltration by leukocytes and proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells. The proliferation and leukocyte infiltration are typically global and diffuse.

Some glomerular diseases may progress from one pattern to another or may present with considerable overlap between them, as a nephritic–nephrotic syndrome; features of nephrotic syndrome can concurrently occur with any form of nephritic syndrome but are most commonly seen with diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (seen in systemic lupus erythromytosus) and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
