questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A couple with 2 children who are not able to conceive for over an year now present to the OPD. The male partner is diagnosed to be having hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. Which of the following is not true ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Low prolactin levels

A male with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism will have high prolactin levels.

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism:

• Low LH &FSH
• Low testosterone
• Low testicular volume (oligospermia)
• High prolactin levels

Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism:

• High LH and FSH
• Low testosterone
• Low testicular volume (oligospermia)
• High prolactin level

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism:

It can be congenital or acquired. Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is divided into anosmic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann syndrome) and congenital normosmic isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism).

Acquired hypogonadotropic hypogonadism can be caused by drugs, infiltrative or infectious pituitary lesions, hyperprolactinemia, encephalic trauma, pituitary/brain radiation, exhausting exercise, abusive alcohol or illicit drug intake, and systemic diseases such as hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis and histiocytosis X.

The clinical characteristics of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism are androgen deficiency and a lack/delay/stop of pubertal sexual maturation. Low blood testosterone levels and low LH and FSH levels confirm the diagnosis. A prolonged stimulated intravenous GnRH test can be useful. In Kallmann syndrome, cerebral MRI can show an anomalous morphology or even absence of the olfactory bulb.

Therapy for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism depends on the patient's desire for future fertility. Hormone replacement with testosterone is the classic treatment for hypogonadism. Androgen replacement is indicated for men who already have children or have no desire to induce pregnancy, and testosterone therapy is used to reverse the symptoms and signs of hypogonadism. Conversely, GnRH or gonadotropin therapies are the best options for men wishing to have children.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An intern is observing the procedure of thoracocentesis. What is the site of needle insertion in this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper border of lower rib

The correct site for needle insertion during thoracentesis is usually at the upper border of the lower rib. This location helps to prevent any injury to the intercostal nerve and vessels.

For thoracocentesis, a posterior approach is preferred. The patient should sit on the edge of the bed, leaning forward with the arms abducted onto a pillow on a bedside stand. The patient might have severe dyspnea, so it is important to assess whether they can maintain this position for 10 minutes before performing the procedure. The entry site for the thoracocentesis is at the superior aspect of the rib.

This prevents any injury to the intercostal nerve and vessels.

While maintaining gentle negative pressure, the needle should be slowly advanced into the pleural space. If a diagnostic tap is being performed, 30-50 mL of fluid will be adequate. If a therapeutic thoracocentesis is being performed, a maximum of 1 liter of pleural fluid should be withdrawn at a given time. Withdrawal of quantities more than this can cause re-expansion pulmonary edema. A chest radiograph should be obtained post-procedure to evaluate for a pneumothorax. The patient should be instructed to inform the doctors if new shortness of breath develops.
questions.learning: Upper border of lower rib — The correct site for needle insertion during thoracentesis is usually at the upper border of the lower rib. This location helps to prevent any injury to the intercostal nerve and vessels.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In a patient with stroke who exhibits homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, which part of the visual (optic) pathway is most likely involved by the lesion?
questions.explanation: "Homonymous hemianopia" is a visual field defect where the same half of the visual field is lost in both eyes. When this defect specifically "spares the macula" (central 5–10 degrees), it is highly characteristic of a lesion in the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe. Macular sparing occurs because the macular region of the visual cortex is located at the occipital pole and has a dual blood supply from both the middle cerebral artery (MCA) and the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). Option C (Optic radiation) lesions usually cause complete hemianopia without macular sparing. Option D (Optic chiasma) lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia. Option A is a visual area, not a lesion site. This finding is most common after a PCA stroke; even if the artery is occluded, the MCA can often maintain perfusion to the macular representation in the cortex. Recognizing macular sparing is a critical localizing sign in clinical neurology

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the schedule of the OPV vaccine?
questions.explanation: As per the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) in India, the primary series of the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) consists of three doses administered at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age. These are typically given alongside other primary vaccines like Pentavalent and Rotavirus. A booster dose of OPV is later given at 16–24 months. Regarding the distractors, the 9th month (Options B and C) is the timing for the first dose of the Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccine and the newly introduced third dose of fIPV (fractional Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine), but not for a standard primary OPV dose. Option D is a vague range that does not align with the standardized multi-dose schedule. Therefore, the specific 6-10-14 week interval is the universally accepted primary schedule for OPV in public health programs
questions.learning: As per the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) in India, the primary series of the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) consists of three doses administered at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A young patient sustained a head injury following a road traffic accident. His family members complain that his behavior has changed following the incident. He is extremely curious and tries touching everything. He forgets everything rapidly, and he tries to keep everything in his mouth. He even tried to eat the plates. They have also noticed him squeezing his genitals. Which of the following structures is most likely to be damaged in this patient?
options: Gray matter around aqueduct of Sylvius
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amygdala

Increased curiosity, hyperorality, memory loss, and increased sex drive are the features of Kluver Bucy syndrome. This occurs due to the damage to the amygdala.

Features of Kluver Bucy syndrome are:

* Fearlessness

* Increased curiosity

* Memory loss

* Patient tries to keep everything in the mouth, even the solid objects that are not meant for eating

* Increased sex drive

Functions of amygdala:

It receives neuronal signals from the neocortex of the temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes, especially from the auditory and visual association areas. It transmits signals to the same cortical areas, thalamus, hypothalamus, and hippocampus. Stimulation of the amygdala leads to alterations in arterial pressure, heart rate, gastrointestinal motility, piloerection, and abnormal tonic circling and clinic movements. It also has role in olfaction.

Other options:

Option A- Gray matter around the aqueduct of Sylvius is the punishment center. Stimulation of punishment centers leads to the inhibition of reward and pleasure centers completely. Punishment and fear will be more prominent than pleasure and reward.

Option C- Lateral nuclei of hypothalamus primarily control hunger and feeding behavior. Stimulation of this area gives a sense of reward

Option D- Damage to the anterior cingulate gyri releases the rage centers of septum and hypothalamus from the prefrontal inhibitory influence. Therefore the patient becomes very aggressive.
questions.learning: Amygdala Increased curiosity, hyperorality, memory loss, and increased sex drive are the features of Kluver Bucy syndrome. This occurs due to the damage to the amygdala.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with fever and altered sensorium. Peripheral blood smear examination reveals multiple ring forms of the parasite. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: The combination of fever and altered sensorium indicates cerebral malaria, which is a severe form of malaria typically caused by Plasmodium falciparum. The presence of multiple ring stages on a peripheral smear strongly supports this diagnosis. Current WHO and national guidelines recommend intravenous Artesunate as the first-line treatment for severe malaria. It is preferred over quinine due to its superior safety profile, faster parasite clearance, and significant reduction in mortality rates. Primaquine (Option A) is used specifically for the radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale to target liver hypnozoites. Quinine (Option B) was historically the drug of choice but has been replaced by artesunate. Chloroquine (Option C) is ineffective in this case due to widespread resistance in P. falciparum. Therefore, prompt administration of IV artesunate is the most critical intervention for this patient
questions.learning: The combination of fever and altered sensorium indicates cerebral malaria, which is a severe form of malaria typically caused by Plasmodium falciparum.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old vegetarian presents with fatigue and weakness that have been present for a few months. On physical examination, pallor is noted. Hemoglobin is 9 g/dL and MCV is increased at 110 fL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Megaloblastic anemia

The most likely diagnosis in this case is megaloblastic anemia, given the patient's vegetarian diet, macrocytosis, and low hemoglobin level.

Megaloblastic anemia can be caused by a deficiency of vitamin B12 or folate. Vegetarians are at increased risk of vitamin B12 deficiency because vitamin B12 is primarily found in animal products. Other conditions can also cause megaloblastic anemia, such as celiac disease, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis. Other causes of high MCV, such as liver disease, alcoholism, and hypothyroidism.

Iron deficiency anemia is characterized by a low hemoglobin level and a microcytic (small cell) anemia. Iron is essential for the production of hemoglobin, and a deficiency of iron can lead to a decrease in hemoglobin levels. However, IDA is typically associated with a low MCV, not a high MCV.

In Aplastic anemia the bone marrow does not produce enough progenitor cells. It can be caused by autoimmune diseases, medications, and radiation. Aplastic anemia can lead to a decrease in all types of blood cells and is associated with a low MCV and a low hemoglobin level, not a high MCV.

Thalassemia is a group of genetic blood disorders that affect the production of hemoglobin. It is characterized by a microcytic anemia. However, thalassemia is not typically associated with a high MCV.
questions.learning: Megaloblastic anemia — The most likely diagnosis in this case is megaloblastic anemia, given the patient's vegetarian diet, macrocytosis, and low hemoglobin level.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A pregnant woman with deafness is evaluated and found to have a 50 dB hearing loss. What is the most likely cause of her hearing impairment?
options: Ossicular fixation with an intact tympanic membrane
Ossicular fixation with a damaged tympanic membrane
questions.explanation: The presentation of progressive hearing loss in a pregnant woman is a high-yield clinical trigger for Otosclerosis. This condition involves abnormal bone remodeling in the labyrinth, frequently causing stapes footplate fixation. Pregnancy is known to accelerate the progression of otosclerosis due to hormonal influences. The resulting conductive hearing loss is typically around 50-60 dB, while the tympanic membrane remains normal and intact. Options B and C are incorrect as otosclerosis is not an inflammatory disease that damages the drum. Option D (erosion with an intact drum) can occur in cholesteatoma, but the specific association with pregnancy makes stapes fixation much more probable. On clinical examination, a pinkish "Schwartz sign" might be seen through the intact drum. Management during pregnancy is typically conservative, such as hearing aids, while definitive surgery (stapedotomy) is postponed until after delivery
questions.learning: The presentation of progressive hearing loss in a pregnant woman is a high-yield clinical trigger for Otosclerosis. This condition involves abnormal bone remodeling in the labyrinth, frequently causing stapes footplate fixation.

questions.explanation:

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the device shown below?
options: It is used to measure infrared rays emitted by red blood cells
It is used for the localisation of calcified plaque
It is used to measure systolic blood pressure
It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel

The given image is of a handheld doppler device. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel.

The Doppler ultrasound device utilizes the doppler effect to assess the movement of red blood cells within blood vessels. The doppler effect is the change in frequency or wavelength of a wave in relation to an observer moving relative to the wave source. The device emits ultrasound waves that reflect off moving red blood cells. The frequency shift between the transmitted and received sound waves is used to calculate the velocity and direction of blood flow.

By analyzing these frequency shifts, the device can provide information about the speed and pattern of blood flow. This is particularly useful in detecting abnormalities such as blockages or stenosis.

Other options:

Option A: Doppler ultrasound does not measure infrared rays. Infrared measurements are typically related to thermal imaging or other specific applications unrelated to blood flow measurement.

Option B: Doppler ultrasound can help identify areas of reduced blood flow due to plaques, it is not specifically used for the localization of calcified plaque. Techniques like computed tomography (CT) or MRI are better suited for visualizing calcified plaques.

Option C: While Doppler can assist in certain vascular assessments, it is not a primary tool for measuring systolic or diastolic blood pressure.
questions.learning: It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel The given image is of a handheld doppler device. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: An ICU patient who was already on endotracheal intubation now requires a tracheostomy. Which type of tube will you use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cuffed tracheostomy tube

A cuffed tracheostomy tube is used in this patient for tracheostomy.

Cuffed tracheostomy is preferred in unconscious patients or patients on ventilators for a long time. When the cuff is inflated, it not only prevents the aspiration of pharyngeal secretions into the trachea but also prevents the leakage of air. The cuff should be deflated every 2 hours for 5 minutes to prevent pressure necrosis of the cartilage and trachea.

Metallic tubes(Option C) and uncuffed tracheostomy(Option A) tubes are not used too commonly because of the risk of displacement and aspiration of secretions into the trachea.
questions.learning: Cuffed tracheostomy tube — A cuffed tracheostomy tube is used in this patient for tracheostomy. Cuffed tracheostomy is preferred in unconscious patients or patients on ventilators for a long time.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman presents to a psychiatrist with a two-month history of persistent low mood, loss of interest in routine activities, reduced appetite, and sleep disturbances. Following detailed assessment, she is diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD). In view of this diagnosis and the requirement for appropriate pharmacological management, which medication would be most suitable to initiate treatment?
questions.explanation: For the initial treatment of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) like Fluoxetine are the first-line pharmacological agents of choice. They are preferred due to their superior safety profile, lower side-effect burden compared to older antidepressants, and high patient acceptability. Divalproex (Option A) and Lithium (Option C) are mood stabilizers primarily used for Bipolar Disorder and are not first-line for unipolar depression. Buspirone (Option B) is an anxiolytic used for Generalised Anxiety Disorder but is not effective as a primary treatment for MDD. Fluoxetine works by increasing the synaptic concentration of serotonin, which helps alleviate the core symptoms of low mood and anhedonia over a period of several weeks. Clinicians must counsel patients that the full therapeutic effect typically takes 2 to 4 weeks to manifest. Monitoring for early side effects like nausea or increased anxiety is essential during the initiation phase of therapy to ensure long-term medication adherence. **************
questions.learning: For the initial treatment of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) like Fluoxetine are the first-line pharmacological agents of choice.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen of a patient is shown below along with the microscopy. The report shows mononuclear cytosis, elevated proteins, and low sugars. Which of the following is the likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculous meningitis

The given clinical scenario along with the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample with cobweb-like clot and slide showing lymphocytic predominance points to a diagnosis of tubercular meningitis.

Tuberculous meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis is caused by the formation of tubercles in the brain parenchyma. This happens during the hematogenous spread of the bacilli during primary infection. It can also be due to the rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space.

Tuberculous meningitis presents as a subacute infection and has a longer course than bacterial meningitis. Ocular nerve palsy is a common association as there is marked meningeal involvement at the base of the brain. The patient can also develop hydrocephalus.

The CSF sample shows a pellicle or cobweb-like clots. Acid-fast bacilli can be best isolated from these. There is usually lymphocytic leukocytosis, low glucose concentration, and elevated proteins. CSF culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis.

The clinical triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity is common to all types of meningitis. Nuchal rigidity is the resistance of the neck to passive flexion and is pathognomonic of meningeal irritation. Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are other features of meningeal irritation. Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) is a complication that presents as papilledema, disorientation, or dilated poorly reactive pupils.

Other options:

Option B - Aseptic meningitis is commonly caused by enteroviruses such as coxsackieviruses, and varicella-zoster virus. It is more benign and usually self-limiting compared to pyogenic meningitis. Gram's staining of the CSF sample shows lymphocytosis but not the organism.

Option C - Bacterial meningitis is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Blood culture can be used for diagnosis. CSF findings are described in the pearl below. Antibiotic prophylaxis is provided to the close contacts of persons with confirmed meningococcal disease.

Option D - Chemical meningitis is a common cause of chronic meningitis. It can arise due to the rupture of tumor contents from a cystic glioma, dermoid cyst, or craniopharyngioma into the CSF.
questions.learning: Tuberculous meningitis — The given clinical scenario along with the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample with cobweb-like clot and slide showing lymphocytic predominance points to a diagnosis of tubercular meningitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the procedure carried out using the instrument shown below?
options: A condensing lens is not required
It is used very close to the patient's eye as possible
A real, inverted image is seen
questions.explanation: The instrument shown is a "Direct Ophthalmoscope". One of its defining characteristics is that it produces a virtual, erect (upright) image of the retina. Therefore, statement C is false. In contrast, an indirect ophthalmoscope produces a real, inverted image. Direct ophthalmoscopy provides high magnification (approximately 15 times) but offers a limited field of view of about 10 degrees. Because it is a handheld device, it does not require a separate condensing lens (statement A), unlike indirect ophthalmoscopy which requires a 20D lens. To obtain the best view, the examiner must be as close to the patient's eye as possible (statement B). While easy to use and portable, the direct ophthalmoscope lacks stereopsis (3D depth perception), which is why indirect methods are preferred for detailed evaluations of the peripheral retina or when examining patients with cataracts
questions.learning: The instrument shown is a "Direct Ophthalmoscope". One of its defining characteristics is that it produces a virtual, erect (upright) image of the retina.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Chvostek's sign is seen in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypocalcemia

The Chvostek's sign is seen in hypocalcemia.

Chvostek's sign is a clinical indicator of hypocalcemia, seen in conditions like hypoparathyroidism and vitamin D deficiency. It is elicited by gently tapping the facial nerve just anterior to the ear, which triggers involuntary twitching of the facial muscles, particularly around the mouth and eye.

While a positive Chvostek's sign suggests neuromuscular excitability due to low calcium levels, it is not always specific, as mild twitching can also occur in healthy individuals. This sign is often assessed alongside Trousseau's sign to confirm hypocalcemia. Trousseau’s sign indicates hypocalcemia and is demonstrated by inflating a blood pressure cuff above the systolic level for 180 seconds. This causes an involuntary carpal spasm, resulting in contraction of the hand and fingers. It signifies increased neuromuscular excitability due to low calcium levels.

Symptoms and signs of hypocalcemia include:

* laryngeal spasms

* mild digital circumoral numbness

* cardiac arrhythmias

* paresthesia

* Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign, as shown in the images below.
questions.learning: Hypocalcemia — The Chvostek's sign is seen in hypocalcemia. Chvostek's sign is a clinical indicator of hypocalcemia, seen in conditions like hypoparathyroidism and vitamin D deficiency.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Relative bradycardia is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Brucellosis

Among the given options, relative bradycardia is seen in brucellosis.

Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the Brucella species, typically contracted through direct contact with infected animals or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products. The clinical presentation includes undulating fever, relative bradycardia, musculoskeletal symptoms like arthritis and myalgia, general malaise, hepatosplenomegaly, neurological symptoms in neuro brucellosis, presenting as meningitis or encephalitis. In men, epididymal-orchitis can occur, presenting as testicular pain and swelling.

Laboratory diagnosis of brucellosis includes:

* Polymerase chain reaction

* Blood culture with the Castaneda method

* Serological methods include standard agglutination test (SAT), complement fixation test, Coomb’s antiglobulin test, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).

* Tests for animals and animal products: Milk ring tests and Rose Bengal card tests.

Treatment includes antimicrobial therapy with IM streptomycin and oral doxycycline. The prevention of brucellosis can be achieved by pasteurizing milk and other milk products.

Relative bradycardia, also known as Faget's sign, is observed when patients exhibit a lower heart rate than anticipated in relation to an increase in body temperature. Body temperature is commonly regarded as a factor that independently influences heart rate. It is estimated that for each 1°C (1.8°F) rise in temperature, the heart rate typically increases by approximately 15-20 beats per minute.

While this pulse-temperature dissociation is not highly sensitive or specific for establishing a diagnosis, it can still prove beneficial in resource-limited settings due to its easy accessibility and simplicity.

Infectious causes of relative bradycardia include:

* Salmonella typhi

* Brucella (brucellosis)

* Francisella tularensis

* Coxiella burnetii (Q fever)

* Leptospira interrogans

* Legionella pneumophila

* Rickettsia spp.

* Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus)

* Corynebacterium diphtheriae

* Plasmodium spp. (malaria)

Noninfectious causes include:

* Drug fever

* Beta-blocker use

* Central nervous system lesions

* Malignant lymphoma

* Factitious fever

It was found that relative bradycardia as a feature of a specific disease only occurs in diseases caused by organisms that are both gram-negative and intracellular.

Other options:

Shigellosis, pertussis, and dengue show tachycardia on clinical examination. ( Option A, B & C)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the 2 vessels shown below, assume the pressure along both the vessels is the same and both follow linear flow pattern. What will be the amount of blood flow in A compared to B
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 8 times

The relationship between the flow in a long narrow tube, the viscosity of the fluid, and the radius of the tube is expressed mathematically in the formula called as Poiseuille's law :

Blood flow (F) inside the vessel depends on:

• Pressure difference: directly proportional
• Viscosity: inversely proportional
• Radius: directly proportional to the fourth power
• Length of the vessel: inversely proportional

Here, the radius is doubled so the flow increases by 2 to the power of 4 = 16.

the length of the vessel is also doubled, so the flow decreases by half (÷2) = 8

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman at 28 weeks of gestation presents for a routine checkup and is asymptomatic. On examination, a soft early to mid-systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border, with no associated thrills, heaves, or other abnormal findings. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Physiological murmur of pregnancy

During pregnancy, increased plasma volume and cardiac output produce a physiological flow murmur, typically heard as a soft (grade I–II), early-to-mid systolic ejection murmur along the left sternal border or pulmonary area. It is not associated with thrills, heaves, or other abnormal cardiac findings and requires no treatment.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mitral stenosis: Characterized by a mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap, not a systolic murmur.
• B. Aortic stenosis: Produces a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, often with a thrill.
• D. Ventricular septal defect: Causes a loud pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, frequently associated with a palpable thrill.
questions.learning: Physiological murmur of pregnancy During pregnancy, increased plasma volume and cardiac output produce a physiological flow murmur, typically heard as a soft (grade I–II), early-to-mid systolic ejection murmur along the left sternal border or pulmonary area.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In preterm labor, which drug has a neuroprotective role?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MgSO4

In preterm labor, MgSO4 (magnesium sulfate) is considered to have a neuroprotective role. Studies have demonstrated that magnesium exposure (compared with no exposure) significantly lowers the risks for cerebral palsy.

The combination of corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate has been associated with lower rates of neurodevelopmental impairment and death compared to corticosteroids alone.

The proposed mechanisms of action include:

• reduced presynaptic release of glutamate
• blockade of glutamatergic NMDA receptors
• potentiation of adenosine action
• improved calcium buffering by mitochondria
• blockage of calcium entry via voltage-gated channels

MgSO4 is used as an anticonvulsant in the management of eclampsia and as prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia. The therapeutic level of magnesium in eclampsia is 4–7 mEq/L. Measurement of serum magnesium levels is indicated to monitor magnesium toxicity (if serum creatinine > 1.0 mg/dL).

Loss of patellar reflex is the first sign of MgSO4 toxicity and occurs when the plasma magnesium level reaches 10 mEq/L. Elevated magnesium levels above 10 mEq/L weaken breathing, while 12 mEq/L or higher levels can lead to respiratory paralysis and arrest. Other signs of magnesium toxicity include urine output <30 mL/h, chest pain, and heart block visual changes, flushing, muscle paralysis, and drowsiness.

In suspected toxicity, MgSO4 therapy should be stopped and a slow IV infusion of 1g calcium gluconate 10 mL (10% solution) is given.

Other options:

Options B, C, and D: Nifedipine (calcium channel blocker), and ritodrine, isoxsuprine (beta-adrenergic agonists) are used as tocolytics in preterm labor.
questions.learning: MgSO4 — In preterm labor, MgSO4 (magnesium sulfate) is considered to have a neuroprotective role. Studies have demonstrated that magnesium exposure (compared with no exposure) significantly lowers the risks for cerebral palsy.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department in an unconscious state. Examination reveals needle track marks on the upper limbs along with hypertension, tachycardia, and hyperthermia. Based on these findings, which type of poisoning should be suspected?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms represent a "sympathomimetic toxidrome," characterized by hypertension (elevated BP), tachycardia (increased HR), and hyperthermia (high body temperature). Cocaine is a potent CNS stimulant that causes these exact signs by blocking the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine. Heroin (Option A) is an opioid; a patient would typically present with a "triad" of pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, and bradycardia, which is the opposite of this presentation. Cannabis (Option C) poisoning generally does not cause severe hypertension or high fever. LSD (Option D) is a hallucinogen that can cause some sympathetic arousal but is rarely associated with unconsciousness and severe systemic instability compared to cocaine. The presence of "needle track marks" indicates intravenous drug abuse, which is common for both cocaine and heroin addicts. In a comatose patient with a racing heart and high fever, cocaine toxicity must be suspected and managed with supportive care and benzodiazepines to control the sympathetic surge
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms represent a "sympathomimetic toxidrome," characterized by hypertension (elevated BP), tachycardia (increased HR), and hyperthermia (high body temperature).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Foot drop is caused by damage to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Common peroneal nerve

Foot drop is caused by damage to the common peroneal nerve.

The common peroneal nerve is a component of the sciatic nerve. In the posterior thigh, it supplies the short head of the biceps femoris. It curves around the neck of the fibula deep to peroneus longus and divides into superficial and deep peroneal nerves.

• The superficial peroneal nerve innervates peroneus longus and peroneus brevis which are the evertors of the foot and to the skin over the dorsal area of the foot except for the first webspace and lateral side of the little toe.
• The deep peroneal nerve innervates all muscles of the anterior compartment which are the dorsiflexors of the foot, extensor digitorum brevis, first two dorsal interossei muscles, and skin between great and second toes.

Hence, injury to the common peroneal nerve will lead to:

• Weakness of dorsiflexion of foot or foot drop
• Loss of eversion
• Loss of extension of toes
• Sensory loss

• Anterior and lateral side of the leg
• Dorsum of the foot including the medial side of the great toe

Th image given below shows the course of common peroneal nerve.
questions.learning: Common peroneal nerve Foot drop is caused by damage to the common peroneal nerve. The common peroneal nerve is a component of the sciatic nerve.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most useful test in vesicovaginal fistula?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cystoscopy

Cystoscopy is the most useful test and also the investigation of choice for vesicovaginal fistula (VVF).

Cystoscopy or cystourethroscopy helps to visualize the size of the fistulas, the exact location of multiple fistulas and their proximity to the ureteral orifice. It can also assess the bladder mucosa for any injuries.

The 3-swab test (Option B) is done to identify the types of genitourinary fistula.

In this test, three sterile pieces of cotton swabs are serially placed in the vaginal cavity, while 50-100ml of methylene blue solution is instilled in the bladder using a catheter. The cotton swabs are placed one at the vault, one at the middle, and one just above the introitus.

Interpretation:

• Uppermost swab gets wet and not stained - the leak is from the ureter, as seen in ureterovaginal fistula
• Middle swab gets stained - the leak is from the bladder, as seen in vesicovaginal fistula
• Lowermost swab gets stained- the leak is from the urethra,as seen in urethrovaginal fistula

The below image shows the 3-swab test.

Option C: MRI is usually not needed for the diagnosis of VVF. They can be used to study vesicouterine fistulas.

Option D: Cystometry is done to measure the capacity of the bladder. It is used to investigate urge incontinence.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Immediately after childbirth, assessment of uterine position is important for postpartum care. What is the normal position of the uterus immediately following delivery?
questions.explanation: After the third stage of labor (delivery of the placenta), the uterus undergoes immediate contraction to prevent postpartum hemorrhage. This physiological process, known as involution, causes the fundus to become firm and globoid. Immediately after delivery, the fundus of the uterus is typically felt at a level roughly midway between the pubic symphysis and the umbilicus, which is below the umbilicus (Option C). Within a few hours, the uterus may rise slightly to the level of the umbilicus due to the relaxation of pelvic floor muscles and bladder filling. Option A (below pubic symphysis) is incorrect as the uterus only returns to its true pelvic, non-palpable position around 2 weeks postpartum. Option D (above umbilicus) is often an abnormal finding, potentially suggesting a full bladder or uterine atony with retained blood. Monitoring this "below the umbilicus" position is standard for ensuring uterine contraction
questions.learning: After the third stage of labor (delivery of the placenta), the uterus undergoes immediate contraction to prevent postpartum hemorrhage. This physiological process, known as involution, causes the fundus to become firm and globoid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man, working in a dye manufacturing industry, presents with urinary complaints. Ultrasound shows markedly thickened and irregular bladder walls. What is the most definitive management approach for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient's occupational history as a dye manufacturing worker is a classic risk factor for developing bladder cancer (exposure to aromatic amines). The ultrasound finding of thickened and irregular bladder walls in a symptomatic older male strongly suggests muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). For MIBC, the most definitive management approach is Radical cystectomy (removal of the bladder and associated lymph nodes) with urinary diversion. Cystoscopy with transurethral removal (TURBT) (Option A) is used for initial diagnosis and treatment of non-muscle-invasive disease. BCG instillation (Option B) and intravesical Mitomycin C (Option D) are adjuvant therapies for non-muscle-invasive tumors to prevent recurrence. Because MIBC has a high risk of systemic spread, radical surgery is necessary for a potential cure. This often follows neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy to improve survival. Recognizing high-risk occupational histories is vital for suspecting aggressive bladder malignancies in the clinical setting
questions.learning: The patient's occupational history as a dye manufacturing worker is a classic risk factor for developing bladder cancer (exposure to aromatic amines).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Nerve fibre least susceptible to local anesthetic is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. C

The nerve fibre least susceptible to local anaesthetic is type C. The order of susceptibility of nerve fibres to local anaesthetics is B >A-δ > A-γ > A-β > A-α > C i.e

• B fibres are the most susceptible/least resistant
• C fibres are the least susceptible/most resistant

Factors that increase the sensitivity of nerve fibres are :

• Smaller diameter
• Unmyelinated nerves
• Anatomical and physiological factors

*Note: Although theoretically, C fibres are supposed to be the most susceptible to local anaesthetics, practically it was found to be the least susceptible.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Choose the correct order of suctioning during neonatal resuscitation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mouth-nose

During neonatal resuscitation, the mouth is suctioned first and then the nares, in order to decrease the risk of aspiration. A 12 or 14 French suction catheter is used, with the suction pressure kept between 80-100mmHg.

Routine suctioning of the trachea during neonatal resuscitation is not recommended. The suctioning of the esophagus and stomach is avoided if not indicated specifically, as it can produce a vagal response due to stimulation in the posterior pharynx, resulting in apnea and/or bradycardia.

The steps in neonatal resuscitation follow the ABCs, Airway, Breathing, and Circulation.

The neonatal resuscitation algorithm is given below:

Chest compression should be initiated over the lower third of the sternum at a rate of 90/minutes. The ratio of chest compression to ventilation is 3: 1 (90 compressions: 30 breaths). The thumb technique (preferred) and 2 finger technique are the two different techniques used for performing chest compression. Umbilical vein cannulation is the preferred method for the administration of medications.
questions.learning: Mouth-nose During neonatal resuscitation, the mouth is suctioned first and then the nares, in order to decrease the risk of aspiration. A 12 or 14 French suction catheter is used, with the suction pressure kept between 80-100mmHg.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Based on the graphs provided showing different occupational groups and their risk of developing fever, which occupation demonstrates the highest likelihood of experiencing fever?
questions.explanation: The bar graph (A) shows the proportion of individuals with fever (blue) and no fever (orange) across different occupational groups. To determine which occupation has the highest likelihood of fever, we compare the relative height of the blue (fever) portion in each category. 1. White-collar workers have the highest blue segment, close to about 90%, indicating the largest proportion of fever cases. 2. Industrial workers show a moderate level (around 60–65%). 3. Farmers have slightly lower levels (around 55–60%). 4. Housewives have the lowest proportion of fever (around 35–40%). The pie chart (B) shows the distribution of total workers, not the risk of fever, so it does not affect the answer to this question. Thus, based on the highest proportion of fever cases, white-collar workers demonstrate the greatest likelihood of experiencing fever

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which inhalational anesthetic agent has a blood–gas partition coefficient most similar to that of nitrous oxide?
questions.explanation: The blood-gas partition coefficient determines the solubility of an anesthetic in the blood and directly influences the speed of induction and emergence. Nitrous oxide has a very low coefficient (approximately 0.47), which explains its rapid effects. Among the volatile agents, Desflurane has the most similar coefficient (approximately 0.42), making it the least soluble volatile agent. Sevoflurane (Option C) has a slightly higher coefficient of 0.65. Isoflurane (Option A) has a coefficient of 1.4, and Halothane (Option D) is the most soluble with a coefficient of 2.4, leading to a much slower recovery. Because desflurane is so insoluble, it provides the fastest emergence of all currently used volatile agents, allowing patients to wake up very quickly even after long procedures. However, its use is limited by its high cost and pungent odor, which can cause airway irritation. Identifying these coefficients is essential for understanding the clinical pharmacokinetics of inhalation anesthesia
questions.learning: The blood-gas partition coefficient determines the solubility of an anesthetic in the blood and directly influences the speed of induction and emergence.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During resuscitation, when is the given position indicated?
options: Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing absent
Unconsciousness with pulse present and breathing absent
Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing present
Unconsciousness with pulse absent and breathing present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing present

The position illustrated in the picture is known as the recovery position, and it is used in the management of patients who are unconscious but with pulse present and breathing present.

The recovery position can help prevent complications such as aspiration and airway obstruction in unconscious individuals. Additionally, it is crucial to monitor the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation continuously while they are in the recovery position and seek immediate medical assistance. An unresponsive patient who is breathing spontaneously in the supine position is at risk of airway obstruction from their tongue, mucus, vomit, etc. A modified lateral position is used and the following 6 principles are considered while choosing which variation of recovery position to use,

1.

The victim should be in as near a true lateral position as possible, with the head dependent to allow free drainage of fluid.

2.

The position should be stable.

3.

Avoid any pressure on the chest that impairs breathing.

4.

It should be possible to turn the victim on his or her side and to return to the back easily and safely, with concern for a possible cervical spine injury.

5.

Good observation of and access to the airway should be possible.

6.

The position itself should not cause injury to the victim.

Other options

Option A: Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing absent - In this situation, the patient is in cardiac arrest and requires immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), not the recovery position. CPR involves chest compressions and rescue breaths to support circulation and respiration.

Option B: Unconsciousness with pulse present and breathing absent - In this case, the patient is experiencing respiratory arrest. Rescue breathing or bag-valve-mask ventilation should be initiated to support the patient's breathing. The recovery position is not indicated in this scenario.

Option D: Unconsciousness with pulse absent and breathing present - This option is not physiologically plausible, as the absence of a pulse implies a lack of circulation, and breathing cannot be present without circulation.
questions.learning: Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing present — The position illustrated in the picture is known as the recovery position, and it is used in the management of patients who are unconscious but with pulse present and breathing present.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An infant is brought with complaints of excessive watering of the eyes and photophobia. The image is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital glaucoma

The clinical scenario of excessive watering and photophobia in an infant and the given image with corneal enlargement and haze suggest a likely diagnosis of congenital glaucoma.

Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is caused by impaired aqueous outflow due to a maldeveloped anterior chamber angle.

It can be classified as

• True congenital glaucoma - IOP is elevated during intrauterine life.
• Infantile glaucoma - manifests before 3 years of age.
• Juvenile glaucoma (least common) - IOP rises between 3 and 16 years of age.

Clinically, the child presents with lacrimation, photophobia, and blepharospasm.

PCG may also present with:

• Corneal haze (due to diffuse edema secondary to raised IOP)
• Buphthalmos (a large eye that results from stretching due to raised IOP before 3 years of age). The thin sclera appears blue due to underlying uveal tissue.
• Haab striae (curvilinear healed breaks in Descemet's membrane)
• Corneal scarring
• Optic disc cupping

Evaluation is done under general anesthesia. Initially, IOP measurement is performed (10–12  mmHg is normal). A corneal diameter measuring greater than 12 mm is highly suggestive of an infant under the age of 1 year.

Management is essentially surgical and goniotomy and/or trabeculectomy may be done.

Other options:

Option B: Congenital cataract occurs due to disturbance in lens growth leading to the development of opaque lens fibers. It can be idiopathic, hereditary, or secondary to metabolic disorders and infections. It presents with leukocoria (white reflex in the pupillary area), wandering eye movement, squint, and nystagmus.

Option C: Mucopolysaccharidoses are inherited metabolic disorders presenting with corneal opacification, pigmentary retinopathy, glaucoma, and optic atrophy.

Option D: Ophthalmia neonatorum presents in neonates with conjunctival discharge and chemosis, and tenderness of the eyeball secondary to infections.
questions.learning: Congenital glaucoma — The clinical scenario of excessive watering and photophobia in an infant and the given image with corneal enlargement and haze suggest a likely diagnosis of congenital glaucoma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with self- mutilating behavior such as biting the lips and fingers, delayed developmental milestones, hyperuricemia, and a family history of similar symptoms in male relatives. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of self-mutilation (biting lips and fingers), developmental delay, and hyperuricemia in a young male is diagnostic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. This X-linked recessive disorder is caused by a complete deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT). HGPRT is essential for the purine salvage pathway; its absence leads to the massive overproduction of uric acid and neurological dysfunction through poorly understood mechanisms. Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency (Option A) and Adenosine deaminase deficiency (Option D) cause forms of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), not self-mutilation. Adenine phosphoribosyl transferase deficiency (Option C) results in 2,8-dihydroxyadenine urolithiasis (kidney stones). Lesch-Nyhan is characterized by "orange sand" (uric acid crystals) in the diaper during infancy. Management includes allopurinol to control hyperuricemia and prevent gout/stones, but there is no effective treatment for the severe behavioral and neurological components. The family history in male cousins reinforces the X-linked inheritance pattern
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of self-mutilation (biting lips and fingers), developmental delay, and hyperuricemia in a young male is diagnostic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old male was diagnosed with a submandibular gland tumour and underwent removal of the tumour following which lingual nerve was found to be damaged. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Taste sensation of posterior one-third of tongue is lost.
Taste sensation of anterior two-thirds of tongue is lost.
General sensation of posterior one-third of tongue is lost.
General sensation of anterior two-thirds of tongue is lost.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. General sensation of anterior two-thirds of tongue is lost.

General sensation from the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve, which is injured in this case.

In the anterior two-thirds of the tongue,

* General sensation is carried by the lingual nerve.

* Taste sensation is carried by chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve.

In the posterior one-third of the tongue,

* Both general and taste sensations are carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Valleculae is supplied by the internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve.

General sensory

Special sensory

Anterior 2/3rds

Lingual nerve (CN V)

Chorda tympani (CN VII)

Posterior 1/3rd

Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

Posterior most tongue (vallecullae, epiglottis)

Internal laryngeal nerve (CN X)

Internal laryngeal nerve (CN X)
questions.learning: General sensation of anterior two-thirds of tongue is lost. General sensation from the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve, which is injured in this case.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis, palpable purpura, myalgia, and pulmonary hemorrhage was found to have p-ANCA positivity. Which of the following is the likely vasculitis in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Microscopic polyangiitis

p-ANCA–positive pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with palpable purpura and pulmonary hemorrhage is characteristic of microscopic polyangiitis.

It is a non-granulomatous small-vessel vasculitis involving capillaries, venules, and arterioles.

Organ damage:

- Kidney → RPGN (crescentic GN)

- Lung → Pulmonary hemorrhage

- Skin → Purpura

| ANCA Type | Antigen | Disease Association

| --------- | ------- | -------------------

| p-ANCA /Microscopic polyangiitis | MPO (myeloperoxidase) | MPA, EGPA

| c-ANCA /Granulomatosis with polyangiitis | PR3 (proteinase-3) | GPA (Wegener)

| Feature | MPA | GPA | PAN

| ------- | --- | --- | ---

| Vessel size | Small | Small | Medium

| ANCA | p-ANCA (MPO) | c-ANCA (PR3) | Negative

| Granulomas | ❌ | ✔ | ❌

| Lung involvement | Hemorrhage | Nodules + cavitation | ❌

| Kidney | RPGN | RPGN | Mild

GPA is usually c-ANCA with granulomas, PAN spares lungs, and Behçet’s is not ANCA-associated.
questions.learning: Microscopic polyangiitis p-ANCA–positive pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with palpable purpura and pulmonary hemorrhage is characteristic of microscopic polyangiitis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the type of fixation shown in the image?
options: Periarticular fracture of knee, spanning fixator
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Periarticular fracture of knee, spanning fixator

The image shows a periarticular fracture of the knee and a spanning external fixator used to stabilize the fracture.

External fixators are used if the fracture is associated with severe soft tissue damage. It is also used if internal fixation is risky due to wound contamination. The spanning external fixator will stabilize the fracture until the condition of soft tissue improves.

The technique of an external fixator is that the bone will be fixed above and below the fractures with screws and wires. These screws and wires are then connected to rigid bars. This method is used in fractures of the tibia, femur, pelvis, bones of the hand, etc.

In the image, the bones above and below the knee joint are fixed using a spanning external fixator and hence the fracture is likely to be a periarticular fracture of the knee.

The complications of external fixation include over-distraction, damage to soft tissue structures, and pin-track infections.

Another external fixator that is commonly used in an open type of fracture is the Ilizarov fixator. It is also used for the reconstruction of the limbs and for emergency stabilization in multiple long bone fractures.
questions.learning: Periarticular fracture of knee, spanning fixator — The image shows a periarticular fracture of the knee and a spanning external fixator used to stabilize the fracture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following image of a FAST scan in a trauma patient suggests:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Positive fast

The image of FAST in a trauma patient suggests Positive FAST as there is a fluid collection in the abdominal cavity. The thin anechoic area located between the liver(on the left) and the Kidney(on the right) is a collection of fluid visualized in this RUQ Sonogram image.

FAST stands for Focused assessment with sonography for trauma. It is a rapid diagnostic examination to assess patients with potential thoracoabdominal injuries. It is performed within 2-4 minutes.

Technique:

• Patient in the supine position
• 3.5-5.0 MHz convex transducer
• Following regions are scanned :

• Subxiphoid: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries
• Right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch
• Left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury
• Suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

An "extended FAST or eFAST" scan may be performed: left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Sequentially order of FAST is:- pericardial sac, the Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ), Left Upper Quadrant (LUQ), and pelvis.

4 ‘Ps’ are evaluated in sequence: Pericardial sac → Perihepatic region → Perisplenic region → Pelvis.

Note:-

In Pneumoperitoneum, air is collected in the peritoneal cavity which is usually hyperechoic not anechoic and would appear white in the ultrasound image.
