questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text:
Which of the following muscles are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve?

1. Abductor hallucis
2. Flexor digitorum accesorius
3. Flexor hallucis brevis
4. First lumbrical
5. First interossei
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 and 5

From the given list, the muscles supplied by the lateral plantar nerve are the flexor digitorum accesorius and the first interossei.

The sole of the foot is supplied by the medial and lateral plantar nerves which are both branches of the tibial nerve.

All the muscles of the sole of the foot are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve, except for the following four muscles which are supplied by the medial plantar nerve:

1. Abductor hallucis
2. Flexor digitorum brevis
3. Flexor hallucis brevis
4. First lumbrical

The sensory supply of the sole of the foot is as shown in the illustration below.

The muscles of the sole of the foot are arranged in 4 layers as shown below:

1st layer: It consists of the abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi.

2nd layer: It consists of flexor accessorius and the four lumbrical muscles,the tendons of flexor hallucis longus and flexor digitorum longus run in the same plane as the muscles of the second layer.

3rd layer: It consists of the shorter intrinsic muscles of the toes, which are flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis and flexor digiti minimi brevis.

4th layer: It consists of plantar and dorsal interossei and the tendons of tibialis posterior and fibularis longus.
questions.learning: 2 and 5 From the given list, the muscles supplied by the lateral plantar nerve are the flexor digitorum accesorius and the first interossei. The sole of the foot is supplied by the medial and lateral plantar nerves which are both branches of the tibial nerve.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A truck driver presents with multiple painful genital ulcers on the scrotum following unprotected sexual intercourse, along with tender lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of multiple, painful genital ulcers associated with painful regional lymphadenopathy (buboes) is the classic hallmark of Chancroid. Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the gram-negative bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi. A chancre (Option A), seen in primary syphilis, is characteristically a painless ulcer with a clean base and painless lymph nodes. Donovanosis (Option B) presents with painless, "beefy-red," granulomatous ulcers that bleed easily, without significant lymphadenopathy. Herpes simplex (Option D) typically presents with multiple, very painful, superficial vesicles that rupture to form shallow ulcers, rather than the deeper, necrotic ulcers of chancroid. Chancroid is often described as having a "dirty" base with undermined edges. Treatment involves macrolide antibiotics like azithromycin or ceftriaxone. This condition is an important risk factor for the transmission of HIV
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of multiple, painful genital ulcers associated with painful regional lymphadenopathy (buboes) is the classic hallmark of Chancroid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a drooping of the eyelid, miosis and anhidrosis. A diagnosis of Horner syndrome is made. Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Sympathetic plexus around the internal carotid artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cervical sympathetic chain

Horner syndrome results from interruption of the sympathetic pathway supplying the eye, commonly at the cervical sympathetic chain.

Lesion causes ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis due to loss of postganglionic sympathetic fibres.
questions.learning: Cervical sympathetic chain Horner syndrome results from interruption of the sympathetic pathway supplying the eye, commonly at the cervical sympathetic chain.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The glycosaminoglycan present in the cornea responsible for transparency is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratan sulfate

Keratan sulfate is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal transparency.

Note:

Keratan sulfate is made of repeating units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose. 2 types of keratan sulfate are seen:

* Keratan sulfate I is present in the cornea.

* Keratan sulfate II is mainly present in the cartilage.

Both keratan sulfate I and dermatan sulfate (KS I and DS) play roles in corneal transparency. However, DS is widely distributed in the body, mainly in the skin. Hence, KS I is the single best choice for this question.

Other factors contributing to transparency of cornea are:

* Peculiar arrangement of corneal lamellae (Maurice theory)

* Peculiar refractive index of corneal lamellae (Goldmann theory)

* Avascularity of cornea

* Corneal crystallins

* Balance between intraocular pressure and swelling pressure
questions.learning: Keratan sulfate Keratan sulfate is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal transparency. Note: Keratan sulfate is made of repeating units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A postmenopausal woman presents with irregular uterine bleeding, and endometrial biopsy reveals endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia is a benign condition with a low risk of progressing to cancer. In postmenopausal women with irregular bleeding, the first-line medical management is progestin therapy to reverse the hyperplasia. The Levonorgestrel Intrauterine System (LNG-IUS) is highly effective as it provides high local progestin concentrations to the endometrium. OCPs (Option A) and Estradiol (Option B) are contraindicated because estrogen stimulates further endometrial proliferation, worsening the condition and increasing malignancy risk. Danazol (Option D) is an androgenic agent with significant side effects and is far less effective than modern progestin options. If medical management fails or symptoms recur, a hysterectomy may be considered as the definitive surgical option
questions.learning: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia is a benign condition with a low risk of progressing to cancer. In postmenopausal women with irregular bleeding, the first-line medical management is progestin therapy to reverse the hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a large breast lump measuring 9 × 10 cm. Histopathological examination reveals increased stromal cellularity with a characteristic leaf-like architecture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a large, rapidly growing breast mass in a middle-aged woman is highly suspicious for a Phyllodes tumor. The definitive diagnostic clue provided is the histopathological finding of "increased stromal cellularity" and a "distinctive leaf-like structure" (cleft-like spaces lined by epithelium). The name "Phyllodes" is derived from the Greek word for "leaf-like." Giant fibroadenoma (Option B) can present similarly as a large mass but lacks the leaf-like stromal overgrowth and increased cellularity seen here. Inflammatory carcinoma (Option C) presents with skin changes like peau d'orange and redness rather than a discrete large lump. Ductal carcinoma (Option D) typically appears as a hard, irregular, fixed mass often with nipple changes or nodal involvement. Phyllodes tumors can be benign, borderline, or malignant and are treated with wide local excision with a 1 cm margin to prevent local recurrence
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a large, rapidly growing breast mass in a middle-aged woman is highly suspicious for a Phyllodes tumor. The definitive diagnostic clue provided is the histopathological finding of "increased stromal cellularity" and a…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. Examination reveals normal breast development with absent axillary and pubic hair. Pelvic examination shows a normally developed vagina with clitoromegaly and a microphallus. Ultrasound reveals masses in the inguinal region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome

Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome (PAIS) is a disorder of sex development (DSD) caused by partial resistance of tissues to androgens due to mutations in the androgen receptor.

• 46, XY karyotype
• Testes present (often located in inguinal canal or abdomen)
• Variable virilization due to partial androgen action
• Ambiguous genitalia (e.g., clitoromegaly or microphallus)
• Primary amenorrhea
• Breast development may be present due to aromatisation of testosterone to estrogen
• Reduced or absent pubic/axillary hair due to impaired androgen effect

Why other options are incorrect:

• Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS): normal female external genitalia ; without clitoromegaly.
• MRKH syndrome: 46,XX with normal pubic/axillary hair and absent uterus/vagina, normal ovaries.
• Gonadal dysgenesis: streak gonads and poor breast development.
questions.learning: Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome (PAIS) is a disorder of sex development (DSD) caused by partial resistance of tissues to androgens due to mutations in the androgen receptor. • 46, XY karyotype • Testes…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the subsequent medications can lead to the development of gynecomastia?
questions.explanation: Gynecomastia is the benign enlargement of male breast tissue due to an imbalance between estrogen and androgen action. Spironolactone (Option C) is a potassium-sparing diuretic well-known for causing gynecomastia as a side effect . It works as a direct androgen receptor antagonist and also inhibits testosterone synthesis, effectively tilting the hormonal balance in favor of estrogen. Tamoxifen (Option A) is actually a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) used to treat painful gynecomastia in men. Oxytocin (Option B) is a reproductive hormone without significant effects on breast tissue growth in males. Clomiphene citrate (Option D) is an ovulation-inducing agent that can occasionally cause breast symptoms but is not a primary recognized cause of clinical gynecomastia compared to spironolactone. Therefore, due to its potent anti-androgenic activity, Spironolactone is the definitive answer. Patients on long-term therapy are often monitored for this bothersome but reversible side effect
questions.learning: Gynecomastia is the benign enlargement of male breast tissue due to an imbalance between estrogen and androgen action. Spironolactone (Option C) is a potassium-sparing diuretic well-known for causing gynecomastia as a side effect .

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 39-year-old woman presents to the outpatient department with a complaint of bloody nipple discharge. Clinical examination reveals that the discharge is arising from a single lactiferous duct. Given this localized finding, what is the most appropriate management or treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: A spontaneous bloody nipple discharge originating from a single duct in a 39-year-old woman is most likely caused by an intraductal papilloma. The standard-of-care surgical management for this presentation is a Microdochectomy. This precise procedure involves the excision of the single, offending lactiferous duct and its surrounding tissue through a periareolar incision. Hadfield’s operation (Option A), or total duct excision, is reserved for multi-duct discharge or more extensive disease. IV antibiotics and incision (Option B) are used for treating an acute breast abscess, not a ductal growth. Microdiscectomy (Option C) is a neurosurgical procedure for the spine. While most intraductal papillomas are benign, they can occasionally contain areas of atypia or early cancer; therefore, histological examination of the excised duct is mandatory. Microdochectomy effectively stops the discharge while preserving the rest of the breast tissue
questions.learning: A spontaneous bloody nipple discharge originating from a single duct in a 39-year-old woman is most likely caused by an intraductal papilloma. The standard-of-care surgical management for this presentation is a Microdochectomy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with blunt trauma to the abdomen. On evaluation, liver injury was noted for which primary repair was done. Coagulation function was monitored intraoperatively, using the method shown below. What is the method used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thromboelastography

In the case of liver injury, intraoperative monitoring of coagulation function is done by thromboelastography which is shown in the given image.

Thromboelastography (TEG) is a non-invasive test that quantifies the ability of whole blood to form a clot. It is useful in intraoperative coagulation status assessment. The dynamic changes in the viscoelastic properties of a blood sample during the clotting can be detected and quantified by thromboelastography. Underlying coagulation deficiencies show different shapes in the TEG. They are shown in the image as follows

Advantages of thromboelastography:

•

Blood coagulability, including coagulation cascade, platelet function, and fibrinolysis can be assessed.

•

It is a simple bedside test

•

Can diagnose coagulopathic bleeding

•

Can be used as a guide in transfusion therapy and decrease the use of blood products

•

Can detect dynamic changes in blood coagulation during resuscitation

•

Predict the clinical efficacy of therapeutic agents affecting blood coagulability

Other options:

Option B: Plethysmography is a semiquantitative method to measure segmental blood flow and velocity in the carotid and peripheral vascular systems. It is safe, inexpensive and easy to use. It is useful in the diagnosis of vascular disease.

Option C: Sonography or ultrasound is a cheap and easily available imaging method. It is used as a first-line imaging method to assess liver, biliary, renal tract, obstetric, and gynecological disease. It is also useful in guiding needle placement during interventional procedures. Ligaments, tendon and muscle injuries can also be studied by an ultrasound.

Option D: Elastography is a newer imaging modality, which detects the changes in elasticity of tissues. It is based on the concept that the pathological process alters the elastic properties of tissue. It is useful in differentiating malignant and benign breast neoplasms, identifying traumatic changes in the muscles and tendons, helping to decide the biopsy site accurately, assess liver fibrosis and steatosis.
questions.learning: Thromboelastography — In the case of liver injury, intraoperative monitoring of coagulation function is done by thromboelastography which is shown in the given image.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Common site for congenital diaphragmatic hernia is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Posterolateral

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia most commonly occurs through the foramen of Bochdalek, a posterolateral defect of the diaphragm.

It results from failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane, leading to herniation of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity.

Anterior defects (foramen of Morgagni) are less common and usually right-sided.
questions.learning: Posterolateral Congenital diaphragmatic hernia most commonly occurs through the foramen of Bochdalek, a posterolateral defect of the diaphragm. It results from failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane, leading to herniation of abdominal contents…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inferior vena cava

Inferior vena cava has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation.

The blood gets oxygenated in the placenta and this passes to the umbilical vein. From the umbilical vein, 50% of the blood enters the hepatic circulation and 50% bypasses the liver to enter the inferior vena cava. From here, the blood enters the heart via the right atrium. The right atrium also receives deoxygenated blood from the superior vena cava. This mixed blood is distributed to the body via aorta.

Therefore, inferior vena cava has the highest concentration of oxygen in the fetal circulation.
questions.learning: Inferior vena cava Inferior vena cava has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation. The blood gets oxygenated in the placenta and this passes to the umbilical vein.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents after a motorcycle road traffic accident with no reported pain or injury. During examination, blood is observed at the tip of the urethral meatus, and the bladder is non-palpable. What would be your next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wait for bladder to fill

The given clinical scenario showing blood at the tip of the urethral meatus following a road traffic accident (RTA) is a clinical hallmark of a urethral injury. The next best step in this scenario is to wait and watch.

Injuries to the urethra are more common in males. They are of:

Part of the urethra
Injury type
Clinical features

Bulbar urethra
(distal urethral injury)
Blunt trauma to the perineum
Butterfly hematoma (perineal bruising), urinary retention, and bleeding from the urethral tip

Bulbomembranous junction
(proximal urethral injury)
Road traffic accidents
Blood at the tip of the meatus and urinary retention
High-riding prostate on digital rectal examination (Vermooten sign)

Retrograde urethrography using water-soluble contrast is used for localizing the site of urethral injury.

The patient should be managed with analgesia and antibiotics. If the bladder is full, it should be drained with a catheter placed by percutaneous suprapubic puncture using a Seldinger technique.

Other options:

Option A: Foley catheterization should not be done since it might convert a partial tear into a complete tear.

Option C: Nephrogram is not done but retrograde urethrogram is performed in urethral injury.

Option D: Suprapubic Cystostomy is done only in cases where the bladder is full or the patient is unable to urinate following a pelvic fracture/ RTA.
questions.learning: Wait for bladder to fill — The given clinical scenario showing blood at the tip of the urethral meatus following a road traffic accident (RTA) is a clinical hallmark of a urethral injury.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following correctly represents the fractional inactivated polio vaccine (fIPV) dosing schedule under the National Immunization Schedule?
options: At birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 16-24 months, 5 years
questions.explanation: Fractional Inactivated Polio Vaccine (fIPV) is administered as a 0.1 ml intradermal dose. Under the current National Immunization Schedule (NIS), the primary doses are given at 6 weeks and 14 weeks. Recently, a third dose was added to be administered at 9 completed months of age. Option A is incorrect because fIPV is not given at 10 weeks. Option B represents the full schedule for Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV), which is given as 2 drops at birth and subsequently alongside IPV. Option D is not a standard immunization schedule. Unlike the live OPV, fIPV is a killed vaccine that provides safe humoral immunity without the risk of Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP). The 9-month dose is specifically given in the left upper arm
questions.learning: Fractional Inactivated Polio Vaccine (fIPV) is administered as a 0.1 ml intradermal dose. Under the current National Immunization Schedule (NIS), the primary doses are given at 6 weeks and 14 weeks.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A diabetic man presents with facial pain and blackish discoloration of the nasal cavity. CT imaging reveals sinus involvement with bone erosion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled diabetes is a major risk factor for mucormycosis, a fulminant and angioinvasive fungal infection. The presence of a black eschar (necrotic tissue) on the nasal mucosa or palate is a hallmark clinical sign. The fungus, usually Rhizopus species, invades blood vessels causing thrombosis, infarction, and invasive bone destruction as seen on the CT. Acute bacterial sinusitis (Option A) causes purulent discharge and pain but lacks tissue necrosis and bone erosion. Allergic fungal sinusitis (Option B) is a non-invasive condition that expands rather than destroys bone. Nasal polyps (Option C) are benign mucosal growths that do not cause pain or necrotic changes. Management requires urgent surgical debridement and high-dose IV liposomal amphotericin B
questions.learning: Uncontrolled diabetes is a major risk factor for mucormycosis, a fulminant and angioinvasive fungal infection. The presence of a black eschar (necrotic tissue) on the nasal mucosa or palate is a hallmark clinical sign.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child presents with a fever and a rash. Urine examination showed cells with owl's eye appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cytomegalovirus

The most likely causative agent is cytomegalovirus (CMV) based on the clinical symptoms and the presence of the owl's eye appearance on urinary examination.

CMV is the largest virus in the herpes family of viruses. It causes the following conditions:

• Immunocompetent individuals - asymptomatic or mononucleosis-like infection such as fever and rash
• Neonates - devastating systemic infections
• Immunosuppressed individuals - serious, life-threatening, disseminated CMV infections of the lungs (pneumonitis) and gastrointestinal tract (colitis)

CMV spreads through contact with salivary secretions and sexual contact, blood transfusion, and organ transplantation.

Laboratory diagnosis is by recovery of the virus from urine, saliva, or other bodily fluids into human fibroblast cells. Antibody demonstration using ELISA is used for diagnosis of primary infection.

A cytomegalic pneumocyte containing characteristic intranuclear basophilic inclusion surrounded by a clear halo known as an owl’s eye appearance.

Other options:

Option B: Epstein Barr virus: Conditions associated with EBV infection are

• Glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis): fever, pharyngitis, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy
• Hodgkin lymphoma
• Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
• Burkitt's lymphoma
• Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
• EBV‐associated lymphoproliferative disease

Option C: Herpes simplex virus causes cutaneous infections like herpes labialis caused by viral reactivation in febrile patients. It presents as blisters around the mouth, cheeks, and forehead. Gingivostomatitis and pharyngitis are the most frequent manifestations of primary herpes infections. HSV esophagitis presents as dysphagia, sub-sternal pain, and weight loss.

Option D: Acute congenital toxoplasmosis may manifest as fever, jaundice, petechial rashes, microphthalmia, cataract, glaucoma, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, myocarditis, cerebral calcifications, and chorioretinitis.

Most infections in adults who are immunocompetent are usually asymptomatic. Active progression of infection is more likely in immunocompromised individuals.
questions.learning: Cytomegalovirus — The most likely causative agent is cytomegalovirus (CMV) based on the clinical symptoms and the presence of the owl's eye appearance on urinary examination.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study utilizes office records from the past 20 years to compare the incidence of a disease between factory workers exposed to aniline dye and unexposed clerical staff. What type of epidemiological study does this represent?
questions.explanation: This study is a retrospective study (specifically a retrospective cohort) because it utilizes existing past records to assess exposure and outcomes that have already occurred. Subjects were grouped by their historical exposure status (aniline dye vs. clerical) and followed through the records to determine disease incidence. A prospective study (Option A) would follow individuals forward in time from the present into the future. A case-control study (Option C) would start by identifying individuals who already have the disease and looking back for exposure; here, the study started with exposure groups. An ecological study (Option D) compares whole populations or geographic areas rather than using individual-level data from office records. Retrospective studies are generally less expensive and time-consuming but are dependent on the accuracy of historical documentation
questions.learning: This study is a retrospective study (specifically a retrospective cohort) because it utilizes existing past records to assess exposure and outcomes that have already occurred.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: When asked about her age, a woman states that she is 39 years old and explains this by saying she is married to an older man and has two children aged 15 and 18 years. Which psychiatric disorder does this presentation suggest?
questions.explanation: Circumstantial speech is a thought disorder where the patient provides excessive, unnecessary, and tedious details before eventually reaching the point or answering the original question. In this case, the woman was asked her age but detailed her marriage and children first, although she did ultimately answer "39 years old". Derailment (Option A) involves a loosening of associations where speech shifts randomly between unrelated topics without any logical connection. Flight of ideas (Option C), often seen in mania, is characterized by rapid, pressured shifting between topics, often with only superficial associations. Tangentiality (Option D) is similar to circumstantiality, but the key difference is that the patient never actually returns to answer the original question. Recognizing these patterns is essential for accurate psychiatric diagnosis and mental status examinations. Circumstantiality is frequently seen in individuals with personality disorders or organic brain syndromes
questions.learning: Circumstantial speech is a thought disorder where the patient provides excessive, unnecessary, and tedious details before eventually reaching the point or answering the original question.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a type of superior mediastinal tumor?
questions.explanation: The superior mediastinum is the space in the thoracic cavity above the plane of the sternal angle (T4-T5). Common tumors in this region often originate from structures normally located there. Retrosternal thyroid goiters (Option B) frequently extend into the superior mediastinum. Lymphomas (Option C), particularly Hodgkin's disease, commonly present with superior mediastinal lymphadenopathy. The thymus (Option D) is a classic superior mediastinal structure, and thymomas or thymic cysts are typical tumors found here. While ectopic parathyroid tissue can occasionally be found in the mediastinum, parathyroid tumors (Option A) are fundamentally neck lesions. Even when ectopic, parathyroid adenomas are more commonly found in the "anterior" mediastinum rather than the superior compartment. Therefore, among the choices provided, a parathyroid tumor is the least typical "type" of superior mediastinal tumor compared to the well-recognized thyroid, thymic, and lymphoid pathologies. Clinically, a superior mediastinal mass often presents with Superior Vena Cava (SVC) syndrome or tracheal compression
questions.learning: The superior mediastinum is the space in the thoracic cavity above the plane of the sternal angle (T4-T5). Common tumors in this region often originate from structures normally located there.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: At what time is a blood sample typically taken to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation: The optimal timing for collecting a blood sample to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism is between 48 and 72 hours after delivery. This delay is critical to avoid the physiological "TSH surge" that occurs immediately after birth, which can lead to false-positive results if testing is done too early. While umbilical cord blood (Option A) can be used for initial screening at birth, it is less reliable for a definitive diagnosis. Samples taken at 24 hours (Option B) or 23–48 hours (Option C) are still within the window where TSH levels may be naturally elevated, complicating the interpretation. A heel prick for dried blood spots is the standard method used for universal newborn screening during this 72-hour window. If the TSH is significantly elevated (>20 mIU/L), a follow-up venous blood sample is required to confirm the diagnosis and initiate timely levothyroxine therapy to prevent intellectual disability
questions.learning: The optimal timing for collecting a blood sample to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism is between 48 and 72 hours after delivery. This delay is critical to avoid the physiological "TSH surge" that occurs immediately after birth, which can lead to…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which is the narrowest part of the adult laryngeal airway?
questions.explanation: In the adult larynx, the glottis—specifically the rima glottidis, which is the narrow opening between the true vocal cords—represents the narrowest part of the airway. This site is critical for voice production and regulating airflow. The supraglottic region (Option A), which contains the epiglottis and false cords, is wider than the glottic opening. The subglottic region (Option C) is located below the vocal cords; while it is the narrowest part of the larynx in infants and children, it is wider than the glottis in adults. The trachea (Option D) is a significantly larger tubular structure and is much wider than any part of the laryngeal apparatus. Understanding these anatomical differences is vital for intubation and airway management, as the glottis is the primary point of resistance in adults, whereas the subglottis is the limiting factor in pediatric patients
questions.learning: In the adult larynx, the glottis—specifically the rima glottidis, which is the narrow opening between the true vocal cords—represents the narrowest part of the airway.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the context of mitral stenosis, which clinical feature is typically observed?
questions.explanation: A loud, snapping first heart sound (S1) is a hallmark of mitral stenosis. This occurs because the mitral leaflets are thickened but still mobile, and the high pressure gradient in the left atrium causes them to slam shut forcefully at the start of systole. An absent S1 (Option B) is more characteristic of severe mitral regurgitation where the leaflets fail to coapt. An S3 gallop (Option C) is associated with volume overload and heart failure, which is not typical for the restricted filling of mitral stenosis. Muffled heart sounds (Option D) suggest pericardial effusion or severe obesity. Other classic findings of mitral stenosis include an opening snap and a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position
questions.learning: A loud, snapping first heart sound (S1) is a hallmark of mitral stenosis. This occurs because the mitral leaflets are thickened but still mobile, and the high pressure gradient in the left atrium causes them to slam shut forcefully at the start of systole.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-month-old baby comes with complaints of deafness, cataract, and patent ductus arteriosus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Congenital rubella syndrome

The most likely diagnosis is congenital rubella syndrome based on the clinical findings.

Triad of Gregg is seen in babies with congenital rubella syndrome. The features include:

• Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
• Cataract
• Sensorineural Hearing loss (SNHL)

Rubella or German measles is a serious infection in pregnancy that causes abortions or severe fetal defects if infection occurs in the first trimester. Transmission of the virus occurs through nasopharyngeal secretions (droplet transmission). The mother usually has a fever and generalized body rash. The rash is maculopapular in nature that begins from the face and spreads to the trunk and extremities later. The incidence and severity reduce as the pregnancy advances and is rare after 20 weeks of gestation.

There is no specific treatment for rubella virus infection in mothers. Post-exposure passive immunization can be beneficial if given within 5 days of exposure to droplets. The incidence of this disease has reduced due to the availability of MMR vaccines. MMR vaccines can be administered only to non-pregnant females as it is a live, attenuated virus. Pregnancy should be avoided for at least 1 month after vaccination.

Other options:

Option A: Herpes simplex infection can be acquired in utero, intrapartum, or during the neonatal period. The intrauterine infection causes skin vesicles, eye findings (chorioretinitis, keratoconjunctivitis), and microcephaly/hydranencephaly. Intrapartum infection presents with either:

• Skin, eye, and mouth disease
• Encephalitis
• Disseminated disease with sepsis-like presentation

Option B: Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs due to primary infection in immunologically normal pregnant women. First-trimester infection results in severe disease and third-trimester disease result in milder disease. It presents with a triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracerebral calcifications.

Option C: Pregnant females infected with cytomegalovirus (CMV) present with infectious mononucleosis-like symptoms, that is fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and polyarthritis. Transmission to the fetus increases as pregnancy advances and is maximum in the third trimester. Congenital infection includes growth restriction, microcephaly, intracranial (periventricular) calcifications, chorioretinitis, mental and motor deficits, hepatosplenomegaly, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenic purpura. Most infected neonates are asymptomatic at birth and later present with these symptoms. Sensorineural hearing loss is a common sequela of congenital CMV infection.

Other infections which cause congenital malformations are:

Organism
Defects

Toxoplasma

Hydro/microcephaly, convulsions, chorioretinitis, diffuse cerebral calcifications

Parvovirus
Non-immune hydrops

Syphilis

Hutchinson's triad:

• Interstitial keratitis
• Hutchinson's teeth
• Eighth nerve deafness
questions.learning: Congenital rubella syndrome — The most likely diagnosis is congenital rubella syndrome based on the clinical findings. Triad of Gregg is seen in babies with congenital rubella syndrome.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics?
options: Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule
Inhibits the Na-CI pump in late distal convoluted tubule
Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl pump in the descending limb of loop of Henle
Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl pump in the ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule

Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits Na+-Cl- symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride.

Thiazide diuretics:

They may be used for the treatment of hypertension, heart failure, nephrolithiasis due to idiopathic hypercalciuria, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). They block the Na+/Cl- co-transporter in the DCT. This results in the loss of sodium, chloride, and water contributing to the diuretic effect. The diuretic effect of thiazide leads to decreased osmotic pressure due to the loss of Na+, Cl-, and water leading to compensatory reabsorption of uric acid thus resulting in hyperuricemia. The intracytoplasmic Na+ concentration also decreases due to the blockade of the co-transporter. To compensate, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger pumps sodium from the systemic circulation into the epithelial cells in exchange for calcium. The declining calcium levels inside the cell will draw more calcium from the lumen into the systemic circulation. This results in hypercalcemia. There is also increased loss of Mg2+, K+, and H+.

Mechanisms of antihypertensive action: Decreases plasma and ECF volume by diuresis thereby decreasing cardiac output. Even when the compensatory mechanisms restore the Na+ levels and plasma volume, a low BP is maintained by a reduction in total peripheral resistance. This reduction in total peripheral resistance is due to the persistence of a small sodium and volume deficit even after compensation. The decreased intracellular sodium is responsible for increased compliance of the vessel wall and a reduced response to constrictor stimulus.

Thiazides are the diuretic of choice for uncomplicated hypertension.

Advantages of thiazide as an antihypertensive are:

* It can be given as once a day dose and has a flat dose-response curve

* Decreased incidence of postural hypotension and relative freedom from CNS side effects

* No tolerance

* No fluid retention

* Decreased risk of osteoporotic fractures due to its hypocalciuric action

* Low cost

* Effectiveness in isolated systolic hypertension

* Thiazides are ineffective both as antihypertensive and diuretic in patients with chronic renal failure.
questions.learning: Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits Na+-Cl- symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 73-year-old man with a long history of smoking and known coronary artery disease presents with blackened toes, pain, coldness of the affected areas, and occasional ulcers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a 73-year-old smoker with pre-existing coronary artery disease (CAD) who now has cold, painful, and black (necrotic/gangrenous) toes is classic for Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) caused by atherosclerosis. Smoking and CAD are major risk factors. Atherosclerotic plaques narrow the arteries of the lower limbs, leading to chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI). Buerger's disease (Option A), or thromboangiitis obliterans, also causes digital gangrene in smokers, but it typically affects much younger males (usually under 45) and is not usually associated with CAD in this manner. Raynaud's disease (Option C) involves reversible vasospasm, usually in response to cold, and does not typically lead to systemic gangrene in an elderly man with generalized vascular disease. Giant cell arteritis (Option D) affects large arteries, primarily the branches of the external carotid, and presents with temporal headaches or jaw claudication. Thus, given the patient's age and extensive cardiovascular history, atherosclerosis is the most probable cause of his critical limb ischemia and gangrene
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a 73-year-old smoker with pre-existing coronary artery disease (CAD) who now has cold, painful, and black (necrotic/gangrenous) toes is classic for Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) caused by atherosclerosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about Finerenone? 1. It causes less hyperkalemia than spironolactone 2. It has a cardioprotective effect 3. It gets accumulated in the kidneys 4. It causes a significant reduction in blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2

Solution – Finerenone:

• It is a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA)
• Used mainly in:

• Chronic kidney disease (CKD) with diabetes
• Cardiovascular protection

Statement 3: Gets accumulated in kidneys

• Opposite is true
• Finerenone has Even distribution (heart + kidney)

• Unlike eplerenone/spironolactone→ kidney accumulation

Statement 4: Significant BP reduction

• Only mild antihypertensive effect
• Not used as a primary antihypertensive

Steroidal MRAs (spironolactone, eplerenone) → kidney-predominant distribution → more BP reduction + more hyperkalemia

Finerenone (non-steroidal) → equal heart:kidney distribution → cardioprotective + less hyperkalemia + minimal BP effect

| Feature | Finerenone | Spironolactone

| ------- | ---------- | --------------

| Type | Non-steroidal MRA | Steroidal MRA

| Tissue distribution | Balanced (heart + kidney) | Kidney predominant

| Hyperkalemia | Less | More

| Anti-androgen effects | None | Gynecomastia

| Cardioprotection | Strong | Moderate

| BP reduction | Mild | Moderate

| CKD use | Preferred | Limited

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with a sudden onset of breathlessness. Based on the radiological image provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The radiological image displays the characteristic "Steeple Sign," which represents subglottic narrowing of the airway. This finding is pathognomonic for Laryngotracheobronchitis, commonly known as Croup. Croup typically presents in children with sudden shortness of breath, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. Epiglottitis (Option A) would show a "thumbprint sign" on a lateral X-ray due to supraglottic swelling and is a more severe, life-threatening emergency. Bronchitis (Option C) involves inflammation of the lower bronchi and does not cause subglottic narrowing. Laryngomalacia (Option D) is a congenital condition causing chronic stridor due to a floppy epiglottis, typically diagnosed clinically rather than by an acute "steeple sign". Thus, the visual narrowing of the upper trachea confirms croup as the diagnosis
questions.learning: The radiological image displays the characteristic "Steeple Sign," which represents subglottic narrowing of the airway. This finding is pathognomonic for Laryngotracheobronchitis, commonly known as Croup.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In the given image which vein is mainly affected?
questions.explanation: The image displays varicose veins, which are dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by valve incompetence. The varicosities follow the anatomical path of the great saphenous vein (GSV), which runs along the medial aspect of the leg and thigh. The short saphenous vein (Option B) runs along the posterior part of the leg and calf; its involvement would show varicosities on the back of the leg rather than the medial side. The femoral vein (Option C) is a deep vein, and although its valves can be incompetent, varicosities are a superficial venous system pathology. Perforator veins (Option D) connect the superficial and deep systems; while their incompetence contributes to the formation of varicosities, they are not the primary vein being visualized as affected in the medial limb. Thus, the location confirms the GSV as the main vessel involved
questions.learning: The image displays varicose veins, which are dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by valve incompetence. The varicosities follow the anatomical path of the great saphenous vein (GSV), which runs along the medial aspect of the leg and thigh.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a severe headache and neck stiffness. There is no history of fever. The CT brain taken is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subarachnoid haemorrhage

The given clinical scenario of an afebrile patient with a severe headache, neck stiffness with CT head showing hyperdense areas in the basal cisterns and sulci, is highly suggestive of Subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. It usually occurs due to bleeding from a ruptured aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. Most of the ruptured aneurysms are located at the circle of Willis.

Patients present with a sudden and severe headache referred to as thunderclap headache, which may be associated with vomiting, decreased consciousness, and seizures. Neck stiffness and photophobia may develop after a few hours.

Non-contrast CT scan is the imaging modality of choice if done within 12 hours. It shows an increased density of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces. A lumbar puncture should be done if there is a strong suspicion of SAH but negative CT findings. It is ideally done 12 hours later. This allows for red blood cell lysis to occur and bilirubin to be detected in the CSF.

Other options:

Option A: Bacterial meningitis is characterised by high fever, neck stiffness, and positive Brudzinski's sign.

Option B: Subdural haemorrhage is often due to the rupture of bridging veins that crosses the subdural space. In subdural hemorrhage, the CT shows crescentic opacity.

Option D: Extradural haemorrhage is mostly due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Since the dura matter tends to adhere to the skull, the hemorrhage is seen in CT as a biconvex dense area. They usually do not cross cranial sutures.

Pearl PF2181: Types of Intracranial Hemorrhage

1. Extradural hemorrhage/epidural hematoma (EDH)

* Source: Arterial - middle meningeal artery (m/c)

* Cause: Trauma - fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone

* Lens or lentiform shaped opacity

* Presence of a characteristic lucid interval

* Treatment: Surgical evacuation of large/rapidly evolving EDH

2. Acute subdural hemorrhage (SDH)

* Source: Venous - bridging veins

* Cause: Trauma

* Common in old age, alcoholics, patients on anticoagulants, shaken baby syndrome (a form of child abuse seen in infants and toddlers)

* Clinical features: Acute SDH may be associated with a lucid interval; chronic SDH is associated with drowsiness, headache

* CT findings: Crescent opacity

* Treatment: May resolve spontaneously or require surgical drainage

3. Acute on chronic SDH

* Source: Venous - bridging veins

* Cause: Usually, trivial trauma in old age or patients on anticoagulants

* Crescent clots

* Presence of a history of headache, confusion, and being prone to falls

4. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

* Source: Arterial

* Causes: Trauma (most common), berry aneurysm (2nd most common)

* M/c sites: Terminal ICA, MCA bifurcation, top of basilar artery

* Clinical features: Characteristic thunderclap headache

* CSF: Xanthochromia

* Hyperdensity in the subarachnoid space

* Treatment: Early repair by clipping/coiling of berry aneurysm. Nimodipine and IV fluids with monitoring to prevent vasospasm.

5. Intra-parenchymal hemorrhage

* Most common type of intracranial hemorrhage

* Cause: Hypertension (most common cause)

* Hyperdensity within the brain parenchyma

* Site: Putamen of the basal ganglia (most common)

* Treatment: Correction of any identified coagulopathy by infusing prothrombin complex concentrates, FFP, or fresh platelets as required; surgical evacuation for cerebellar hematoma >3 cm in size
questions.learning: Subarachnoid haemorrhage — The given clinical scenario of an afebrile patient with a severe headache, neck stiffness with CT head showing hyperdense areas in the basal cisterns and sulci, is highly suggestive of Subarachnoid haemorrhage.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old laborer working at a construction site presented with fever and hemoptysis. The sputum sample collected for examination showed the following. The smear will be stained by which of the following sequences?
options: Methylene blue - malachite green- acetic acid-water
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carbol fuschin - acid-alcohol - methylene blue

The given clinical vignette of fever and hemoptysis in a labourer with the sputum smear showing acid-fast bacilli is suggestive of tuberculosis. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, detected on sputum smear, is appreciated by Ziehl-Neelsen staining, which would includes carbol fuschin - acid - alcohol - methylene blue.

Acid-fast bacteria (like MTB) in a stained Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) smear appear bright red against a blue background. Steps involved in ZN staining are:

• Place the sample on slide evenly spread it with rotational movement
• Air-dry the slide and fix it by passing it over a flame
• Apply carbol fuschin stain and heat to fix it.
• Wash with water to remove excess stain
• Decolourise with alcohol
• Apply Methylene blue/Malachite green stain
• Wash with water to remove excess stain
• View under the microscope

Kinyoun modified the classical ZN staining such that heat fixing is not required. It is called the cold method. It involves increasing the concentration of phenol acid and the duration of staining. The slide is then washed with water and decolourized with acid alcohol. Counterstaining with Loeffler's methylene blue or malachite green is done for a minute and viewed under a microscope. Acid-fast bacteria in a stained smear appear bright red against a blue background.

The image attached below summarizes the steps.

Option A: It depicts the order of Gram staining, which was discovered by Hans Christian Gram in 1884.

• Primary staining with para-rosaniline dye (crystal violet, methyl violet or gentian violet).
• Application of dilute solution of iodine.
• Decolorisation with an organic solvent (ethanol, acetone, aniline).
• Counterstaining with the dye of contrasting colour (carbol fuchsin, safranine, neutral red).

Option B: It includes the steps for performing Albert's stain which is used for detected Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

• A heavy smear of the bacterial isolate is prepared on a glass slide and allowed to dry without fixing.
• Albert’s stain is applied for (3-4) minutes. Then it is washed with water and Albert’s iodine is applied for one minute.
• Wash with water and let dry with blotting paper.
• Examine the slide under oil immersion.

Corynebacterium diphtheriae are slender bacilli with an arrangement resembling the letters V or L. They have metachromatic granules at the poles of bacilli which are also called polar bodies, volutin, or Babes-Ernst granules. Albert staining is useful in the demonstration of metachromatic granules. The presence of metachromatic granules helps to distinguish C.diphtheriae from diphtheroids which lack them. The images below show Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
questions.learning: Carbol fuschin - acid-alcohol - methylene blue — The given clinical vignette of fever and hemoptysis in a labourer with the sputum smear showing acid-fast bacilli is suggestive of tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: The 4A Test is a screening tool for detection of delirium. Which of the following parameters are included in the 4AT tool? I. Alertness II. Apnoea III. Abbreviated Mental Test (AMT4) IV. Attention Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

The 4AT (4 ‘A’s Test) is a rapid bedside screening tool used for the detection of delirium and cognitive impairment, particularly in older hospitalized patients. It is quick to administer (usually <2 minutes) and does not require special training.

The four components of the 4AT are:

1. Alertness ✔
2. Abbreviated Mental Test-4 (AMT4) ✔
3. Attention ✔
4. Acute change or fluctuating course ✔
questions.learning: I, III and IV — The 4AT (4 ‘A’s Test) is a rapid bedside screening tool used for the detection of delirium and cognitive impairment, particularly in older hospitalized patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman undergoes hemithyroidectomy for a suspicious thyroid nodule. On postoperative day 1, she is comfortable and tolerating oral intake. Her voice is mildly hoarse. Neck drain shows minimal serosanguinous output and her airway is patent. Which of the following postoperative findings would be least expected after hemithyroidectomy?
options: Airway compromise due to neck hematoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypocalcemia with tetany

Hypocalcemia is due to parathyroid injury or devascularization and classically occurs after total thyroidectomy rather than hemithyroidectomy.

In hemithyroidectomy, at least one lobe and most parathyroids remain intact → calcium levels are usually preserved.

Hypocalcemia with tetany is least expected after hemithyroidectomy because at least two parathyroid glands remain intact on the contralateral side, preserving calcium homeostasis.

Expected complications after hemithyroidectomy

• Hoarseness of voice: due to transient recurrent laryngeal nerve neuropraxia

• Postoperative hemorrhage: can cause neck swelling

• Neck hematoma → airway compromise: surgical emergency requiring immediate wound opening

Why hypocalcemia is uncommon

• Significant hypocalcemia usually occurs after total thyroidectomy due to:

o Removal of parathyroids

o Devitalization of parathyroid blood supply

• In hemithyroidectomy, contralateral parathyroids maintain normal calcium levels.
questions.learning: Hypocalcemia with tetany Hypocalcemia is due to parathyroid injury or devascularization and classically occurs after total thyroidectomy rather than hemithyroidectomy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45 year male presented to OPD with complaints of swelling on the upper back. It has been present for nearly a year and has not increased in size. On examination, the swelling is non pulsatile, and slip sign is positive approximately measuring 5*5 cm. Which of the following statements is likely true?
options: Excision can be done if the patient makes a request
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Excision can be done if the patient makes a request

The clinical scenario of a 45-year-old male presenting with a non-pulsatile swelling on the upper back, which has not increased in size for nearly a year and measures approximately 5*5 cm with a positive slip sign, suggests a benign lesion like a lipoma. If the patient requests it, excision can be performed.

Lipomas are benign tumors of adipose tissue. It can occur anywhere and at any depth. It can be encapsulated or diffuse, superficial or deep.
On examination, they are nontender and non-pulsatile. Because of the soft consistency, they may appear to be fluctuant but they are not. The slip sign is positive.
Diagnosis is mostly clinical. Biopsy is rarely indicated in case of clinical doubt of malignant transformation. All lipomas need not be excised. Lipomas can be excised on suspicion of malignant transformation and sometimes at the patient's request.
Imaging is required in cases of deep-seated tumors only.

Other options:

Option A: Lipomas have a very low risk of malignant transformation into liposarcoma.
Option B: While FNAC (Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology) can be used to confirm the diagnosis, it is not always necessary for a typical lipoma.
Option C: PET scans are generally not needed for benign conditions like lipomas. They are used in cases where malignancy is suspected.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient came with complaints of hair loss. His wife mentions that she has noticed some behavioral changes. The doctor notices that there is a loss of eyebrows on the lateral side. He then comes to a conclusion by examining the nails. What is the type of poisoning in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thallium

The given scenario of hair loss, loss of eyebrows on the lateral side along with behavioral and nail changes point to thallium poisoning.

Thallium poisoning occurs due to an overdose or idiosyncrasy. Thallium sulfate and thallium acetate are the two salts of thallium used in dyes, in the glass industry, and as rodenticides and pesticides.

Mild cases of poisoning have features of joint pain, loss of appetite, and drowsiness. Severe cases present with colic, vomiting, muscle pain, convulsions, psychosis, tremors, delirium, and coma are seen in severe cases. Hair loss is seen after 2 weeks and a characteristic feature is loss of the outer thirds of the eyebrows. Mees lines are seen on the nails. Maculopapular rashes in a butterfly pattern on the face are characteristic.

In chronic poisoning, alopecia, skin rashes, peripheral neuropathy, and mental confusion are present.

Treatment is mainly by stomach wash with potassium iodide or Prussian blue, activated charcoal. Hemodialysis is useful and forced diuresis can be given.

The image below shows Mees lines.
questions.learning: Thallium — The given scenario of hair loss, loss of eyebrows on the lateral side along with behavioral and nail changes point to thallium poisoning. Thallium poisoning occurs due to an overdose or idiosyncrasy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Compared to a pregnant female, a lactating female would require a higher level of nutrient supplementation for which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcium

According to the Recommended daily allowance (RDA) guidelines set by the National Institute of Nutrition (NIN), the requirement of calcium intake is increased in a lactating woman (1200mg/d) when compared to that of a pregnant woman (1000mg/d). Calcium intake of 1200mg/d is advised in postmenopausal women as well.

The RDA of vitamin A is increased by 50mcg in lactation as compared to pregnancy. But the increased vitamin A demand is met from the diet and it is not given as a supplement nutrient. Vitamin A supplements are given only when there is vitamin A deficiency.

The RDA of iron and folic acid is decreased during lactation compared to pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty swallowing, especially solids, over several months, accompanied by significant weight loss and cachexia. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate for evaluating this patient?
questions.explanation: In an elderly patient (70 years old) presenting with progressive dysphagia for solids and significant weight loss, esophageal cancer must be the primary suspicion. The best diagnostic choice is Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (UGIE). UGIE allows for direct visualization of the tumor and, most importantly, provides the ability to take biopsies for histological confirmation, which is required for a definitive diagnosis. Barium swallow (Option C) can show a "rat-tail" or irregular narrowing, but it cannot provide a tissue diagnosis. Manometry (Option B) is used to diagnose motility disorders like Achalasia, which characteristically presents with dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the start. Barium meal follow-through (Option D) is used for the small intestine, not the esophagus. Once the cancer is confirmed via UGIE biopsy, CT or PET/CT is used for staging. Early diagnosis via endoscopy is critical for determining the feasibility of surgical resection or palliative therapy
questions.learning: In an elderly patient (70 years old) presenting with progressive dysphagia for solids and significant weight loss, esophageal cancer must be the primary suspicion.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-month-old former 28-week preterm infant is admitted with cough, wheezing, and feeding difficulty. Examination shows moderate respiratory distress with nasal flaring and intercostal retractions. Nasopharyngeal swab is positive for RSV. The infant has a history of bronchopulmonary dysplasia and oxygen requirement at discharge. Which of the following is the most appropriate antiviral therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ribavirin aerosol therapy

Severe RSV infection in high-risk infants (e.g., premature infants, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease) may be treated with aerosolized ribavirin, an antiviral that inhibits viral RNA synthesis. It is reserved for severe RSV disease in hospitalized high-risk patients.

Key distinctions:

A. Nirsevimab: Long-acting monoclonal antibody for RSV prevention

C. Oseltamivir: Antiviral for influenza, not RSV

D. Palivizumab: Monoclonal antibody used for RSV prophylaxis, not treatment
questions.learning: Ribavirin aerosol therapy Severe RSV infection in high-risk infants (e.g., premature infants, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease) may be treated with aerosolized ribavirin, an antiviral that inhibits viral RNA synthesis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statement is true about orbital cellulitis?
options: It is present anterior to the orbital septum
Presents with proptosis, orbital swelling, normal pupil, and extraocular movements
Ethmoid sinusitis is the most common etiology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ethmoid sinusitis is the most common etiology

Orbital cellulitis is a postseptal infection of the orbit, most commonly arising from ethmoid sinusitis due to the thin lamina papyracea.

Key clinical features:

• Proptosis
• Painful and restricted extraocular movements
• Decreased vision ± afferent pupillary defect
• Eyelid edema, fever

Ethmoid sinusitis is the most common source of orbital cellulitis spread.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A) Anterior to septum = preseptal cellulitis, not orbital
• B) Requires IV antibiotics, not just topical
• C) EOM are restricted and painful, not normal
questions.learning: Ethmoid sinusitis is the most common etiology Orbital cellulitis is a postseptal infection of the orbit, most commonly arising from ethmoid sinusitis due to the thin lamina papyracea.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to you with inability to form words but can make noises. He also knows what he wants to say. What area of the brain has been damaged in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Broca’s area

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Broca's aphasia in which the Broca's area will be affected.

In Broca's aphasia/ Motor aphasia / Non-fluent aphasia, areas 44 and 45 in the prefrontal and premotor facial regions of the cerebral cortex are affected. The affected individuals will have difficulty forming verbal or written words. The comprehension aspect of speech is preserved but the person cannot repeat or name the words and lacks fluency.

Patients in whom the area is severely affected may have very few words to express all of their emotions.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following advices to be given by the ASHA to Mrs. M, assuming pregnancy has been confirmed, regarding personal hygiene measures: 1. Minimum 12 hours sleep at a stretch at night 2. Avoid resting immediately after mid-day meals 3. Avoid intake of extra fluids to avoid constipation 4. Avoid taking purgatives like castor oil to relieve constipation How many of the four advices listed above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Two

Let’s assess each advice:

1. Minimum 12 hours of sleep at a stretch at night — Incorrect

• Pregnant women generally require adequate rest and sleep, but 12 hours of continuous nighttime sleep is not a standard recommendation.

2. Avoid resting immediately after mid-day meals — Correct

• Avoiding lying down immediately after meals helps reduce indigestion and heartburn during pregnancy.

3. Avoid extra fluids to prevent constipation — Incorrect

• Adequate fluid intake helps prevent constipation. Pregnant women should be encouraged to maintain adequate hydration.

4. Avoid purgatives such as castor oil for constipation — Correct

• Castor oil and other strong purgatives should be avoided during pregnancy because they can stimulate intestinal contractions and potentially cause uterine contractions.

Therefore, 2 statements are correct → B. Two.
questions.learning: Minimum 12 hours of sleep at a stretch at night — Incorrect • Pregnant women generally require adequate rest and sleep, but 12 hours of continuous nighttime sleep is not a standard recommendation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the best management approach for gastroschisis in a neonate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primary closure

A neonate with gastroschisis would need an immediate primary closure. Primary closure under general anesthesia or gradual reduction using a preformed silo may be performed. Parenteral nutrition is often needed for several weeks to support intestinal recovery.

Gastroschisis is an abdominal wall defect located on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly) allowing protrusion of the intestines, stomach, bladder, and sometimes ovaries or undescended testes. The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion as they herniate through the abdominal wall directly into the amniotic cavity. The affected bowel loops can be damaged by exposure to amniotic fluid.

Risk factors include teenage pregnancy, recreational drug use, smoking, and genitourinary infection during pregnancy. After birth, careful management is required to prevent twisting or kinking of the blood supply to the intestines. The abdomen is wrapped with transparent plastic wrap, a nasogastric tube is inserted, and fluid resuscitation is initiated.

Management: Immediate surgical intervention is required after birth to prevent complications such as infection, dehydration, and damage to the exposed abdominal organs. Surgical repair typically involves gently placing the protruding abdominal contents back into the abdominal cavity and closing the abdominal wall defect surgically. This approach helps protect the exposed organs, prevent complications, and facilitate normal abdominal wall development.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the given histopathology slide.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Brunner's gland

The slide shows section of the duodenum and marked structures glands located on the duodenum called Brunner's glands

Brunner's glands (or duodenal glands) are compound tubular submucosal glands present in the upper duodenum (above the sphincter of Oddi).

The alveoli of duodenal glands are lined mostly by mucous secreting columnar cells. Their ducts pass through the muscularis mucosae and empty into the intestinal crypts (of Lieberkuhn).

The duodenum can be easily differentiated from the jejunum or ileum by the presence of these submucosal glands. The jejunum and ileum do not have glands in their submucosa.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presented with diarrhoea for a few weeks. His family members report observing abnormal behaviour that they had not noticed earlier. Recently, he has developed a rash around his neck, as shown below. This rash flares up when exposed to sunlight. Which of the following supplements is most likely to benefit the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nicotinamide

The above clinical scenario of a patient with diarrhoea, abnormal behaviour (probably dementia) and rash around his neck (casal's neck) points to a diagnosis of pellagra which is secondary to nicotinamide/ niacin/ vitamin B3 deficiency. Hence this patient will benefit from nicotinamide supplements.

Niacin deficiency is mostly seen among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which are low in niacin and tryptophan. Excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis (beefy tongue) and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4 D's of pellagra are Diarrhea, Dermatitis, Dementia, and if untreated, Death.

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone. It is treated by oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The leading cause of preventable childhood blindness is:
questions.explanation: The leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide, especially in developing countries like India, is vitamin A deficiency (VAD). It is a major public health problem affecting young children due to malnutrition. Vitamin A is essential for maintaining the integrity of the conjunctival and corneal epithelium and for normal vision (especially night vision). Deficiency leads to a spectrum of ocular changes collectively called xerophthalmia, which includes: 1. 1. Night blindness 2. 2. Conjunctival xerosis 3. 3. Bitot’s spots 4. 4. Corneal xerosis 5. 5. Keratomalacia (can lead to irreversible blindness) If detected early, VAD is completely preventable and treatable through vitamin A supplementation and proper nutrition. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Refractive error: Common cause of visual impairment, but not blindness (C) Retinopathy of prematurity: Important cause, but not the leading one globally (D) Injuries: Preventable but less common cause
questions.learning: The leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide, especially in developing countries like India, is vitamin A deficiency (VAD). It is a major public health problem affecting young children due to malnutrition.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male patient presented with purulent discharge from an opening located in the perianal region. The patient is put in a lithotomy position and the opening is located at the 11 o'clock position, 4 cm from the anal margin. What will be the likely position of the internal opening and where does the internal opening start?
options: 12 o'clock and at external anal spinchter
11 o'clock and at internal anal spinchter
6 o'clock and crypt of the dentate line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6 o'clock and crypt of the dentate line

The likely location of the internal opening is at 6'O clock position which is the posterior midline of the anal canal and the opening starts at the crypt of the dentate line.

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of fistula-in-ano with the external opening located at 11’O clock position, 4 cm from the anal margin. This means that the anal margin is located anterior to the coronal midsection. The location of the internal opening of the fistula can be identified based on Goodsall's rule.

Goodsall’s rule:

* Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract.

* Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly tract in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline.

However, exceptions to this rule often occur. Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline.

Thus, according to the exception to Goodsall's rule, this patient likely has an internal opening at the 6'O clock position as the external opening is located more than 3 cm from the anal margin track.

A fistula-in-ano is a chronic abnormal hollow tract or cavity that is lined with granulation tissue. It has a primary internal opening in the anorectal lumen and a secondary external opening in the perianal skin. An anal fistula may also be present if the patient has Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, malignancy, foreign body, lymphogranuloma venereum, or actinomycosis. Patients usually present with intermittent discharge and pain.

Intersphincteric fistulas are the most common type. Other types of anal fistulae are transphincteric fistula, suprasphincteric fistula, and extrasphincteric fistula.

Patients usually present with intermittent purulent discharge and pain.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 20-year-old patient presented to the clinic with a history of malabsorption, diarrhea, and poor appetite. Duodenal biopsy of the patient showed crypt hyperplasia, villi atrophy, and CD8+ cells in lamina propria. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Celiac disease

The clinical presentation and the histopathological findings are suggestive of celiac disease.

Celiac disease is an autoimmune gluten-induced enteropathy where HLA DQ2 and DQ8 are expressed. In the small intestine, peptides of gluten are presented to helper T cells which mediate mucosal inflammation. Antiendomysial and anti-tTG antibodies are found in serological studies.

Clinically, malabsorption syndrome with diarrhea, abdominal pain, and marked weight loss is seen along with chronic refractory anemia. Dermatitis herpetiformis is seen in 10% of patients with celiac disease. Microscopic findings show villi atrophy, villi flattening, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial T lymphocytes (IEL).

Option A: Environmental enteropathy / tropical sprue is seen in tropical areas with poor sanitation. It is believed to be caused by one or more infectious agents that respond to antibiotics. Mucosa shows variable villous atrophy.

Option C: Whipple's disease is a multisystemic disease caused by T.whipplei. Small intestinal biopsy shows PAS-positive macrophages.
questions.learning: Celiac disease — The clinical presentation and the histopathological findings are suggestive of celiac disease. Celiac disease is an autoimmune gluten-induced enteropathy where HLA DQ2 and DQ8 are expressed.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following features is not characteristic of the El Tor biotype of Vibrio cholerae, the organism responsible for epidemic diarrhea?
options: Resistant to El Tor phage V
Not susceptible to group IV phage
questions.explanation: Vibrio cholerae is divided into two main biotypes: Classical and El Tor. The El Tor biotype is actually "susceptible" to El Tor phage V; therefore, statement A is "not" a characteristic. The Classical biotype is resistant to phage V. The other statements are accurate descriptions of the El Tor biotype: it has "intrinsic resistance to Polymyxin B" (Option B, unlike Classical) , it is "Voges-Proskauer (VP) positive" (Option C, unlike Classical) , and it is "not susceptible to Group IV phage" (Option D, unlike Classical). Additionally, El Tor vibrios are generally more robust in the environment and are responsible for the current (seventh) cholera pandemic. These laboratory tests are used in epidemiological surveillance to track the spread of different cholera strains during outbreaks. Understanding biotype differences helps in predicting the severity and duration of diarrhea epidemics in a population
questions.learning: Vibrio cholerae is divided into two main biotypes: Classical and El Tor. The El Tor biotype is actually "susceptible" to El Tor phage V; therefore, statement A is "not" a characteristic.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Banding technique used for dicentric chromosomes is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. C banding

The banding technique used for dicentric chromosomes is C banding.

Heterochromatin includes non-coding regions of DNA, such as centromeric regions. The staining of these constitutive heterochromatins, is done by C-banding using silver salt staining. A dicentric chromosome having two centromeres can hence be identified by C banding.

Various techniques are used in karyotyping to study chromosomes. Staining with various compounds produces various results and helps us to understand the chromosomes better.

Common techniques used are:

• Q banding - Fluorescence staining with quinacrine mustard.
• G banding - Giemsa staining after partial denaturation of chromatin. It is the most common technique used in cytogenetics to produce a visible karyotype by staining condensed chromosomes.
• R banding - Reverse Giemsa staining. In this, the light and dark areas are reversed.
• C banding - staining of heterochromatin with silver salts.
• T banding - staining the telomeres of chromosomes.
questions.learning: C banding — The banding technique used for dicentric chromosomes is C banding. Heterochromatin includes non-coding regions of DNA, such as centromeric regions.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A person is diagnosed to have diabetes on his 45th birthday. When will you recommend a dilated fundus examination for him?
options: When he complains of decrease in vision
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediately

A 45 year old diagnosed with diabetes mellitus is likely to have type 2 diabetes and thus, he should undergo screening for diabetic retinopathy immediately.

Duration of diabetes is the most important risk factor for developing diabetic retinopathy, especially proliferative diabetic retinopathy. The recommendations for first fundus examination in diabetic retinopathy is:

• Within 3-5 years of diagnosis in type 1 diabetes
• Immediately in type 2 diabetes.

Later, the screening is continued once every year in both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes. In the event proliferative diabetic retinopathy develops, screening is done more frequently - once every 2 months.
questions.learning: Immediately — A 45 year old diagnosed with diabetes mellitus is likely to have type 2 diabetes and thus, he should undergo screening for diabetic retinopathy immediately.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which organization does not fund The National TB program of India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. UNICEF

The funding for the National TB program of India is done by all, except option D, UNICEF.

The procurement of Anti TB drugs, equipment like microscopes, and diagnostics like CBNAAT cartridges are done mainly from the Domestic Budgetary Sources, that is the budget allocated by the Govt. of India for this program, World Bank, and The Global Fund.

The Central Medical Services Society (CMSS), an independent and autonomous body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare procures the drugs and other materials through the DBS and World Bank funding.

However, The Global Fund is made use of by the Global Drug Facility which is administered and housed by the United Nations Office for Project Services.
