questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is true regarding neurovascular anatomy of the uterus?
options: The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the external iliac artery.
The uterine artery crosses the ureter 3.5 cm lateral to the internal os.
The venous channels of the uterus drain into the internal iliac veins.
The somatic distribution of the uterine pain is the area of the abdomen supplied by T5 and T6.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The venous channels of the uterus drain into the internal iliac veins.

• A. The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the external iliac artery: Incorrect. The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, not the external iliac artery.
• B. The uterine artery crosses the ureter 3.5 cm lateral to the internal os: Incorrect. The uterine artery crosses over the ureter approximately 1.5–2 cm lateral to the internal os, not 3.5 cm.
• C. The venous channels of the uterus drain into the internal iliac veins: Correct. The uterine venous plexus drains predominantly into the uterine veins → internal iliac veins.
• D. The somatic distribution of the uterine pain is the area of the abdomen supplied by T5 and T6: Incorrect. Uterine pain is primarily referred through T10–L1 segments. Fundal pain may be referred around T10, while cervical pain is transmitted via pelvic visceral afferents.
questions.learning: The venous channels of the uterus drain into the internal iliac veins. • A. The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the external iliac artery: Incorrect.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the radiological image of the condition given below.
questions.explanation: The skull X-ray demonstrates a classic “cotton wool appearance,” characterized by patchy areas of sclerosis interspersed with lytic regions. This pattern is highly suggestive of Paget’s disease of bone, a disorder involving abnormal bone remodeling. In this condition, there is excessive and disorganized activity of osteoclasts followed by osteoblasts, leading to thickened, enlarged, and structurally weak bone. The skull vault often appears widened with irregular dense patches, giving the typical cotton wool look. Clinically, Paget’s disease may present with bone pain, deformities, increased head size, and sometimes hearing loss due to involvement of skull bones. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Multiple myeloma: Produces multiple punched-out lytic lesions without surrounding sclerosis, giving a “raindrop skull” appearance. (C) Hyperparathyroidism: Causes a “salt and pepper skull” due to diffuse demineralization and loss of trabecular pattern. (D) Sickle cell anemia: Shows a “hair-on-end” appearance due to marrow hyperplasia and vertical trabeculations. Thus, the presence of patchy sclerosis forming a cotton wool pattern confirms Paget’s disease
questions.learning: The skull X-ray demonstrates a classic “cotton wool appearance,” characterized by patchy areas of sclerosis interspersed with lytic regions. This pattern is highly suggestive of Paget’s disease of bone, a disorder involving abnormal bone remodeling.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man from Nellore, Andhra Pradesh, presents with characteristic dental lesions. Based on his geographic background and the typical appearance of these lesions, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image displays "mottling of enamel," characterized by brownish stains and pitting, which is the pathognomonic clinical sign of dental fluorosis. This condition occurs due to chronic ingestion of excessive fluoride during the period of tooth development. The geographic clue—Nellore, Andhra Pradesh—is highly significant as several districts in Andhra Pradesh are known endemic belts where groundwater contains high fluoride levels. Selenosis (Option A) typically leads to hair loss and nail changes. Plumbism (Option B), or lead poisoning, often presents with a bluish-black "Burtonian line" on the gums rather than enamel mottling. Lathyrism (Option D) is a neurological disorder caused by consuming grass pea and does not affect the teeth. Dental fluorosis is a permanent cosmetic and structural defect. In severe cases, it can be accompanied by skeletal fluorosis, which causes crippling bone and joint deformities. Prevention relies on providing defluoridated water or alternate water sources in endemic regions
questions.learning: The image displays "mottling of enamel," characterized by brownish stains and pitting, which is the pathognomonic clinical sign of dental fluorosis. This condition occurs due to chronic ingestion of excessive fluoride during the period of tooth development.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a translucent, bluish cystic swelling in the oral cavity, suggestive of a ranula, which is a mucus-filled cyst typically caused by salivary gland obstruction. Which site is the most common location for the development of a ranula?
questions.explanation: A ranula is a clinical term for a large mucocele specifically located on the floor of the mouth. It most frequently originates from the sublingual salivary gland, though it can occasionally involve the submandibular duct. The anatomical floor of the mouth provides the space where extravasated mucus can accumulate, forming the classic bluish, translucent, "frog-belly" cystic mass. Sites such as the tonsil (Option B), uvula (Option C), and cingula (Option D) are not associated with the development of ranulae. While mucoceles can occur on the lips or buccal mucosa, the term "ranula" is reserved exclusively for those occurring in the sublingual space. Understanding the site of origin is essential for surgical management, which often requires excision of the cyst along with the offending sublingual gland to prevent recurrence. Therefore, given the physiological and anatomical context of mucus retention cysts, the floor of the mouth is the definitive common site for ranula presentation
questions.learning: A ranula is a clinical term for a large mucocele specifically located on the floor of the mouth. It most frequently originates from the sublingual salivary gland, though it can occasionally involve the submandibular duct.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient complains that he feels like the room is spinning when he gets up from lying down or turning his head. He has no history of loss of consciousness. Which of the following could be the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

The given clinical scenario, with complaints of dizziness associated with postural change and no history of loss of consciousness is suggestive of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

BPPV is one of the common causes of recurrent vertigo, and the episodes are brief (<1min) and are always provoked by changes in head position. The attacks are caused by free-floating calcium carbonate crystals usually dislodged from the posterior canal.

A positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver confirms the diagnosis of BPPV. In this maneuver, the patient begins sitting up with their head turned 45 degrees toward the ear to be tested. Then the patient is made to lie down quickly with their head past the end of the bed. Then, the patient's neck is extended 20 degrees below the horizontal. The clinician then watches the patient's eyes for torsional and up-beating nystagmus, which should persist for no more than one minute. This would indicate a positive test.

Epley's maneuver is performed to reposition the crystals into the macula from the semicircular canals. This is only a temporary cure and there is a high rate of recurrence.
questions.learning: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo — The given clinical scenario, with complaints of dizziness associated with postural change and no history of loss of consciousness is suggestive of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which staining method is commonly used for identifying Cryptococcus?
questions.explanation: The India ink stain is the classic and most rapid method used for the presumptive identification of Cryptococcus neoformans, particularly in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples. Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast; the ink particles are too large to penetrate the thick polysaccharide capsule, creating a characteristic clear halo around the budding yeast cells against a dark background. Albert's stain (Option A) is used for Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Auramine-rhodamine (Option D) is a fluorescent stain for acid-fast bacilli like Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Silver staining (Option B) can visualize Cryptococcus in tissue sections but is not the primary rapid diagnostic tool for CSF. Identifying the capsule via India ink is a life-saving diagnostic step in immuno compromised patients (like those with HIV/AIDS) presenting with meningitis. Although more sensitive antigen tests are now available, the India ink prep remains a foundational tool in clinical microbiology for the immediate visualization of this pathogen
questions.learning: The India ink stain is the classic and most rapid method used for the presumptive identification of Cryptococcus neoformans, particularly in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which blood component is not separated by centrifugation in the blood bank?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Albumin

Albumin is not separated by centrifugation in the blood bank.

In blood banks, centrifugation is used to separate the main components of blood into distinct layers for storage and transfusion purposes. These components include:

1. Red Blood Cells (RBCs): Separated by centrifugation and stored for patients with anemia or significant blood loss. (Option A)
2. Platelets: Isolated through centrifugation of plasma-rich blood for use in patients with bleeding disorders. (Option B)
3. Cryoprecipitate: Derived from plasma by controlled freezing and thawing, which allows the collection of clotting factors (e.g., Factor VIII, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor). (Option C)

Albumin is a plasma protein that is extracted through a process called fractionation, not simple centrifugation. This involves the use of chemical, temperature, and pH adjustments to isolate albumin from plasma.
questions.learning: Albumin Albumin is not separated by centrifugation in the blood bank. In blood banks, centrifugation is used to separate the main components of blood into distinct layers for storage and transfusion purposes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Cell in cell appearance is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Entosis

Cell in cell appearance is seen in entosis.

Entosis is a phenomenon where a cell engulfs a cell of the same type. While cells that are internalised by this mechanism are initially viable. But, the majority of them undergo a non-apoptotic form of cell death. It plays a physiological role in the elimination of cells detached from a surface.

Other options:

Option A: Necrosis is a pathologic process of irreversible cell death following severe injury. It is associated with local inflammation due to damaged cell membranes. Some microscopic features of necrosis are as follows:

• Dilation of mitochondria
• Nuclear changes: karyolysis, pyknosis, and karyorrhexis.
• Myelin figures replacing dead cells.

Option B: Apoptosis is a pathway of programmed cell death. In apoptosis, Mitochondrial and death receptor pathways activate caspases resulting in the formation of apoptotic bodies which are then phagocytosed.

Option C: Necroptosis is a type of cell death which is a hybrid of both necrosis and apoptosis. It is also called programmed necrosis/caspase-independent programmed cell death(since it does not result in caspase activation).
questions.learning: Entosis Cell in cell appearance is seen in entosis. Entosis is a phenomenon where a cell engulfs a cell of the same type.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: If Bajra is mixed with black seeds, what is used to separate them?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 20 % salt water

20% saltwater is used to separate bajra from black grains or seeds. They can also be removed by hand-picking and air floatation.

Note:

Food items like bajra, rye, sorghum, and wheat have a tendency to house the ergot fungus called Claviceps purpurea.The safe limit for ergot alkaloids in grains is 0.05 mg per 100 grams.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-month-old male infant presents with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. He is diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of rare disorders characterized by the absence of both T and B lymphocyte function. Approximately 15% of SCID cases are caused by a deficiency of the enzyme Adenosine deaminase (ADA), which is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. The lack of ADA leads to the toxic buildup of dATP in lymphocytes, which halts their development and function. ADA deficiency typically presents in infancy with the "classic SCID triad": recurrent infections, diarrhea, and failure to thrive. OTC deficiency (Option B) leads to hyperammonemia. HGPRT deficiency (Option C) results in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (gout/self-mutilation). Phosphomannose isomerase (Option A) is involved in protein glycosylation. ADA-SCID is a pediatric emergency because it is fatal without treatment; management options include hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, enzyme replacement therapy, or gene therapy
questions.learning: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of rare disorders characterized by the absence of both T and B lymphocyte function. Approximately 15% of SCID cases are caused by a deficiency of the enzyme Adenosine deaminase (ADA), which is inherited in…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common association with Tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease. Among the provided genetic disorders, Downs syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most frequently associated condition . While the most common heart defect specifically in Down syndrome is an endocardial cushion defect (AVSD), TOF occurs at a significantly higher rate in this population than in the general public. Klinefelter's (Option A, 47,XXY) and Turner's (Option D, 45,X) syndromes have different cardiac associations, such as coarctation of the aorta in Turner's. Edwards syndrome (Option B, Trisomy 18) features severe multi-organ defects and VSDs but is less commonly associated with surviving TOF cases than Down syndrome. TOF involves four specific defects: VSD, pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta. Therefore, in clinical genetics and pediatrics, Trisomy 21 is recognized as the most frequent chromosomal association for children born with TOF
questions.learning: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease. Among the provided genetic disorders, Downs syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most frequently associated condition .

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient present in the ward when asked, "what is your name?" repeats the same sentence back to you. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Echolalia

Echolalia is a type of complex vocal tic, where there is the repetition of last-heard words of others.

Tics are semi-voluntary neuropsychiatric events characterized by brief rapid motor movements or vocalizations. These are typically performed in response to irresistible premonitory urges.

Motor and vocal tics are divided into simple and complex types.

Simple motor tics
Complex motor tics

Composed of repetitive, rapid contractions of functionally similar muscle groups.

More purposeful and ritualistic than simple tics.

Examples:

Eye-blinking

Neck-jerking

Shoulder-shrugging

Facial-grimacing

Head shaking

Examples:

Grooming behaviours

Smelling objects

Jumping

Touching behaviours

Echopraxia (imitation of observed behaviour)

Copropraxia (display of obscene gestures)

Simple vocal tics
Complex vocal tics

It consists of sounds that do not form words.
Repeating words or phrases out of context.

Examples:

Coughing

Throat-clearing

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old medical student has been preparing for exams for several nights with inadequate sleep and irregular meals. Laboratory tests reveal mild hypoglycemia. Which of the following hormones is most likely to show an increase in secretion during this period of fasting, stress, and deep sleep recovery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Growth hormone

Growth hormone increases during fasting, stress, and deep sleep.

Growth hormone is secreted from the somatotropes located in the anterior pituitary. Its main role is the growth of the human body. The growth hormone levels show diurnal variation and variation across different age groups. Adolescents have the highest circulating levels of growth hormone, followed by children and adults. The levels are relatively low during the day and the pulsatile release of this hormone occurs during sleep.

Stimuli that increase GH secretion:

* Hypoglycemia, deoxyglucose, fasting, starvation

* Exercise

* Protein meal, infusion of arginine

* Glucagon

* Deep sleep

* Estrogens and androgens

* Stressful stimuli

Important regulators of growth hormone:

* Growth hormone-releasing hormone- stimulates the production of the hormone

* Somatostatin- inhibits the release of GH

* Ghrelin- increases the GH release

Actions of growth hormone:

* Growth of cartilage, bones, and organs.

* Increases amino acid uptake and protein synthesis in the cells and decreases protein breakdown.

* Diabetogenic action: Increases the hepatic glucose release and decreases the glucose uptake by muscles and fat.

* Increases fat utilization. It is ketogenic and increases circulating free fatty acid levels.

Stimuli that decrease GH secretion

• Drugs like Apomorphine, L-Dopa

• Somatostatin (GHIH)
• Exogenous GH
• Somatomedins (IGF-1)
• Cortisol

• ↑ Blood glucose

GHIH - Growth hormone inhibiting hormone

A patient with dengue hemorrhagic shock can be discharged after the return of appetite.

Criteria for the discharge of patients recovering from dengue:

• Platelet count >50,000/cu.mm

• Visible clinical improvement

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 10-year-old presents with muscle cramps, especially following high-intensity exercise. What is the type of glycogen storage disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. McArdle's disease

A clinical scenario of a patient with muscle cramps with exertion is suggestive of McArdle's disease, which is due to the deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase.

A unique feature associated with McArdle is the improvement in symptoms after rest for a few minutes. This is termed the second wind phenomenon. This occurs due to the increased blood flow to the muscles, liver glycogen release and increased utilisation of free fatty acids (FFAs) for energy production after resting for a few minutes. This compensates for the impaired ATP generation from glycogenolysis. Patients with McArdle disease can benefit from engaging in regular aerobic exercises, such as walking or cycling, which can help increase their exercise tolerance and cardiovascular fitness. However, they should avoid high-intensity exercises or activities that can trigger muscle cramps and rhabdomyolysis. Glucose administration before exercise can improve tolerance. Vitamin B6 is also recommended.

McArdle disease, also known as type V glycogen storage disorder, is an autosomal recessive condition. It typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation.

Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. Due to high-intensity exercise, sudden persistent muscle contraction occurs. This leads to severe muscle damage resulting in a massive release of muscle proteins and myoglobin in the blood. Myoglobinuria secondary to rhabdomyolysis leads to the passage of burgundy-coloured urine in some patients.

Rarely, it can present during infancy as hypotonia, muscle weakness, and respiratory complications. It is generally fatal. Muscle biopsy to measure glycogen content is the standard diagnosis.

Other options:

Option B: Cori's disease (type III glycogen storage disorder) – It is caused by a deficiency of glycogen debranching enzyme. Patients with Cori's disease present with hepatomegaly, growth retardation, and hypoglycemia. Muscle weakness may be present, but not muscle cramps or myoglobinuria.

Option C: Pompe's disease results from a deficiency in the enzyme lysosomal alpha-glucosidase.

Option D: Andersen disease (type IV glycogen storage disorder) – It is caused by the deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme. This disease presents with hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, and liver failure. It does not cause muscle cramps or myoglobinuria.
questions.learning: McArdle's disease — A clinical scenario of a patient with muscle cramps with exertion is suggestive of McArdle's disease, which is due to the deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase.

The reference woman used in the calculation of recommended daily allowance (RDA) weighs about 55 Kgs and is aged between 19-39 years, nonpregnant, non-lactating with a height of 1.61 meters, and a BMI of 21.2, is free from disease and physically fit for active work.

On each working day, she must be engaged in 8 hours of occupation/work, which usually involves moderate activity. When not at work she spends 8 hours in bed, 4-6 hours in sitting and moving about, 2 hours in walking, and in active recreation or household duties.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: From the given flowchart, identify: A-the management technique used and B- the critical path.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A- Network analysis, B-Machinery installation

In the given image management technique, A is network analysis, and the critical path B is machinery installation.

The provided flowchart visually represents a sequence of events, indicating that the management technique used is network analysis. The critical path, identified as the longest sequence of dependent tasks, is the machinery installation/ equipment installed (10 months).

Network analysis is a systematic approach used to plan, organize, and manage complex projects by breaking them down into interconnected tasks. It helps in identifying the sequence of activities, estimating time requirements, and optimizing resource allocation.

Techniques like the Critical Path Method (CPM) and Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT) are commonly used to determine the most efficient workflow and identify critical tasks that directly impact project timelines. Network analysis is widely applied in fields such as construction, logistics, healthcare, and IT project management, ensuring better decision-making, risk assessment, and overall efficiency in achieving project goals.

Pearl PF1998: Network Analysis in Health Management

A network is a graphic plan of all events and activities to be completed in order to reach an end objective.

Two types of network analysis: PERT and CPM

1. Programme Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT)

* An arrow diagram of all events in logical sequence is drawn.

* Time to finish each activity can be calculated and critical activities can be identified.

* It aids in planning, scheduling and monitoring of the project.

2. Critical Path Method (CPM)

* The longest path of the network is called the critical path.

* A delay in the critical path will cause a delay in the entire project.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old lactating woman presents with breast pain, fever, localized redness and warmth, point tenderness, a positive fluctuation test, and mild unilateral axillary lymphadenopathy, while the opposite breast is normal. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A breast abscess is a localized collection of pus that typically arises as a complication of untreated or inadequately treated lactational mastitis. The clinical features of pain, fever, localized erythema, and warmth are shared with mastitis. However, the pathognomonic finding here is the "positive fluctuation test" and "point tenderness," which indicate the presence of a fluid-filled cavity (pus). Lactational mastitis (Option A) presents with diffuse inflammation without a focal, fluctuant mass. Breast carcinoma (Option B) usually presents as a painless, hard mass in older patients and does not typically cause acute fever or fluctuation. Fibroadenoma (Option D) is a benign, firm, "mouse in the breast" mass seen in younger women, lacking signs of infection. Axillary lymphadenopathy is a reactive finding to the nearby infection. Management of a breast abscess in a lactating mother requires incision and drainage or ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, along with appropriate antibiotics and encouragement to continue breastfeeding or pumping from the affected side to maintain drainage

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Alkali disease of livestock is caused by an excess of which of the following minerals?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Selenium

Excess of selenium causes alkali disease in livestock.

Clinical types of selenium intoxication

• Acute selenosis
• Subacute selenosis (i.e., blind staggers type)
• Chronic selenosis (i.e., alkali disease type)

Alkali disease occurs when animals consume moderate levels of selenium for a period of weeks to months.

The common clinical signs of chronic selenosis in horses, cattle, and swine are loss of hair (horses and cattle lose long hair from the mane and tails), emaciation, hoof lesions, weight reduction, and lameness.

Correct answer: C. Diagnostic Study - CONSORT

The guidelines used for reporting the results of RCT are CONSORT (consolidated standards of reporting trials).

To improve the quality of reporting of health research, certain standards have been developed. These standards vary according to the type of study in question. questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A vital layer, also known as “Schmutzdecke”, is seen in which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Slow sand filter

The Schmutzdecke (German for “dirty layer” or “vital layer”) is a biologically active layer that develops on the surface of a slow sand filter. It consists of algae, bacteria, protozoa, fungi, and organic matter and is responsible for the major purification of water by removing microorganisms and organic impurities.

• A. Air filter ✗

• Does not contain a Schmutzdecke.

• B. Rapid sand filter ✗

• Purification occurs mainly by physical filtration after coagulation and sedimentation.
• No biological layer (Schmutzdecke) is formed.

• C. Slow sand filter ✓

• The Schmutzdecke is its characteristic feature and provides biological purification.

• D. Reverse osmosis filter ✗

• Uses a semipermeable membrane under pressure; no biological layer is involved.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding scabies? (NEET PG 2017)
options: Presence of Circle of Hebra lesions
Scalp and face are spared in infants
Norwegian scabies is the most severe form
Burrows are found in the stratum corneum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scalp and face are spared in infants

Scabies is an infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. The female mite burrows into the stratum corneum, producing intense pruritus (especially at night) and characteristic skin lesions.

Why Option B is Incorrect:

• In adults, the scalp and face are usually spared.
• In infants and young children, however, the scalp, face, neck, palms, and soles are commonly involved.
• Therefore, the statement “Scalp and face are spared in infants” is incorrect.

Important Features of Scabies:

• Burrows are thin, wavy, grayish lines found in the stratum corneum.
• Circle of Hebra: Ring of papules and vesicles around affected areas, a classical sign of scabies.
• Norwegian (Crusted) Scabies: A severe, highly contagious form characterized by extensive hyperkeratotic crusted lesions and a very high mite burden, often seen in immunocompromised patients.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient exhibits an abnormal gait in which the legs cross over each other while walking, producing a characteristic scissoring pattern. This finding suggests increased muscle tone due to excessive neural activity. Hyperactivity of which nerve is most likely responsible for this scissoring gait?
questions.explanation: A "scissoring gait" is caused by excessive adduction of the thighs, leading to the legs crossing over each other during ambulation. This is primarily driven by hyperactivity or spasticity of the hip adductor muscles, which are innervated by the obturator nerve. This gait pattern is commonly seen in patients with upper motor neuron lesions, such as those with cerebral palsy. The superior gluteal nerve (Option A) innervates the gluteus medius and minimus; its weakness causes a Trendelenburg gait. The inferior gluteal nerve (Option B) supplies the gluteus maximus, and its dysfunction leads to difficulty in standing up or climbing stairs. The femoral nerve (Option D) supplies the quadriceps, primarily facilitating knee extension. Because the scissoring movement is a direct result of overactive adduction, the obturator nerve's role in supplying the adductor longus, brevis, and magnus makes it the correct choice

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient has significant distress on reading text off paper or screen. On examination of his eyes, all domains including visual acuity are essentially normal except for Schirmer's test which reads 5mm. What is the best way to treat this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lubricants

The given clinical scenario is most likely to be one of dry eye or keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS). The best initial management would be to lubricate the eye.

Treatment of dry eye includes medical treatment (lubricating eyedrops, most commonly methylcellulose derivatives) or surgical treatment (lacrimal punctum occlusion using silicone plugs).

The tests used to diagnose dry eye (KCS) are:

1. Schirmer test

Inference

* 15 mm: Normal

* 5-10 mm: Moderate keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS)

* < 5 mm: Severe KCS

2. Tear film break-up test (TBUT)

Inference

* 15-35 seconds: Normal

* < 10 seconds: Unstable tear film

3. Rose Bengal staining

Inference

* A pattern: Confluent staining → Severe KCS

* B pattern: Extensive staining → Moderate KCS

* C pattern: Fine punctate stains → Mild KCS

4. Tear osmolarity test

Abnormal osmolarity is defined by

* An elevated reading, >300 mOsm/L, indicating loss of homeostasis, or

* When the inter-eye difference is >8 mOsm/L, indicating instability of the tear film.
questions.learning: Lubricants — The given clinical scenario is most likely to be one of dry eye or keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS). The best initial management would be to lubricate the eye.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Vessel A has a length of L and diameter of D and vessel B has 2L and 2D. Considering the flow is laminar through both the cylinders, the flow through B is how many times as much as the flow through A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8 times

Flow through B will be 8 times more than the flow through A.

According to Poiseuille Hagen formula,

F= ΔP x π/8 x 1/n x r4/L

F = flow

ΔP = pressure difference between two ends of the tube

η = viscosity

r = radius of the tube

L = length of the tube

Hence flow directly varies to the 4th power of radius and inversely varies to length.

Flow through B = (2r)4/2L = 8 times

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Utilizing the provided X-ray, identify the type of fracture using the Salter-Harris classification?
questions.explanation: The Salter-Harris classification system is used to describe fractures involving the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) in children. A Type 2 fracture, the most common type, occurs when the fracture line passes through the growth plate (physis) and then extends upwards through the metaphysis. The X-ray shows the characteristic "Thurston Holland fragment," which is the triangular piece of metaphysis that remains attached to the epiphysis. Type 1 (Option A) involves the growth plate only. Type 3 (Option C) passes through the growth plate and extends through the epiphysis into the joint space. Type 5 (Option D) is a crush injury of the growth plate, which is often difficult to see on initial X-rays. Type 2 fractures generally have a good prognosis because the germinal layer of the growth plate remains intact. Management usually involves closed reduction and immobilization, as the fracture does not enter the joint surface

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents with leukocoria and is diagnosed with persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV). The child subsequently undergoes lens extraction. What is the most common postoperative complication in such cases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinal detachment

PHPV, now more commonly termed persistent fetal vasculature (PFV), results from failed regression of the embryonic hyaloid vascular system. This leaves behind fibrovascular tissue stretching from the optic disc to the posterior lens surface.

This fibrovascular stalk exerts chronic traction on the retina. When surgery removes the lens (and often the associated vitreous/fibrovascular tissue), the support structures are further disrupted, and the pre-existing tractional forces can precipitate retinal detachment — making it the most frequent postoperative complication.

Clarifying the distractor:

• Vitreous hemorrhage can certainly occur, given the vascularity of the fibrous tissue — but in exam contexts, retinal detachment is designated the most common complication due to the underlying tractional pathology.

Why the other options don't fit?

• A. Orbital cellulitis: An infectious complication, not a mechanistic consequence of PHPV surgery
• D. Keratitis: Unrelated to the posterior segment pathology driving PHPV
questions.learning: Retinal detachment PHPV, now more commonly termed persistent fetal vasculature (PFV), results from failed regression of the embryonic hyaloid vascular system.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug regimen is commonly used as the initial phase of treatment for tuberculosis during the first two months?
questions.explanation: The standard WHO and national guidelines for the treatment of drug-sensitive tuberculosis involve two phases. The initial (intensive) phase lasts for the first 2 months and consists of a four-drug regimen: Isoniazid (H), Rifampicin (R), Pyrazinamide (Z), and Ethambutol (E). These four drugs are used together to rapidly kill the bacterial population and prevent the emergence of drug resistance. Streptomycin (Option A) was historically part of the regimen but is now reserved for specific resistant cases due to its toxicity and need for injections. Linezolid (Option C) and Levofloxacin (Option D) are second-line drugs used for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) rather than standard initial therapy. Following the 2-month intensive phase, patients enter a 4-month continuation phase, typically with only H and R. The use of Ethambutol is specifically important to cover potentially isoniazid-resistant strains in the initial bacterial load. Patients must be monitored for side effects like optic neuritis while on this medication

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes Ayushman Bharat in this context?
options: Umbrella scheme includes Pradhan Mantri Jan Aarogya Yojna and sub centres
Benefit to 40% of poor and vulnerable population
Covers only tertiary health care centers
Cashless, paperless service by only government hospitals
questions.explanation: Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) is a flagship health insurance scheme designed to provide financial protection to the bottom 40% of India's poor and vulnerable population. It offers an annual health cover of ` 5 lakhs per family for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization. Option A is partially correct but the scheme actually includes "Health and Wellness Centres" rather than just standard sub-centres. Option C is incorrect as it covers both secondary and tertiary care. Option D is incorrect because the cashless, paperless service is provided at both government and empanelled private hospitals. The scheme is a major step toward Universal Health Coverage in India, aiming to reduce out-of-pocket expenditures that often lead to poverty. Therefore, the defining demographic reach of the scheme is the protection of the most vulnerable 40% of the citizenry

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Mayo’s repair is done for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Umbilical hernia

Mayo’s repair (also called the vest-over-pants repair) is a tissue repair technique used for umbilical hernia, in which the fascial edges are overlapped to reinforce the defect.

Why not the other options?

• A. Inguinal hernia: Common repairs include Lichtenstein, Shouldice, Bassini.
• B. Femoral hernia: Common repairs include McVay (Cooper’s ligament), Lockwood, Lotheissen, McEvedy.
• D. Incisional hernia: Usually treated with mesh repair.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What are the characteristics of dermoid cyst? I. Germ cell ovarian tumour II. Bilateral in 15–20% cases III. Torsion is common IV. Rupture is common Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and III

A dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma) is the most common benign ovarian germ cell tumor, occurring predominantly in women of reproductive age (20–40 years). It arises from totipotent germ cells and contains tissues derived from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm). The following statements are correct:

• I. Germ cell ovarian tumour: Dermoid cyst is a benign germ cell tumor and is the most common ovarian germ cell neoplasm.
• II. Bilateral in 15–20% cases: Approximately 10–20% of dermoid cysts are bilateral.
• III. Torsion is common: Ovarian torsion is the most common complication because the cyst is usually mobile and has a long pedicle.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Rupture is common: Rupture is uncommon. When it occurs, it may cause chemical peritonitis due to spillage of sebaceous material, but it is much less common than torsion.
questions.learning: I, II and III — A dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma) is the most common benign ovarian germ cell tumor, occurring predominantly in women of reproductive age (20–40 years).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A chronic tobacco consumer went to the dental clinic with bleeding lesions on his tongue and was diagnosed with carcinoma of the tongue. Which of the following papillae, which do not have taste buds, is least likely to be involved in such a cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Filiform

Among the different types of papillae on the tongue, the one that does not have taste buds is the filiform papillae.

Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections that are mainly present on the dorsal part of the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue. The filiform papillae do not contain taste buds. They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

Other papillae of the tongue are:

Circumvallate papillae are 8-12 in number which are large cylindrical structures. They form a V-shaped row just in front of the sulcus terminalis. Usually, the entire papillae are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Taste buds are present in the lateral wall of these papillae which surrounds the papillae circumferentially.

Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red and are mainly present on the lingual margins and also on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. They are supplied by the facial nerve.

Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at the sides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a polysaccharide vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant protein vaccine.

Polysaccharide vaccines are a type of subunit vaccine containing the capsular polysaccharide antigen. They generate a T-cell independent response.

Examples include:

• Pneumococcus
• Meningococcus
• Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib)

Recombinant protein vaccines: With the help of recombinant DNA technology, the purified recombinant proteins from the cultured microorganisms result in cleaner vaccine preparations with a better safety profile.

Examples include:

• HBV
• HPV
• Lyme disease
• Cholera toxin-B
• COVID-19

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The mother of a 14-month-old normally developing baby comes to you for feeding advice. Which of the following would be appropriate for her as per the IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness) Program? I. Breastfeed as often as the child wants II. Keep the child in your lap and feed with your own hands III. Offer food from the family pot IV. Give 3 to 4 meals each day Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, III and IV

According to the IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness) guidelines, children aged 12–24 months should continue breastfeeding on demand, receive family foods, and be fed 3–4 meals per day along with 1–2 nutritious snacks to ensure adequate growth and development.

• I. Breastfeed as often as the child wants. ✔

• Continued breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond is recommended along with complementary feeding.

• II. Keep the child in your lap and feed with your own hands. ✘

• This is recommended for younger infants or children requiring active assistance.
• At 14 months, the child should be encouraged to self-feed, with the caregiver providing supervision and assistance as needed.

• III. Offer food from the family pot. ✔

• After 1 year of age, children should receive family foods that are appropriately prepared (soft, mashed, or chopped if needed).

• IV. Give 3 to 4 meals each day. ✔

• Children aged 12–24 months should receive 3–4 meals daily, along with 1–2 healthy snacks if required.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray shows diffuse, bilateral alveolar opacities in a classic "bat-wing" or butterfly pattern, which is characteristic of pulmonary edema. The central distribution of these opacities, combined with cardiomegaly (an enlarged heart silhouette), strongly suggests a cardiogenic cause, such as left heart failure. Other common findings include Kerley B lines, which represent septal edema. Hydrothorax (Option B) and Pleural Effusion (Option C) appear as homogeneous opacities with a meniscus sign that blunts the costophrenic angles, rather than diffuse infiltrates throughout the lung parenchyma. Pulmonary Fibrosis (Option D) typically presents with reticular opacities, honeycombing, and reduced lung volumes, which differ from the fluffy alveolar pattern seen here. Treatment for cardiogenic pulmonary edema focuses on diuretics and oxygen to reduce volume overload

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child has been diagnosed with febrile seizures, and the parents are seeking guidance on treatment options. In pediatric neurology, which medication is most commonly recommended as first-line therapy to manage or control febrile seizures?
questions.explanation: For an acute seizure in a child, including a prolonged febrile seizure, a fast-acting benzodiazepine is the first-line treatment of choice to terminate the event. Midazolam (given intranasally or buccally) or Diazepam (rectally) are the most frequently recommended initial treatments (Option C) . These are preferred for their rapid onset and ease of administration outside the hospital. Sodium valproate (Option A) and Phenobarbitone (Option D) are used for the long-term maintenance of epilepsy but are not the primary choice for acute termination of a simple febrile seizure. Phenytoin (Option B) is an alternative for status epilepticus but is not the "initial" choice before benzodiazepines. Most febrile seizures are brief and self-limiting, requiring only fever control; pharmacological intervention is reserved for seizures lasting more than 5 minutes. Therefore, because of its rapid efficacy in stopping acute convulsions, Midazolam is the definitive initial choice for active seizure management
questions.learning: For an acute seizure in a child, including a prolonged febrile seizure, a fast-acting benzodiazepine is the first-line treatment of choice to terminate the event.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient who is a known case of COPD presented with acute exacerbation and is admitted to the ICU. Which of the following statements is correct with regards to the initial management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Non-Invasive PPV should be given

Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) should be the first mode of ventilation used in COPD patients with acute respiratory failure provided there are no absolute contraindications. This approach improves gas exchange, reduces work of breathing and the need for intubation, decreases hospitalization duration and enhances overall survival outcomes.

Invasive positive pressure ventilation is only considered after failure of NIPPV, resulting in severe respiratory distress, life threatening hypoxemia, severe hypercarbia and/or acidosis, markedly impaired mental status, respiratory arrest or hemodynamic instability (Option B).

Apart from NIPPV, short-acting inhaled beta 2 agonists (albuterol, salbutamol) with or without short-acting anticholinergics (ipratropium) and Long-acting anticholinergics (tiotropium) are recommended as the initial bronchodilators. Maintenance therapy with long-acting beta 2 agonists (formoterol) must be started as soon as possible.

Systemic corticosteroids are useful in the treatment of acute exacerbations of COPD as they reduce airway inflammation and improve lung function over time. However, the effects are not immediate. NIPPV on the other hand provides immediate relief to the patient and reduces the work of breathing. Therefore, it would not be the best choice in this case. (Option C)

Antibiotics can also be considered, as they reduce duration of hospitalisation. Treatment is given for 5 days.

Permissive hypercapnia refers to a ventilation strategy where tidal volume is reduced in order to avoid hyperinflation-associated lung trauma. It is not preferred at the initial presentation. It is only permitted once invasive PPV is started following NIPPV failure (Option D)

An exacerbation of COPD is defined as an event characterized by dyspnea and/or cough and sputum that worsen over < 14 days. Exacerbations of COPD are often associated with increased local and systemic inflammation caused by airway infection, pollution, or other insults to the lungs.
questions.learning: Non-Invasive PPV should be given Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) should be the first mode of ventilation used in COPD patients with acute respiratory failure provided there are no absolute contraindications.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A man with multiple myeloma who has undergone several cycles of chemotherapy presents with progressive fatigue, recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, and easy bruising. CBC reveals severe pancytopenia. Which of the following is the most important dose-limiting toxicity of melphalan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bone marrow suppression

Melphalan is an alkylating agent (nitrogen mustard) commonly used in the treatment of multiple myeloma. Its dose-limiting toxicity is bone marrow suppression (myelosuppression), which manifests as anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and pancytopenia, leading to fatigue, recurrent infections, and bleeding tendencies. The patient has:

• Multiple myeloma receiving melphalan
• Progressive fatigue
• Recurrent infections
• Easy bruising
• Severe pancytopenia

These findings are characteristic of melphalan-induced bone marrow suppression, the principal dose-limiting toxicity.

Why not the other options?

• B. Hemorrhagic cystitis: Characteristic adverse effect of cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide due to the metabolite acrolein; prevented with MESNA.
• C. Pulmonary fibrosis: Classically associated with bleomycin and busulfan, not melphalan.
• D. Peripheral neuropathy: Most commonly caused by vincristine, bortezomib, and taxanes, not melphalan.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A wound was left open initially, with debridement and cleaning for 5 days before closure by sutures. What type of wound healing is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tertiary intention

Primary intention

• Clean wound (edges are brought together )→ closed immediately (ie sutured)
• Heals with minimal inflammation, minimal scar fast healing and minimal granulation tissue formation → Example: surgical incision

Secondary intention :-

• The Wound left open completely
• Heals by:

• Granulation tissue
• Wound contraction
• Epithelialization

• Slower healing, heals with more scarring.
• Done for large diabetic ulcers, large traumatic wounds

Tertiary intention:-

• Wound is not closed immediately due to:

• Contamination / infection risk
• Devitalized tissue

• It is kept open for a few days (usually 3–5 days)
• During this time:

• Debridement is used to remove dead tissue (that hampers healing)
• Irrigation + dressings reduce bacterial load

• Once the wound looks clean and granulation tissue is formed, it is sutured.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which classification system is shown in the image below that is used to stage gastric cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bormann's classification

The image shows Bormann classification used for advanced gastric cancer.

Gastric carcinoma can be classified as early gastric cancer and advanced gastric cancer.

* Early gastric cancer involves mucosa, submucosa with or without lymph node involvement. Early gastric cancer can be further classified using the Japanese classification.

* Advanced gastric cancer involves the muscularis layer, with or without adjacent structures. Its macroscopic appearances have been classified using Bormann classification.

The given image shows the pathological types of early gastric cancer as per Japanese system.

Other options:

Option A: AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer) is for squamous cell carcinoma. It is classified based on the extent of differentiation.

Option D: Hinchey classification is used for diverticulitis.

Pearl PF1130: Borrmann’s classification of stomach cancer

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which glands are primarily affected in Bromhidrosis? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Both Apocrine and Eccrine Glands

Bromhidrosis (osmidrosis) is a condition characterized by offensive body odor resulting from the breakdown of sweat by skin bacteria.

Both apocrine and eccrine sweat glands contribute to bromhidrosis:

• Apocrine glands

• Located mainly in the axillae, areola, and anogenital region.
• Produce protein- and lipid-rich secretions.
• Bacterial degradation of these secretions is the major cause of body odor.

• Eccrine glands

• Distributed throughout the body.
• Excess sweating (hyperhidrosis) can promote bacterial growth and contribute to odor formation.

Types of Bromhidrosis

• Apocrine bromhidrosis – most common form
• Eccrine bromhidrosis – associated with hyperhidrosis, poor hygiene, certain foods, and metabolic disorders

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Apocrine glands alone: Major contributor but not the only glands involved.
• Eccrine glands alone: Can contribute but are not solely responsible.
• Sebaceous glands: Produce sebum and are not the primary glands involved in bromhidrosis.
questions.learning: Both Apocrine and Eccrine Glands Bromhidrosis (osmidrosis) is a condition characterized by offensive body odor resulting from the breakdown of sweat by skin bacteria.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy weighing 30 Kgs has been posted for surgical resection of a tumor. What is the daily maintenance fluid required for this child while he’s NPO?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1700 mL

The daily maintenance fluid required for a child weighing 30 Kg is 1700 ml.

Bodyweight method for calculating the daily maintenance fluid volume (also known as Holliday-Segar method) is used.

Bodyweight
Fluid required per day

0–10 Kg
100 mL/Kg

11–20 Kg
1000 mL + 50 mL/Kg for each Kg >10 Kg

>20 Kg
1500 mL + 20 mL/Kg for each Kg >20 kg

Calculation:

In the question, the weight of the child is given as 30 Kgs.

So, the formula for >20 Kg is used.

1500 mL + (20 mL x weight more than 20 Kgs)

Since the child weight is 30 Kgs, he/she is 10 Kgs more.

Therefore, fluid required is

= 1500 mL + (20 mL x 10)

= 1500 mL + 200 mL

= 1700 mL.
questions.learning: 1700 mL The daily maintenance fluid required for a child weighing 30 Kg is 1700 ml. Bodyweight method for calculating the daily maintenance fluid volume (also known as Holliday-Segar method) is used.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following cases is the drug given below contraindicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malpresentation of fetus

The drug given in the image is Oxytocin, and it is contraindicated in the malpresentation of the fetus.

The smooth muscle contraction seen with the use of oxytocin is physiological, i.e., it causes fundal contraction and cervical relaxation that helps in the delivery of the fetus, and makes oxytocin a good agent for the induction of labor.

Uses of oxytocin:

* To accelerate abortion and to stop bleeding following evacuation of the uterus

* Used as an adjunct to induction of abortion along with other abortifacient agents (PGE1 or PGE2)

* To induce labor by ripening the cervix before induction

* Augmentation of labor

* Following the expulsion of the placenta as an alternative to ergometrine.

* In active management of the third stage of labor

* To minimize blood loss and control postpartum hemorrhage.

* Oxytocin is involved in the regulation of preterm and term labor, but the exact mechanisms are not fully understood.

Contraindications of Oxytocin-

* Hypersensitivity to the hormone itself or any part of its synthetic version

* Vaginal deliveries that are in themselves contraindicated. These include:

* Active genital herpes infection in the mother,

* Vasa previa,

* Complete placenta previa,

* Invasive cervical cancer

* Abnormal position (most notably including a transverse lie)

Other options:

Option B- Recent studies have shown that induction of labor with a modified oxytocin infusion is a safe and effective alternative for selected gravidas with heart disease where elective delivery is warranted.

Option C- Oxytocin is used to induce or augment labor, including in some cases of premature labor when delivery is necessary. It's not contraindicated in this situation.

Option D- There's no specific contraindication for oxytocin use in hypothyroidism. Thyroid disorders don't typically interfere with oxytocin administration during labor.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old male patient presented to the hospital with palpitations. Physical examination showed a diastolic murmur in the left 3rd intercostal space. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic regurgitation

A diastolic murmur best heard at the left 3rd intercostal space (Erb’s point) is classic for aortic regurgitation.

It is an early diastolic, high-pitched decrescendo murmur due to backflow from aorta to LV. In AR:

• The aortic valve does not close properly
• Blood flows backward from aorta → left ventricle during diastole

This causes:

• Volume overload of the LV
• Increased stroke volume

Aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation are systolic murmurs.

Aortic regurgitation produces high pulse pressure, causing several classic signs:

| Sign | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Water hammer pulse | Bounding pulse

| Corrigan pulse | Rapid rise and fall pulse

| De Musset sign | Head nodding

| Quincke sign | Capillary pulsation

These occur due to large stroke volume and rapid diastolic runoff.

Tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic and best heard at the left lower sternal border.
questions.learning: Aortic regurgitation — A diastolic murmur best heard at the left 3rd intercostal space (Erb’s point) is classic for aortic regurgitation. It is an early diastolic, high-pitched decrescendo murmur due to backflow from aorta to LV.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding indirect ophthalmoscopy?
options: The image produced is erect and real
Condensor needs to be kept very close to the eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It provides 3-5x magnification

An indirect ophthalmoscope produces an inverted real image of 3 to 5 times magnification.

Advantages of the binocular indirect ophthalmoscope are:

* Visualization through hazy media is possible due to strong in built illumination system.

* Field of view is much larger than direct ophthalmoscopy.

* Examination of peripheral retina up to ora serrata is possible.

* Depth perception of the lesion is possible due to stereopsis with binocular indirect ophthalmoscope.

* Visualization of fundus in very high refractive error is also possible, where it may not be possible to focus the lesion with direct ophthalmoscope.

* A real, Inverted image is formed (Option A).

* There is an arms distance between the condensing lens and the patient's eye (Option C).

Other options:

Option D: 15 times magnification is seen with a direct ophthalmoscope.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 22-year-old female with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep, rapid breathing for one day. She is dehydrated and has a fruity breath odor. Her random blood glucose is 400 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis shows: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 20 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L. What is the most likely acid–base disorder?
options: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to the accumulation of ketoacids (β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) resulting from absolute insulin deficiency. The body compensates by hyperventilation (Kussmaul respiration), leading to a fall in PaCO₂ as a form of respiratory compensation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis: Incorrect. DKA causes a high anion gap acidosis, and patients hyperventilate rather than retain CO₂.
• C. Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation: Incorrect. Vomiting can cause metabolic alkalosis, but the predominant disturbance in DKA is metabolic acidosis.
• D. Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation: Incorrect. The primary abnormality is metabolic, not respiratory.
questions.learning: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to the accumulation of ketoacids (β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) resulting from absolute insulin deficiency.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the time taken for the embryo to travel from point 1 to 8?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8 days

The embryo takes approximately 8 days to travel from point 1 (fertilization) to point 8 (implantation) (typically 6-7 days).

Timeline of implantation:

• 3-4 days after fertilization: The morula (12-16 cells) enters the uterus.
• 4th day after fertilization: The advanced morula reaches the uterine lumen.
• 4-5 days after fertilization: The early blastocyst stage is seen.
• 6-7 days after fertilization: The blastocyst implants in the uterus. Implantation corresponds to 20-22 days of the menstrual cycle.

The blastocyst normally implants in the functional layer of the uterine endometrium. In the secretory phase, the endometrium comprises three layers: stratum compactum, stratum spongiosum, and stratum basale. The first two layers, collectively known as the stratum functionale or functional layer, are crucial for implantation. If implantation does not occur, this functional layer is shed off during menstruation. However, if implantation occurs, the functional layer is retained as the decidua, marking the beginning of a successful pregnancy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery runs in close relation to the region of the skull depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: The image identifies the Pterion, a critical anatomical landmark where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and greater wing of the sphenoid bones meet. The anterior (frontal) branch of the middle meningeal artery (MMA) runs directly deep to the Pterion on the internal surface of the skull. This area is clinically significant because the skull is thin at the Pterion, making it vulnerable to fractures from lateral head trauma. A fracture here can rupture the MMA, leading to an epidural (extradural) hematoma, which typically presents with a "lucid interval" followed by rapid neurological deterioration. The anterior cerebral artery (Option A) is located deep in the longitudinal fissure between brain hemispheres. The internal carotid (Option B) enters the skull base far more medially. The deep temporal arteries (Option D) supply the temporalis muscle on the external surface of the skull. Rapid surgical intervention via a burr hole at the Pterion is often required to evacuate an MMA-related hematoma

questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A 34-year-old medical student has fever, chest pain, severe breathlessness, and dry cough. Chest X-ray shows right homogeneous opacity. Ultrasound lung confirms massive pleural effusion on the right side. Which of the following statements are correct? 1. A therapeutic pleural tap should be done to relieve dyspnoea and sent for analysis. 2. If pleural fluid analysis is inconclusive, a thoracoscopy may be done. 3. Thoracoscopy should be done under general anesthesia. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2 only

• 1. Therapeutic pleural tap should be done: Correct

• A massive pleural effusion causing severe breathlessness is an indication for therapeutic thoracentesis to relieve dyspnea.
• The aspirated fluid should also be sent for diagnostic analysis, including protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cell count, Gram stain/culture, and cytology as appropriate.

• 2. Thoracoscopy if pleural fluid analysis is inconclusive: Correct

• If the cause remains undiagnosed after pleural fluid analysis, thoracoscopy (medical thoracoscopy/VATS) can be performed for direct visualization and pleural biopsy.
• It is particularly useful when malignancy or tuberculosis is suspected.

• 3. Thoracoscopy should be done under general anesthesia: Incorrect

• Medical thoracoscopy is generally performed under local anesthesia with conscious sedation.
• VATS (video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery) is performed under general anesthesia.

questions.text: Which of the following is used in the treatment of hemophilia A? a) Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) b) Cryoprecipitate c) Factor VIII concentrates d) Cryo-poor Plasma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. a, b, c

Correct answer is C because hemophilia A is due to factor VIII deficiency, and treatment requires replacement of factor VIII–containing products. Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate contain factor VIII and can be used when specific factor VIII concentrates are unavailable.

| FFP | All clotting factors

| Cryoprecipitate | Fibrinogen, Factor VIII, vWF, XIII

| Cryo-poor plasma | Factor IX, XI, albumin

| Factor VIII concentrate | Only Factor VIII

Cryoprecipitate and factor VIII concentrates are used in hemophilia A, not hemophilia B.

| Feature | Hemophilia A | Hemophilia B

| ------- | ------------ | ------------

| Deficiency | Factor VIII | Factor IX

| Treatment | Cryo, FVIII concentrate | FFP, FIX sources

| Common? | More common | Less common

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and a fever. On examination, the left breast appears as shown in the image below. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and the contralateral breast is normal. Repeated aspirations under antibiotic cover were unsuccessful. A USG done showed fluid collection. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Incision and drainage

This patient with breast abscess has not responded to multiple attempts of aspirations. The next best step in this scenario is to perform incision and drainage.

The given scenario points towards a diagnosis of breast abscess. The initial management of breast abscess includes aspiration of abscess along with supportive measures like a breast support garment, cold compression on the breast and analgesia to aid in symptomatic relief. This often allows resolution without the need for an incision scar and also allows the patient to continue breastfeeding. But her aspirations have been unsuccessful and thus incision and drainage have to be the next step in the management of this patient.

Mastitis occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. This occurs secondary to blockage of the lactiferous duct or due to incomplete emptying of breast milk or due to a retracted nipple. Overgrowth of these bacteria results in the development of breast abscesses.

It is common in new mothers at the beginning of lactation who are inexperienced with breastfeeding or during weaning when nipple trauma occurs due to the infant's growing teeth.

Signs and symptoms of this condition involve:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

The initial treatment should involve providing pain relief with analgesics. The abscess should then be localized preferably under USG guidance and percutaneous aspiration carried out. The pus should be sent for microbiological examination to find the organism and antibiotic sensitivity. Repeated aspirations may be carried out under antibiotics cover if needed.

In some conditions mentioned below, the breast abscess may be unresponsive to repeated aspirations and antibiotic cover. In such cases, incision and drainage are performed. The conditions include:

* Presence of thick pus

* Bacteria resistant to antibiotics

* If just a superficial part has been aspirated in the presence of a multiloculated abscess

* A non-healing breast abscess due to tuberculosis of the breast or inflammatory carcinoma of the breast, or an immunocompromised host.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient presents with a chronic tingling sensation in the forearm. A neurological examination is done and appears to be normal. Which of the following receptors are correctly matched?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pacinian corpuscles-fast vibration

Pacinian corpuscles are responsible for sensing fast vibration. The chronic tingling sensation is mediated by pressure-sensitive Aβ fibers and low-conduction velocity C fibers.

Pacinian corpuscles are the most sensitive mechanoreceptors in the somatosensory system. They are responsive to high-frequency (30–500 Hz) vibratory stimuli and deep pressure. They are also examples of rapidly adapting receptors.

Chronic tingling causing conditions include Diabetes, carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar nerve palsy, radial nerve palsy, tarsal tunnel syndrome, sciatica, vitamin B1,B6,B12 deficiencies, and alcoholism.

Other options

Option A: The Merkel cells are expanded dendritic endings in the epidermis of glabrous skin and respond to sustained pressure and touch.

Option B: Meissner's corpuscle senses tap and flutter. They are present in dermal papillae. They are rapidly adapting receptors.

Option D: Ruffini's corpuscles are enlarged dendritic endings with elongated capsules in the dermis of glabrous and hairy skin. They respond to stretch and fluttering vibrations. They are slowly adapting receptors.
questions.learning: Pacinian corpuscles-fast vibration Pacinian corpuscles are responsible for sensing fast vibration. The chronic tingling sensation is mediated by pressure-sensitive Aβ fibers and low-conduction velocity C fibers.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient who underwent a renal transplant recently came with complaints of watery diarrhoea. The stool sample revealed oocysts of size 30x15 microns. Identify the organism
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystoisospora

The given clinical scenario of a patient with a history of renal transplant and complaints of watery diarrhoea along with  a Kinyoun stain positive image of  pink coloured, acid-fast oocyst with the size of 30x15 microns is suggestive of infection due to Cystoisospora.

Cystoisospora usually causes a self-limiting but protracted diarrhoea, lasting for several years,  majorly in immunocompromised persons and particularly among the HIV infected. Human infection is acquired by ingestion of mature oocysts in food or drink. The parasites generally dwell in the epithelial cells of the small intestine .

Diagnosis involves identifying oocysts in fecal smears, which may sometimes be sparse and overlooked due to their transparent appearance in unstained films. They stain red using the cold acid-fast technique. Concentration methods like zinc sulfate or formol-ether techniques can be used.

The first line of management for isosporiasis is cotrimoxazole for 7-10 days. Patients who do not tolerate cotrimoxazole are treated with nitazoxanide or ciprofloxacin.
