questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are indications of endometrial sampling? I. Endometrial tuberculosis II. Endometrial polyp III. Postmenopausal bleeding IV. Abnormal uterine bleeding Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Endometrial sampling (endometrial biopsy) is a minimally invasive procedure used to obtain endometrial tissue for histopathological examination. It is primarily indicated to evaluate abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, and diagnose specific endometrial diseases such as tuberculosis. The following are indications for endometrial sampling:

• I. Endometrial tuberculosis: Endometrial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing genital tuberculosis, demonstrating granulomatous inflammation and allowing microbiological testing (AFB stain, culture, PCR). ⭐
• III. Postmenopausal bleeding: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation for endometrial carcinoma, and endometrial sampling is indicated, especially when endometrial thickness is >4 mm or bleeding is recurrent. ⭐
• IV. Abnormal uterine bleeding: Endometrial biopsy is recommended in:

• Women ≥45 years with AUB
• Women <45 years with persistent AUB, failed medical treatment, or risk factors for endometrial carcinoma.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Endometrial polyp: The preferred investigations are transvaginal ultrasound, saline infusion sonography, or hysteroscopy. Although a removed polyp is sent for histopathology, endometrial sampling alone is not the investigation of choice for diagnosing an endometrial polyp.
questions.learning: I, III and IV Endometrial sampling (endometrial biopsy) is a minimally invasive procedure used to obtain endometrial tissue for histopathological examination.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with fever, weakness, hypotension, and tachycardia. Peripheral blood smear examination confirms infection with Plasmodium falciparum. In this clinical scenario, which drug is considered the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with signs of "Severe (or Complicated) Malaria," as evidenced by systemic instability (hypotension/shock, tachycardia) and a smear positive for Plasmodium falciparum. Plasmodium falciparum (Option B) is the species most frequently associated with multi-organ failure and death. Vivax (Option A) and Ovale (Option C) can cause severe malaria but are more classically known for relapses due to liver hypnozoites. Malariae (Option D) is usually a chronic, milder infection. In falciparum infections, "sequestration" of infected erythrocytes in capillaries leads to cerebral malaria, pulmonary edema, and acute renal failure. According to WHO guidelines, the immediate treatment for severe malaria is intravenous Artesunate. Falciparum malaria is a true medical emergency, especially when systemic symptoms like hypotension are present, requiring rapid parasite clearance and intensive supportive care to prevent mortality
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with signs of "Severe (or Complicated) Malaria," as evidenced by systemic instability (hypotension/shock, tachycardia) and a smear positive for Plasmodium falciparum.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient undergoing autologous stem cell transplantation requires a recombinant growth factor for myeloid reconstitution. The agent chosen is produced in a expression system and carries a known risk of capillary leak syndrome. Which growth factor and source organism pairing is correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sargramostim — yeast — GM-CSF

Sargramostim is a recombinant form of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) used to accelerate myeloid recovery following bone marrow or stem cell transplantation. Unlike filgrastim, it stimulates multiple myeloid lineages, including neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and eosinophils.

• Sargramostim = recombinant GM-CSF
• Produced using a yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) expression system
• Important adverse effect: Capillary leak syndrome, characterized by hypotension, edema, and fluid extravasation.

Why not the others?

• A. Filgrastim — E. coli — G-CSF → Correct pairing, but not associated with the classic question stem of yeast-derived GM-CSF and capillary leak syndrome.
• C. Pegfilgrastim — E. coli — G-CSF → Pegylated form of filgrastim; same lineage specificity as G-CSF.
• D. Sargramostim — E. coli — GM-CSF → Incorrect source organism; sargramostim is produced in yeast, not E. coli.
questions.learning: Sargramostim — yeast — GM-CSF Sargramostim is a recombinant form of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) used to accelerate myeloid recovery following bone marrow or stem cell transplantation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are the contents of the carotid sheath except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sympathetic chain

The sympathetic chain is not the content of the carotid sheath. It lies posterior to the carotid sheath and anterior to the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae in the neck.

The carotid sheath is a layer of loose connective tissue formed by adjacent portions of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, the pretracheal fascia, and the prevertebral fascia.

Contents of carotid sheath:

• Common and internal carotid arteries,
• Internal jugular vein,
• Vagus nerve
• Ansa cervicalis

Note: The glossopharyngeal, accessory, and hypoglossal nerves lie within the upper part of the carotid sheath.
questions.learning: Sympathetic chain — The sympathetic chain is not the content of the carotid sheath. It lies posterior to the carotid sheath and anterior to the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae in the neck.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old female patient came with a history of fatiguability and constipation for the past 1 year. She has a history of multiple blood transfusions after delivery 4 years ago. She has had a lactational failure and never regained her periods after the delivery. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sheehan syndrome

The most likely diagnosis in a woman with lactational failure and postpartum amenorrhea, now presenting with fatiguability and constipation is Sheehan syndrome. A history of multiple blood transfusions after delivery indicates major obstetric blood loss, which resulted in pituitary ischemia leading to this condition.

Sheehan syndrome is panhypopituitarism due to pituitary ischemia and necrosis following massive obstetrical hemorrhage.

The most severe form presents with shock due to pituitary apoplexy. It is characterized by a sudden onset headache, nausea, visual deficits, and hormonal dysfunction due to acute pituitary hemorrhage or infarction. Less severe forms present with anovulation and amenorrhea.

Damage to specific pituitary cell types leads to lactational failure, loss of axillary and pubic hair, and symptoms of hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency. Prolactin deficiency is most commonly encountered, but adrenal insufficiency is the most life-threatening complication. Hence, the adrenal function should be immediately assessed if there is any suspicion of Sheehan syndrome.

Option B: Hypothyroidism can present with vague symptoms such as fatigue, constipation, and amenorrhea. However, postpartum hypothyroidism usually presents 4-8 months after delivery after a thyrotoxic phase with palpitations and thyroid enlargement.

Option C: Premature ovarian failure presents with menopausal symptoms. It is due to primary ovarian dysfunction. It is diagnosed when serum FSH levels are >30-40 mIU/mL on two occasions, at least one month apart.

Option D: Delayed transfusion reaction presents days to weeks after the transfusion. It may be asymptomatic or with low-grade fever. Coombs test may be positive, unconjugated bilirubin increased, and the rise in hemoglobin levels following the transfusion will be less than expected.
questions.learning: Sheehan syndrome — The most likely diagnosis in a woman with lactational failure and postpartum amenorrhea, now presenting with fatiguability and constipation is Sheehan syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An industrial worker was brought to a medical facility due to health problems. On his workup including laboratory tests, a finding of basophilic stippling of red blood cells (RBC) was observed. Which among the following is he/she likely to be having?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lead poisoning

Lead poisoning (Plumbism) is an important occupational disease seen in workers involved in battery manufacturing, painting, smelting, ceramics, printing, soldering, and recycling industries.

• Lead inhibits the enzymes δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase and ferrochelatase, resulting in defective heme synthesis.
• This leads to:

• Microcytic hypochromic anemia
• Basophilic stippling of RBCs (coarse blue granules due to retained ribosomal RNA)

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Asbestosis: Causes interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, pleural plaques, and mesothelioma; does not cause basophilic stippling.
• B. Farmer’s lung: A hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of moldy hay (Micropolyspora faeni); unrelated to RBC changes.
• D. Brucellosis: A zoonotic bacterial infection causing undulant fever; basophilic stippling is not a feature.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the RCH (Reproductive and Child Health) program guidelines, when should CuT 380A ideally be inserted to ensure maximum compliance? 1. Within 48 hours of delivery 2. Immediate post-partum 3. Within first 5-7 days of menstrual cycle 4. Within 7 days of next menstrual cycle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

CuT-380A is a long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC) widely promoted under India’s Reproductive and Child Health Programme and National Health Mission. It is a copper intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) effective for up to 10 years. IUCD is part of spacing methods in family planning.

As per RCH guidelines, CuT 380A insertion is ideal immediate post-partum, within 48 hours of delivery (PPIUCD), and within 5–7 days of the menstrual cycle, as these timings ensure high acceptance, convenience, and compliance.

Insertion within 7 days of the next menstrual cycle is not an ideal recommended window.

Advantages of CuT-380A are that it is long lasting, reversible, hormone free and cost effective.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 CuT-380A is a long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC) widely promoted under India’s Reproductive and Child Health Programme and National Health Mission.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which receptor is primarily responsible for mediating glucose uptake in skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: GLUT 4 is the primary glucose transporter found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. It is uniquely characterized as the insulin-responsive transporter. Under resting conditions, GLUT 4 is sequestered in intracellular vesicles. When insulin binds to its receptor on the cell surface, or during physical exercise, these vesicles translocate to the plasma membrane, allowing for the rapid uptake of glucose from the blood into the muscle. GLUT 1 (Option A) provides basal glucose uptake in most tissues, including the blood-brain barrier. GLUT 2 (Option B) is a high-capacity, low-affinity transporter found in the liver, pancreas, and kidneys. GLUT 3 (Option C) is the primary transporter for neurons in the brain. The dysregulation of GLUT 4 translocation is a hallmark of insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes. Because exercise can stimulate GLUT 4 translocation independently of insulin, physical activity remains a cornerstone of managing blood sugar levels in diabetic patients
questions.learning: GLUT 4 is the primary glucose transporter found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. It is uniquely characterized as the insulin-responsive transporter.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A defect in which of the following forms the structure marked below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fascia transversalis

The structure marked is the deep inguinal ring, which is formed by a defect in fascia transversalis.

The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia present 1 cm above the inguinal ligament, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. An indirect inguinal hernia arises through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessel.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the ideal thickness of lead aprons for personnel working in a radiology department?
questions.explanation: In the field of radiation protection, the goal is to reduce occupational exposure as much as possible (ALARA principle). For the majority of diagnostic radiology workers, a lead apron with a thickness of 0.5 mm lead equivalent is considered the ideal standard. This thickness provides an excellent balance between radiation attenuation and the physical comfort of the wearer; a 0.5 mm apron can block approximately 95–99% of the scattered X-ray radiation encountered in typical diagnostic settings. While a 1 mm apron (Option B) would provide even higher protection, it is significantly heavier and can cause orthopedic issues with prolonged use. 0.75 mm (Option C) and 2 mm (Option D) are not standard requirements for general diagnostic work. Proper storage (hanging rather than folding) is also essential to prevent the lead from cracking. Consistent use of these personal protective devices, along with thyroid shields and lead glasses, is mandatory for ensuring the long-term safety of radiology personnel
questions.learning: In the field of radiation protection, the goal is to reduce occupational exposure as much as possible (ALARA principle). For the majority of diagnostic radiology workers, a lead apron with a thickness of 0.5 mm lead equivalent is considered the ideal standard.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A child before playing consumed fruit from the garden. After some time he developed a high fever, confusion, photophobia, and unable to urinate. What are the likely causative agent and the appropriate antidote used in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Datura, Physostigmine

The clinical vignette in the question is suggestive of Datura poisoning, for which the appropriate antidote is physostigmine, a reversible acetylcholine esterase antagonist. It is an effective treatment for severe anticholinergic poisoning.

Datura poisoning:

The common names include thorn apple, Jimson weed, and Devil's trumpet. The active ingredients include the anticholinergic alkaloids atropine, scopolamine, and hyoscyamine. The seeds or other parts of the plant can be ingested or smoked.

Toxic manifestations of Datura:

• Mnemonic: "hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, and mad as a hatter"
• Also, remember the D's of Datura

• Dry hot skin (Temp rises up to 42 C, a scarlet rash may also be appreciated).
• Dilatation of pupils along with loss of accommodation
• Diplopia
• Dryness of the mouth and throat, unquenchable thirst
• Dysphagia
• Dilatation of cutaneous blood vessels
• Dysarthria (Difficulty in talking)
• Drunken gait
• Delirium
• Drowsiness
• Death due to respiratory or cardiac failure

Treatment

• Gastric lavage or decontamination with activated charcoal or tannic acid: Gastric emptying is often delayed, and the small, plentiful seeds can become trapped among the gastrointestinal folds after ingestion; thus, gastric decontamination can be an important therapy.
• Physostigmine in severe toxicity given 1-2 mg IM/IV after every half hour as required: It is a physiological antidote. Pilocarpine may also be given.

Medico-legal importance:

In India, Datura is used as a stupefying poison prior to robbery, kidnapping, and rape. It is also known as a rail-road poison, as it is commonly encountered during a journey. Robbers disguised as saints may offer ‘prasad’ mixed with Datura seeds and rob the passengers.

Yellow oleander:

All parts of the plant are poisonous. The active principles are thevatin and thevatoxin, which are cardiac glycosides. The nectar of the flower yields poisonous honey. Symptoms include a burning sensation in the mouth, tingling of the tongue, dryness of the throat, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dilated pupils, irregular action of the heart followed by drowsiness, coma, collapse, and death.

Treatment includes

• Gastric lavage
• Single-dose activated charcoal
• To combat acidosis IV sodium lactate and 5% glucose can be given
• Atropine, adrenaline, or noradrenaline (if blood pressure is low)
• Digoxin-specific antibodies

The given image shows the flowers of Cerebra thevatia.
questions.learning: Datura, Physostigmine — The clinical vignette in the question is suggestive of Datura poisoning, for which the appropriate antidote is physostigmine, a reversible acetylcholine esterase antagonist.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which test is considered the best for evaluating long-term glycemic control in diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation: Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) is the gold standard test for assessing long-term glycemic control in patients with diabetes mellitus. Because red blood cells have a lifespan of approximately 120 days, the HbA1c level reflects the average blood glucose concentration over the preceding 2-3 months. Glycated albumin (Option B) and serum fructosamine (Option C) reflect glycemic control over a much shorter period, typically the past 2-3 weeks. These are useful in specific conditions where HbA1c might be unreliable, such as in patients with hemolytic anemia or hemoglobinopathies. Urine sugar (Option D) is a poor marker as it only indicates that the blood glucose has exceeded the renal threshold at a specific moment and provides no information about long-term trends. For most diabetics, an HbA1c goal of less than 7% is recommended to reduce the risk of long-term microvascular complications like retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy. It is a vital tool for both diagnosis and management

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following intravenous anesthetics functions as an NMDA receptor antagonist?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is a unique intravenous anesthetic that works as a non-competitive antagonist at the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor. It produces a state of "dissociative anesthesia," where the patient appears awake but is detached from their environment and unresponsive to pain. Ketamine is prized for providing intense analgesia and maintaining respiratory drive and blood pressure, making it ideal for trauma or field medicine. Propofol (Option B) and Thiopentone (Option C) primarily function through the enhancement of GABA-A receptors to produce sedation. Midazolam (Option D) is a benzodiazepine that also acts on GABA receptors. Ketamine's primary drawbacks include emergence delirium and vivid dreams, which are often mitigated by combining it with a benzodiazepine. It is also being increasingly used at sub-anesthetic doses for the management of chronic pain and treatment-resistant depression

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A pregnant woman, after undergoing a cesarean section under spinal anesthesia, had a headache that aggravated in sitting position. Which of the following is not advised for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Restricted water intake

The given scenario is suggestive of post-dural puncture headache which worsens with restricted water intake.

Post-dural puncture headache is believed to result from a puncture of the dura (unintentional or intentional) in the setting of neuraxial anesthesia. This causes leakage of CSF from a dural defect leading to intracranial hypotension.

The characteristic feature of a post-dural puncture headache is the frontal or occipital headache. It is associated with nausea, neck stiffness, and lower back pain. Most of the headaches resolve spontaneously within 7 days.

An epidural blood patch is the definitive management. It is ideally performed 24 hours after dural puncture and the development of classic symptoms (Option A).

Supine position, IV fluids, caffeine, stool softeners, and analgesia are other factors that help in relieving the symptoms (options B & D).

Pearl PF0038: PDPH- Post-Dural Puncture Headache

* May follow lumbar puncture, spinal anesthesia, wet epidural tap (in which epidural needle pierced dura).

* Onset 12-72hrs and last for 1-2 weeks.

* Aggravated by sitting and relieved by lying down.

* Incidence increases with the larger needle, cutting point (in comparison to pencil point) needle, young age, females, pregnancy.

* Prevention by thinner needle

Management:

* Supine position

* IV fluids

* Caffeine and analgesia

* Epidural blood patch

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the statement is true regarding laryngomalacia?
options: Most common congenital abnormality in new-born
Surgical management is required in most children
questions.explanation: Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx in newborns and infants. It is characterized by the inward collapse of the supraglottic structures (like the epiglottis and arytenoids) during inhalation. This results in a high-pitched inspiratory stridor (Option A is incorrect as it is not expiratory). The stridor is typically worst in the supine position and improves when the baby is placed prone (Option B is incorrect). In the vast majority of children (over 90%), the condition is self-limiting and resolves spontaneously by the age of 18–24 months as the laryngeal cartilage matures; therefore, surgical management is NOT required in most children (Option D is incorrect). Surgery (supraglottoplasty) is only reserved for severe cases involving failure to thrive, severe cyanosis, or significant sleep apnea. Diagnosis is usually made through flexible laryngoscopy, which shows a classic "omega-shaped" epiglottis. Reassurance and monitoring for adequate weight gain are the cornerstones of management for most affected infants
questions.learning: Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx in newborns and infants. It is characterized by the inward collapse of the supraglottic structures (like the epiglottis and arytenoids) during inhalation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a hospital, a healthcare worker is responsible for segregating biomedical waste according to standard waste management guidelines. As per these guidelines, which category of biomedical waste should be disposed of in a white (translucent) bag?
questions.explanation: According to the current Biomedical Waste Management Rules, the white disposal bag is specifically reserved for sharp waste. This includes needles, syringes with fixed needles, scalpel blades, and lancets. These containers must be puncture-proof and leak-proof to prevent accidental needle-stick injuries to healthcare personnel. Anatomical waste (Option A), such as tissues or body parts, must be placed in yellow bags for incineration. Glassware (Option C), including vials or broken glass, should be placed in blue-labeled containers or boxes. Plastic waste (Option D) like catheters, IV tubes, and gloves is typically disposed of in red bags for autoclaving or chemical treatment before recycling. Proper segregation is vital to ensure that sharps, which pose a high risk for transmitting bloodborne pathogens like HIV, are handled with specific sterilization protocols. Consequently, the healthcare worker must place all sharp items into the designated white container
questions.learning: According to the current Biomedical Waste Management Rules, the white disposal bag is specifically reserved for sharp waste. This includes needles, syringes with fixed needles, scalpel blades, and lancets.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient receiving cholesterol-lowering therapy develops facial flushing and erythema. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Niacin

Niacin (vitamin B3) is an antihyperlipidemic drug that commonly causes facial flushing, warmth, and erythema due to prostaglandin (PGD₂ and PGE₂)-mediated vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels. This adverse effect can be minimized by taking aspirin 30 minutes before niacin or by using extended-release formulations.

• Niacin mechanism: Inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue → ↓ VLDL synthesis → ↓ LDL; also markedly increases HDL (most effective drug for raising HDL).
• Characteristic adverse effect: Flushing due to prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation.
• Other adverse effects: Hyperuricemia (may precipitate gout), hyperglycemia, hepatotoxicity, and pruritus.
• Prevention of flushing: Aspirin or NSAIDs before niacin therapy.
• Lipid effects: ↓ LDL, ↓ Triglycerides, ↑ HDL (greatest HDL increase among lipid-lowering drugs).

Why not the other options?

• A. Atorvastatin: Common adverse effects include myalgia, myopathy, elevated liver enzymes, and rarely rhabdomyolysis; flushing is not characteristic.
• B. Ezetimibe: Inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption; generally well tolerated with occasional gastrointestinal symptoms.
• C. Gemfibrozil: Fibrate associated with myopathy (especially with statins), gallstones, and elevated liver enzymes, not facial flushing.
questions.learning: Niacin Niacin (vitamin B3) is an antihyperlipidemic drug that commonly causes facial flushing, warmth, and erythema due to prostaglandin (PGD₂ and PGE₂)-mediated vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 66-year-old man presented with difficulty in urination, back pain, and an elevated PSA blood test. An X-ray revealed two radiolucent lesions in the bony pelvis and MRI revealed several enlarged lymph nodes in the lower abdomen. Which of the following drugs can most likely be used to treat the given condition? PSA- Prostate-specific antigen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Goserelin

The clinical features and investigations showing elevated PSA, osteolytic lesions and enlarged lymph nodes are suggestive of prostate cancer. Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used in the treatment of prostate cancer.

Androgen deprivation therapy is the primary medical therapy for prostate cancer. The drugs approved for this indication include leuprolide, goserelin, histrelin, buserelin, and triptorelin.

The agonist action of the GnRH analogs causes increased testosterone production, causing a tumor flare. It can be prevented by concomitant administration of an androgen receptor antagonist such as flutamide, bicalutamide, or nilutamide; until downregulation of testosterone is complete.

The combined androgen deprivation therapy with continuous GnRH agonist and an androgen receptor antagonist is as effective as surgical castration, in reducing the levels of serum testosterone and its effects. GnRH agonist can be used in the early and late course of the disease.

Other options:

Option a: Anastrozole is an aromatase inhibitor, used in the treatment of advanced breast cancer.

Option b: Desogestrel is a synthetic progestin without androgenic activity. It is used in combination with ethinyl estradiol for oral contraception.

Option c: Oxandrolone is a synthetic derivative of testosterone (anabolic steroid). It is used in the treatment of bone pain in patients with osteoporosis.
questions.learning: Goserelin — The clinical features and investigations showing elevated PSA, osteolytic lesions and enlarged lymph nodes are suggestive of prostate cancer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with fatigue, gum bleeding, and multiple perifollicular hemorrhages on the lower limbs, along with a bleeding tendency. These findings are most consistent with a deficiency of which enzyme activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prolyl hydroxylase

The clinical features—bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, easy bruising, and fatigue—are classic for scurvy (vitamin C deficiency).

Vitamin C is required as a cofactor for:

• Prolyl hydroxylase
• Lysyl hydroxylase

These enzymes catalyze hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen, which is essential for:

• Stability of the collagen triple helix
• Proper cross-linking of collagen fibers

Why other options are incorrect:

• Lysyl oxidase: Involved in collagen cross-linking but is copper-dependent, not vitamin C dependent
• Tyrosinase: Involved in melanin synthesis
• Alkaline phosphatase: Associated with bone metabolism
questions.learning: Prolyl hydroxylase — The clinical features—bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, easy bruising, and fatigue—are classic for scurvy (vitamin C deficiency).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: LMWH is given by which route?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subcutaneous

LMWH is given by the subcutaneous route.

Heparin, low molecular weight heparin (LMWH), and fondaparinux are not absorbed through GI mucosa and must be given parenterally.

LMWH and fondaparinux are given subcutaneously.

Heparin can be given through intravenous infusion and subcutaneous routes.
questions.learning: Subcutaneous LMWH is given by the subcutaneous route. Heparin, low molecular weight heparin (LMWH), and fondaparinux are not absorbed through GI mucosa and must be given parenterally.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with bronchial asthma is prescribed a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler (MDI) but has difficulty coordinating actuation with inspiration. His physician recommends using a spacer device with the MDI. Which of the following statements is true regarding the use of a spacer with an MDI?
options: It increases systemic absorption of the drug
It decreases drug wastage and oropharyngeal deposition
It makes the inhalation technique more complicated and less effective
It has no effect on drug delivery to the lungs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It decreases drug wastage and oropharyngeal deposition

A spacer (valved holding chamber) improves the effectiveness of a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) by reducing the need for precise coordination between actuation and inhalation. It slows the aerosol particles, allowing more drug to reach the lower airways while reducing drug deposition in the oropharynx and minimizing wastage, thereby improving both efficacy and safety.

• Particularly useful with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): Reduces the risk of oral candidiasis and dysphonia.
• Technique: Actuate one puff at a time into the spacer, followed by slow deep inhalation (or tidal breathing in young children).

Why not the other options?

• A. It increases systemic absorption of the drug: Incorrect. Spacers reduce oropharyngeal deposition and systemic absorption of the swallowed drug, thereby decreasing systemic adverse effects.
• C. It makes the inhalation technique more complicated and less effective: Incorrect. Spacers simplify inhaler use, especially in children, elderly patients, and those with poor hand-breath coordination.
• D. It has no effect on drug delivery to the lungs: Incorrect. Spacers increase pulmonary drug deposition and improve drug delivery.
questions.learning: It decreases drug wastage and oropharyngeal deposition A spacer (valved holding chamber) improves the effectiveness of a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) by reducing the need for precise coordination between actuation and inhalation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old male comes with complaints of hip pain. An X-ray of the hip shows lytic lesions and serum calcium levels are elevated. Bone marrow plasma cells are 42% and the cells seen are given in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Multiple myeloma

In an elderly male patient, the presence of hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, bone marrow plasma cells of more than 10%, and the characteristic Mott cell as seen in the image suggest multiple myeloma.

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia. The incidence of multiple myeloma increases with age, and it is more commonly seen in males than in females.

Signs and symptoms

* Bone pain is the most common symptom

* Pathologic fractures

* Recurrent bacterial infections

* Renal failure

* Normocytic normochromic anemia elevated ESR, Hypercalcemia, normal ALP (ALP is a marker of bone growth and hence is not increased in multiple myeloma)

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%) and presence of Dutcher bodies, Russel bodies, and Mott cells.

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation)

Option A: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is usually asymptomatic at diagnosis but can present with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are usually seen. Peripheral smear contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is often described as a convent-girl appearance.

Option B: Acute lymphocytic leukemia presents with a hypercellular marrow that is packed with lymphoblasts. These lymphoblasts, when compared to myeloblasts, have more condensed chromatin with less prominent nucleoli.

Option C: In chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), patients typically present with a dragging sensation in the abdomen due to splenomegaly or splenic infarct, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss. The peripheral smear contains neutrophils and their precursors of various sizes and configurations like band cells, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and blasts. Hence, the histological picture is described as having a garden party or a college girl appearance.

Pearl PF0569: Some Pathological Cells/Bodies in Multiple Myeloma

Description

Russell bodies

They are globular intracellular accumulations of immunoglobulins (Ig).

Plasma cells filled with multiple Russell bodies are called Mott cells.

Dutcher bodies

PAS-positive intranuclear inclusions containing Ig seen in some of the plasma cells are called Dutcher bodies.

Flame cells

Plasma cells with fiery red cytoplasm are called flame cells.

PAS: Periodic acid Schiff
questions.learning: Multiple myeloma — In an elderly male patient, the presence of hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, bone marrow plasma cells of more than 10%, and the characteristic Mott cell as seen in the image suggest multiple myeloma.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The dose at which dopamine acts on beta 1 receptors is ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2-10 mcg/kg/min

The dose at which dopamine acts on β-1 receptors is 2-10 mcg/kg/min.

The systemic effects of dopamine vary with its concentration in the body.

When administered at an infusion rate of 2-5 mcg/kg/min, it directly stimulates cardiac β receptors. This enhances myocardial contractility and is useful in the management of cardiogenic shock.

At doses of 5-15 mcg/kg/min and above, it stimulates α adrenergic receptors. This causes peripheral arterial and venous vasoconstriction.

At lower doses of <2 mcg/kg/min, it directly stimulates both D1 and D2 receptors. The D1 receptors in renal and mesenteric blood vessels are the most sensitive: i.v. infusion of low dose of DA dilates these vessels subsequently, causing increased renal blood flow and increased urine output.

The clinical indications of dopamine include cardiogenic and vasodilatory shock, congestive cardiac failure and symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine or pacing.

The major side effects are:

• Severe hypertension (especially when taken with nonselective β-blockers)
• Ventricular arrhythmias
• Cardiac ischemia
• Tissue ischemia/gangrene (high doses/extravasation into tissues)
questions.learning: 2-10 mcg/kg/min The dose at which dopamine acts on β-1 receptors is 2-10 mcg/kg/min. The systemic effects of dopamine vary with its concentration in the body.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to an infertility clinic with a history of recurrent pregnancy losses and is diagnosed with a septate uterus. Which corrective procedure is associated with the best obstetric outcomes in this condition?
questions.explanation: A septate uterus is a congenital uterine anomaly associated with the highest risk of recurrent pregnancy loss. The modern "gold standard" procedure that yields the most favorable obstetric outcomes with the least morbidity is Hysteroscopic Transcervical Resection of the Septum (TCRS) (Option D). This minimally invasive technique involves using a hysteroscopic resectoscope or scissors to divide the septum without making an incision in the abdominal or uterine wall. This allows for a shorter recovery time and, most importantly, allows the patient to attempt a vaginal delivery in the future. In contrast, Jones (Option A) and Tompkins (Option C) metroplasties are older, invasive abdominal surgeries that require a Cesarean section for all subsequent deliveries. Strassman metroplasty (Option B) is specifically utilized for the correction of a bicornuate uterus rather than a septate uterus. Therefore, hysteroscopic resection is the definitive contemporary choice
questions.learning: A septate uterus is a congenital uterine anomaly associated with the highest risk of recurrent pregnancy loss. The modern "gold standard" procedure that yields the most favorable obstetric outcomes with the least morbidity is Hysteroscopic Transcervical…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a village, it is observed that several farmers have crossed gait and use a stick for support to stand up and walk. Due to poor yield from farms, they consume meals containing rice and pulses only. Supplementing their diet with which of the following vitamins could have prevented this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

The clinical picture describes lathyrism, seen in famine-affected villages where people consume Kesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) along with rice. The neurotoxin β-ODAP causes spastic paraparesis with scissoring (crossed) gait, forcing patients to use a stick for walking. Vitamin C supplementation reduces the neurotoxicity of the toxin and helps prevent lathyrism.
questions.learning: Vitamin C — The clinical picture describes lathyrism, seen in famine-affected villages where people consume Kesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) along with rice.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient not able to chew the food and food stuck between cheeks and teeth. Which muscle weakness is associated with this clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Buccinator

The correct answer is Buccinator.

Buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth, preventing food from accumulating in the vestibule during mastication.

Weakness leads to food getting trapped between cheek and teeth, a classic sign seen in facial nerve palsy.
questions.learning: Buccinator — The correct answer is Buccinator. Buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth, preventing food from accumulating in the vestibule during mastication.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identical twins have similarities in all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fingerprint pattern

Fingerprint pattern differs in identical twins.

Fingerprints are formed during intrauterine life due to friction ridges. These ridges are created by pressure on the fingers from touching the surroundings. Hence, it is unique to every individual.
questions.learning: Fingerprint pattern Fingerprint pattern differs in identical twins. Fingerprints are formed during intrauterine life due to friction ridges.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drugs are commonly used to prevent or treat chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting?
questions.explanation: The modern management of Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting (CINV) involves a multi-modal approach targeting different neurotransmitter pathways. The combination of a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist (Granisetron), a corticosteroid (Dexamethasone), and an NK1 receptor antagonist (Aprepitant) is the standard and highly effective protocol for highly emetogenic chemotherapy. Granisetron blocks serotonin signals from the gut; Aprepitant blocks substance P in the brain; and Dexamethasone synergistically enhances the anti-emetic effect through mechanisms that are not fully understood. Other options list older, less effective agents like metoclopramide (dopamine antagonist) or doxylamine (antihistamine) which are insufficient as primary prevention for modern high-dose chemotherapy. Using this "triple therapy" has dramatically improved the quality of life for cancer patients by preventing both acute and delayed vomiting episodes. Clinicians must tailor the regimen based on the specific emetic potential of the chemotherapy being administered. This combination represents the current gold standard in supportive oncology care
questions.learning: The modern management of Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting (CINV) involves a multi-modal approach targeting different neurotransmitter pathways.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Iodine has complex effects on thyroid function. Very high concentrations of iodine inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis and release. This effect is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wolff-Chaikoff effect

The Wolff–Chaikoff effect is the transient inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis and release following exposure to large amounts of iodine. It occurs due to inhibition of iodine organification within the thyroid gland and is the basis for using potassium iodide in thyroid storm and before thyroid surgery.

Why not the other options?

• B. Jod-Basedow effect: Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, seen in patients with autonomous thyroid tissue (e.g., multinodular goiter).
• C. Reverse Wolff–Chaikoff effect: Refers to the escape phenomenon, where the thyroid resumes normal hormone synthesis after a few days despite continued iodine exposure.
• D. Reverse Jod-Basedow effect: Not a recognized physiological phenomenon.
questions.learning: Wolff-Chaikoff effect — The Wolff–Chaikoff effect is the transient inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis and release following exposure to large amounts of iodine.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Least frequency of slow waves is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stomach

Among the given options, the least frequency of slow waves is seen in the stomach (4/min).

The Basal electrical rhythm (BER) also called slow-wave, is a rhythmic fluctuation of membrane potential in the gastrointestinal smooth muscle. It is initiated by the interstitial cells of Cajal. The membrane potential fluctuates between -65mV and -45mV.

The BER is seen in all sites of gastrointestinal smooth muscle except in the esophagus and proximal stomach.

The rate of BER in various sites is as follows:

• Stomach: 4/min
• Duodenum: 12/min
• Distal ileum: 8/min
• Cecum: 2/min
• Sigmoid colon: 6/min

The BER does not cause contraction of the smooth muscle. However, when the BER is superimposed by the spike potentials, it increases muscle tension.

Acetylcholine causes an increase in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension. Epinephrine causes a decrease in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension.

Muscle contraction can occur only when the motor stimulus is provided during the depolarisation part of the BER.

Thus, BER does not cause muscle contraction by itself, but controls the rate and organization sites of the muscle contractions, as in coordination of the peristaltic activity and setting the rhythm of segmentation.
questions.learning: Stomach Among the given options, the least frequency of slow waves is seen in the stomach (4/min). The Basal electrical rhythm (BER) also called slow-wave, is a rhythmic fluctuation of membrane potential in the gastrointestinal smooth muscle.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A G3P1A1 woman is admitted to the labor room at term with a cervix dilated to 4 cm, intact membranes, and the fetal head palpable at 3/5 per abdomen. After 4 hours, a repeat examination shows the cervix dilated to 5 cm with an unchanged station, and the cervicograph remains on the right side of the alert line. Which of the following statements about the progress of labor is correct?
options: The head was engaged at the time of presentation
The cervicograph status suggests that intervention is likely to be required
The cervicograph on repeat examination would touch the action line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The cervicograph status suggests that intervention is likely to be required

A partograph (cervicograph) is used to monitor the progress of labor by plotting cervical dilatation against time. Important lines on the partograph:

• Alert line → represents expected normal cervical dilatation
• Action line → placed 4 hours to the right of the alert line and indicates need for intervention if crossed

In this patient:

• Cervical dilatation progressed only from 4 cm to 5 cm in 4 hours
• Fetal station remained unchanged
• Cervicograph lies to the right of the alert line

This indicates abnormal or slow progress of labor and suggests that intervention may soon be required (eg, augmentation or operative delivery).

Additional concepts:

• “3/5 head palpable per abdomen” means the head is not fully engaged
• Engaged head usually corresponds to ≤2/5 palpable abdominally
questions.learning: The cervicograph status suggests that intervention is likely to be required A partograph (cervicograph) is used to monitor the progress of labor by plotting cervical dilatation against time.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Paris green dust is commonly used to kill which of the following?
questions.explanation: Paris green (copper acetoarsenite) is a specialized stomach poison used in public health for mosquito control. It is primarily applied as a dust to the surface of stagnant water bodies to target Anopheles larvae, which are the vectors of malaria. Unlike Culex larvae, which feed at the bottom, Anopheles larvae feed at the water's surface, where they ingest the toxic Paris green particles. Houseflies (Option B) are typically managed with residual sprays or baits like malathion. Bedbugs (Option C) and cockroaches (Option D) require different classes of insecticides, such as pyrethroids or organophosphates, applied to cracks and crevices where they reside. While Paris green was a historical cornerstone of malaria eradication programs, it has largely been superseded by more modern larvicides (like Temephos) and biological control agents (like Bti) due to the environmental risks associated with its arsenic content. However, it remains a classic topic in exams regarding historical vector control strategies
questions.learning: Paris green (copper acetoarsenite) is a specialized stomach poison used in public health for mosquito control. It is primarily applied as a dust to the surface of stagnant water bodies to target Anopheles larvae, which are the vectors of malaria.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the causative agent for granuloma inguinale?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calymmatobacterium granulomatis

The causative agent for granuloma inguinale (donovanosis) is Calymmatobacterium granulomatis. It is now called Klebsiella granulomatis and is a gram-negative bacillus causing chronic ulcerative infection of the vulva.

It is highly contagious and transmitted through repeated sexual or non-sexual contact. The incubation period is 1-12 weeks.

Clinical features:

It begins as a painless nodule which later ulcerates to form multiple beefy red painless ulcers that tend to coalesce; the vulva is progressively destroyed, and minimal adenopathy may occur.

Diagnosis:

Microscopic examination of smears from the lesion/ biopsy specimens reveals pathognomonic intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies and clusters of bacteria with a bipolar (safety pin) appearance. Blue-black stained organisms are seen in the cytoplasm of mononuclear cells.

Management:

Azithromycin 1 g orally once per week or 500 mg daily for at least 3 weeks and until all lesions have completely healed.

The given image below shows the donovanosis in a female patient with a beefy red ulcer:
questions.learning: Calymmatobacterium granulomatis — The causative agent for granuloma inguinale (donovanosis) is Calymmatobacterium granulomatis. It is now called Klebsiella granulomatis and is a gram-negative bacillus causing chronic ulcerative infection of the vulva.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate has bilateral chorioretinitis with intraparenchymal calcifications. She also has hydrocephalus. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Toxoplasma gondi

The presence of bilateral chorioretinitis with intraparenchymal calcifications and hydrocephalus in a neonate is suggestive of congenital toxoplasmosis.

The characteristic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications. Clinical manifestations apart from the triad include hydrops fetalis, intrauterine growth retardation, prematurity, peripheral retinal scars, persistent jaundice, and mild thrombocytopenia.

Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs when a pregnant woman acquires the infection during gestation. The organism may cross to the fetus transplacentally or at the time of vaginal delivery. The severity of the disease in the neonate is greater if the woman gets infected early in her pregnancy. The causative agent is Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan.

The diagnosis is made by the detection of IgM anti-toxoplasma antibodies. IgG can cross the placenta is hence, cannot confirm infection in the infant. IgM immunosorbent agglutination assay (ISAGA) and IgA ELISA are the most useful diagnostic tests.

Spiramycin can be administered for cases of acute infection in early pregnancy to reduce vertical transmission. It does not cross the placenta and therefore cannot be used to treat an infected fetus. Pyrimethamine-sulfonamide (to be avoided in the first trimester) is used when a fetal infection is confirmed or in maternal infections after 18 weeks.

Other options:

Option A: Trypanosoma is a genus of protozoan parasites responsible for diseases like African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) and American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease). These diseases present with different clinical features, such as fever, swollen lymph nodes, and neurological symptoms in African trypanosomiasis, and fever, swelling at the infection site, and cardiomyopathy in Chagas disease.

Option C: Taenia solium is a parasitic tapeworm transmitted through undercooked pork, causing intestinal infection (taeniasis) or more severe cyst formation in tissues, including the brain (cysticercosis). It's prevalent in regions with poor sanitation and where pork is consumed.

Option D: Congenital cytomegalovirus presents with hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. Head neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss. Diagnosis is made by isolating the virus from the urine or blood by polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
questions.learning: Toxoplasma gondi — The presence of bilateral chorioretinitis with intraparenchymal calcifications and hydrocephalus in a neonate is suggestive of congenital toxoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A gasless abdomen is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute pancreatitis

A gasless abdomen is an X-ray feature that can be seen in acute pancreatitis. Patients with acute pancreatitis can have significant vomiting and diarrhea that may produce a gasless abdomen.

Common causes of gasless abdomen include:

• High obstruction: gastric outlet obstruction, congenital atresia
• Small bowel obstruction
• Bowel ischemia
• Ascites
• Acute pancreatitis
• Gastroenteritis
• Large abdominal mass - due to displacement
• Post-surgery following total colectomy, esophagogastrectomy, gastrectomy, and low anterior resection
• A paucity of small bowel gas may be a normal finding in some adults

Note: In intussusception, an X-ray shows small bowel obstruction, a mass, and a paucity of gas in the right iliac fossa.
questions.learning: Acute pancreatitis — A gasless abdomen is an X-ray feature that can be seen in acute pancreatitis. Patients with acute pancreatitis can have significant vomiting and diarrhea that may produce a gasless abdomen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Cervarix vaccine is effective against which of the following Human papillomavirus serotypes?
questions.explanation: The Cervarix vaccine is a bivalent vaccine specifically designed to protect against Human Papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 16 and 18. These two high-risk serotypes are responsible for approximately 70% of all cervical cancers worldwide. HPV 6 and 11 (Option B) are low-risk serotypes that cause approximately 90% of genital warts; protection against these is provided by the quadrivalent (Gardasil) or nonavalent vaccines, but not by Cervarix. Options C and D list incorrect pairings of high and low-risk serotypes. Cervarix is typically administered to girls and young women before the onset of sexual activity to provide maximum preventative efficacy against cervical malignancy and its precursors. The vaccine works by inducing high levels of neutralizing antibodies against the L1 capsid protein of the virus. Universal HPV vaccination remains a primary public health goal for eliminating cervical cancer in many countries
questions.learning: The Cervarix vaccine is a bivalent vaccine specifically designed to protect against Human Papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 16 and 18. These two high-risk serotypes are responsible for approximately 70% of all cervical cancers worldwide.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 31-year-old woman who develops pain and sensory loss over the anterolateral aspect of the thigh following vaginal delivery is most likely experiencing injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
options: The lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh
questions.explanation: Pain and numbness confined to the anterolateral aspect of the thigh are classic for meralgia paresthetica, which results from compression or injury to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (also called the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve). This nerve is a pure sensory nerve that passes beneath the inguinal ligament, making it vulnerable to compression. Such injury commonly occurs after prolonged vaginal delivery, especially when the patient is maintained in a forced lithotomy position for an extended period. Compression may result from leg supports, prolonged hip flexion, or pressure from the fetal head. The sciatic nerve (Option A) causes sensory loss over the posterior leg with associated motor weakness. The obturator nerve (Option B) supplies the medial thigh and affects thigh adduction. The ilioinguinal nerve (Option C) provides sensation to the groin and labia majora. Most cases of meralgia paresthetica are self-limiting and resolve with conservative management, but correct identification of the sensory distribution is essential to exclude more serious motor nerve injuries
questions.learning: Pain and numbness confined to the anterolateral aspect of the thigh are classic for meralgia paresthetica, which results from compression or injury to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (also called the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the diagnosis from the given abdominal X-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rectal foreign body

The image shows a foreign body in the rectum which is most likely a bottle.

A variety of foreign bodies are seen in the rectum many of which are hard to remove due to the difficulty in vacuum creation while removing it through the anus.

The object can be pushed from above into the assistant’s fingers in the rectum, or removed by means of a rectotomy in a proximal area of the rectum.

If there is difficulty in removing then laparotomy is advised.

If a considerable laceration is seen while removing then a temporary colostomy is necessary for healing as there is a high risk of associated necrotizing fascitis which needs broad-spectrum antibiotics. There can be associated bladder or urethral damage.
questions.learning: Rectal foreign body — The image shows a foreign body in the rectum which is most likely a bottle. A variety of foreign bodies are seen in the rectum many of which are hard to remove due to the difficulty in vacuum creation while removing it through the anus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old woman with no comorbidities presented with numbness and paraesthesia of the fingers along with the characteristic finding as shown in the image below. She has no other illnesses and she says these episodes occur when she is under excess stress or during cold temperatures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary Raynaud's phenomenon

In the above clinical scenario of a patient with numbness, parasthesia in episodes following stress or cold exposure, with the image showing a characteristic change in color of the finger, and with the history of no previous illness is most likely of primary Raynaud's phenomenon.

Raynaud's phenomenon:

* Episodic digital ischemia due to the vasospasm of digital arteries.

* Cold exposure or emotional stress can trigger it.

* The blanching/ischemic phase of the phenomenon with pallor/cyanosis is often accompanied by numbness and paraesthesia.

* Capillaries and venules dilate and cyanosis results from the deoxygenated blood that is present in these vessels.

* Color changes are usually well-demarcated and are confined to the fingers or toes.

* In the rewarming phase, digital vasospasm resolves and blood flows into the dilated arterioles and capillaries increase dramatically causing reactive hyperemia which imparts bright red color to the digits.

* Some may experience only pallor cyanosis while others experience both pallor and cyanosis.

Types of Raynaud's:
1.Primary/idiopathic

2. Secondary associated with other diseases like:

*

* Collagen vascular diseases: scleroderma, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, dermatomyositis, polymyositis

* Arterial occlusive diseases: atherosclerosis of the extremities, thromboangiitis
obliterans, acute arterial occlusion

* Neurologic disorders: intervertebral disk disease, syringomyelia

* Blood dyscrasias: cold agglutinins, cryoglobulinemia, cryofibrinogenemia,

* Trauma: vibration injury, electric shock, cold injury, typing, piano playing

* Drugs and toxins: ergot derivatives, methysergide, β-adrenergic receptor
blockers

Management:

* Reassurance, warm clothing, and avoiding cold exposures.

* Reduce or abstain from smoking and reduce stress levels.

* Drug treatments such as CCBs (nifedipine, amlodipine), alpha 1 blockers ( prazosin) are used only for advanced cases.

* In secondary Raynaud's, Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors like sildenafil, tadalafil may improve symptoms.
questions.learning: Primary Raynaud's phenomenon — In the above clinical scenario of a patient with numbness, parasthesia in episodes following stress or cold exposure, with the image showing a characteristic change in color of the finger, and with the history of no previous…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient is undergoing a surgery for removal of a benign tumour from the parotid gland. Which of the following structures should be preserved during this surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Facial nerve

The facial nerve (CN VII) is the most important structure to identify and preserve during parotidectomy.

• The facial nerve enters the parotid gland and divides within it into its major terminal branches.
• The parotid gland is classically divided into superficial and deep lobes by the facial nerve.
• Injury can result in ipsilateral facial paralysis, making preservation essential during surgery.

Why not the other options?

• (a) Facial artery: Runs through the face but is not the critical structure that divides the parotid gland.
• (b) Auriculotemporal nerve: Related to the parotid region and carries secretomotor fibers, but preservation is not the primary surgical concern.
• (c) Zygomatic artery: Not the key structure at risk during parotidectomy.
questions.learning: Facial nerve — The facial nerve (CN VII) is the most important structure to identify and preserve during parotidectomy. • The facial nerve enters the parotid gland and divides within it into its major terminal branches. • The parotid gland is classically…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mr. X, a 46-year-old man, presents with lower back pain and dysuria. Laboratory tests show normocytic normochromic anemia and hypercalcemia. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals an M-spike in the gamma region. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of multiple myeloma?
questions.explanation: This patient presents with the classic symptoms of Multiple Myeloma: back pain (bone lesions), anemia, and hypercalcemia. The finding of an M-spike on serum protein electrophoresis is strongly suggestive of a monoclonal gammopathy. To further support and confirm this diagnosis, testing for Bence Jones protein in the urine is highly appropriate, as it detects the monoclonal free light chains being produced by the malignant plasma cells. Liver function tests (Option A) are generally not helpful for this hematological malignancy. UACR (Option C) is used to monitor diabetic kidney disease, not myeloma. The heat and acetic acid test (Option D) is a general test for proteinuria but is not specific for the monoclonal light chains seen in myeloma. The gold standard for definitive diagnosis would be a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showing clonal plasma cells. Multiple myeloma is a complex disease requiring multidisciplinary management, including chemotherapy, steroids, and often bone-strengthening agents
questions.learning: This patient presents with the classic symptoms of Multiple Myeloma: back pain (bone lesions), anemia, and hypercalcemia. The finding of an M-spike on serum protein electrophoresis is strongly suggestive of a monoclonal gammopathy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, step-ladder–pattern fever, headache, and malaise, with symptoms progressively worsening over the past two weeks. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate to confirm the suspected condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with classical features of enteric (typhoid) fever, including step-ladder pattern fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, and malaise progressing over two weeks. In such cases, the commonly used diagnostic test in many exam settings is the Widal test, which detects antibodies against Salmonella typhi (O and H antigens) in the patient’s serum. The Widal test becomes positive after the first week of infection, making it useful in patients presenting in the second week, as in this case. It is widely used in clinical practice, especially in resource-limited settings, and is often considered the expected answer in theoretical examinations. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Stool culture → Positive in later stages (3rd week) (C) Blood culture → Best in early disease but may take time and may not always be positive later (D) Urine culture → Not specific for typhoid diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient presents with classical features of enteric (typhoid) fever, including step-ladder pattern fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, and malaise progressing over two weeks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis for an elderly female patient with diabetes, as depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: The clinical context of an elderly diabetic patient presenting with aggressive, necrotic facial and orbital inflammation is highly suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis. This is a life-threatening fungal infection caused by molds of the order Mucorales. Diabetic patients, especially those in ketoacidosis, are uniquely susceptible because the fungi thrive in acidic, high-glucose environments. The image shows the typical rapid progression with tissue necrosis and potential black eschar (necrotic tissue) due to the fungus's angioinvasive nature, which causes vascular thrombosis and infarction. Rhinosporidiosis (Option A) typically presents as painless, friable, strawberry-like polyps in the nose. A foreign body (Option C) would cause localized inflammation but not widespread necrotic destruction. Aspergillosis (Option D) can cause invasive sinusitis, but it is generally less hyper-acute than mucormycosis and is more common in severely neutropenic patients. Management of mucormycosis is a medical and surgical emergency involving aggressive debridement, intravenous Amphotericin B, and strict glycemic control. Without rapid intervention, the infection can spread to the brain with nearly 100% mortality
questions.learning: The clinical context of an elderly diabetic patient presenting with aggressive, necrotic facial and orbital inflammation is highly suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presented with recurrent epistaxis. There is no history of trauma associated with it. On examination, there is a firm purplish mass on the left posterior choanae. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Surgical excision

The most probable diagnosis is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma and the most appropriate step in its management is surgical excision.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma(JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumour seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality.

Patients usually present with, profuse, recurrent, and spontaneous epistaxis (most common presentation). A mass may be present in either the postnatal space, resulting in progressive nasal obstruction, or nasopharynx, where it may obstruct both choanae. The mass is firm in consistency, but digital palpation of the same should not be done. If the mass obstructs the eustachian tube, conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion may be observed. Proptosis, swelling of the cheeks, broadening of the nasal bridge, and involvement of 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 6th cranial nerves may occur.

JNA can be diagnosed using CT, MRI, and carotid angiography. Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus due to the presence of a mass in the pterygomaxillary space is a characteristic CT finding of JNA. This is known as the Holman-Miller sign or antral sign, as shown in the image below.

Surgical excision is the treatment of choice though radiotherapy and chemotherapy monotherapy or in combination have also been used. Radiotherapy(Option C) is considered for recurrent inaccessible tumours. Chemotherapy with doxorubicin, vincristine, and dacarbazine is used in the case of very aggressive recurrent tumours and residual tumours. Hormonal therapy can be used as a primary or adjunctive treatment.
questions.learning: Surgical excision — The most probable diagnosis is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma and the most appropriate step in its management is surgical excision.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency room after an RTA with a history of diplopia, epistaxis, and restricted eye movements. The radiological examination is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Orbital floor fracture

The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

Blowout fractures are isolated comminuted fractures caused by direct trauma to the orbit that result in a backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in the intraorbital pressure. This causes a fracture at the weakest point of the orbital wall, which is usually the posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone in the orbital floor. The second most common site for orbital blowout fractures is the medial wall of the orbit.

An isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called a blowout fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum into the maxillary sinus, which may lead to enophthalmos and entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle. The floor is made of zygomatic, maxillary, and palatine bones.

The patient with a blowout fracture usually presents with immediate periorbital edema and blood extravasation in and around the orbit. Proptosis of the eyeball secondary to orbital edema or hemorrhage with paraesthesia along the infraorbital nerve is also very common. Clinical signs: periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis, and subconjunctival haemorrhage. Infraorbital hypoesthesia may be present because of entrapment of the infraorbital nerve.

Imaging by a plain x-ray in water's view or by CT demonstrates depression of bony fragments and orbital contents herniating through the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum. This is called the "hanging drop sign" or "teardrop sign".

Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotics.

Le Fort fracture is the term used to describe different types of maxillary fractures.

Investigations:

* X-ray (Water's view) shows a teardrop opacity in the maxillary sinus.

* A CT scan is used to confirm the site and size of the fracture and entrapment of muscle.

* Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants.

Indications of surgery:

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

* Persistent and progressive diplopia in the primary position

* Entrapment of orbital contents

* Large fracture involving at least half of the orbital floor

If any of these conditions are present, surgical correction is required within 2 weeks.

Pearl PF1981: Le-Fort's classification of Maxillary Fracture

Le-Fort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla

* Fracture line passes through the lower part of nasal septum, maxillary antra and the pterygoid plates

* It separates palate from the rest of the face leading to floating teeth or palate

* Also called Guerin’s fracture.

Le-Fort II is a pyramidal fracture

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, lacrimal bone, floor of the orbit, upper part of the maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates

* X-ray or CT appears like hanging maxilla

* It is associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

Le-Fort III is craniofacial dysjunction i.e., facial skeleton completely disconnected from its cranial attachment

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, ethmo-frontal junction, superior orbital fissure, lateral wall of the orbit, fronto-zygomatic and temporo-zygomatic sutures and the upper part of pterygoid plates

* It is also associated with CSF rhinorrhea.
questions.learning: Orbital floor fracture — The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: According to Herrington classification, the decerebrate rigidity is characterized by all except ______
options: Rigidity occurs in all the muscles of the body
Increase in the rate of discharge of the ɣ efferent neuron
Increased excitability of the motor neuron pool
Decerebration produces no phenomenon akin to spinal shock
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rigidity occurs in all the muscles of the body

In decerebrate rigidity, there is rigidity in extensor muscles of all the four extremities (not all muscles of the body).

Decerebration

• Complete transection of the brain stem between the superior and inferior colliculi permits the brain stem pathways to function independently of their input from higher brain structures. This is called a mid-collicular decerebration.
• This lesion interrupts all input from the cortex (corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts) and red nucleus (rubrospinal tract), primarily to distal muscles of the extremities.
• The excitatory and inhibitory reticulospinal pathways (primarily to postural extensor muscles) remain intact.
• The dominance of drive from ascending sensory pathways to the excitatory reticulospinal pathway leads to hyperactivity in extensor muscles in all four extremities which are called decerebrate rigidity.
• The excitatory input from the reticulospinal pathway activates γ-motor neurons which indirectly activate α-motor neurons (via Ia spindle afferent activity). This is called the gamma loop.

Option 4. Spinal shock is different from decebrate rigidity as it is a transient state that can occur immediately after a spinal cord injury. It is characterized by a temporary loss or depression of spinal reflexes below the level of the injury.
questions.learning: Rigidity occurs in all the muscles of the body — In decerebrate rigidity, there is rigidity in extensor muscles of all the four extremities (not all muscles of the body).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person wants to study about the relationship between smoking and lung cancer, so he collects data about people diseased with lung cancer from government hospitals and the number of cigarette packets sold at the same time period. Which type of study is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ecological

The type of study described is an ecological study as the unit of study is the population. The number of cigarette packets sold at the same time is data about the population.

Option A: The unit of study in a cross-sectional study is an individual.

Option C: There is no experiment done here. Hence, it is not experimental study.

Option D: Quasi-experiments are nonrandomized, pre-post intervention studies done when it is not feasible or ethical to conduct a randomized controlled trial. The unit of study is therefore patients or individuals and not population.
questions.learning: Ecological — The type of study described is an ecological study as the unit of study is the population. The number of cigarette packets sold at the same time is data about the population.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Aprepitant is a drug used in the treatment of some cases of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NK1 antagonist

Key clue:

• Chemotherapy-induced nausea & vomiting (CINV)

Think of the “big 3 antiemetic pathways”:

1. Serotonin (5-HT3)
2. Dopamine (D2)
3.

Substance P (NK1)

4.

Aprepitant belongs to the Substance P pathway. Aprepitant = Neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist

5. Blocks Substance P

Acts at:

• Vomiting center (medulla)
• Chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ)

Chemotherapy

↓

Enterochromaffin cells release serotonin

↓

5-HT3 activation → acute vomiting

+

Substance P release (brainstem)

↓

NK1 receptor activation → delayed vomiting

Aprepitant blocks NK1 receptors

↓

Prevents delayed phase vomiting

| Phase | Mediator | Drug

| ----- | -------- | ----

| Acute (0–24 hr) | Serotonin (5-HT3) | Ondansetron

| Delayed (>24 hr) | Substance P | Aprepitant

| Drug | Mechanism | Use

| ---- | --------- | ---

| Aprepitant | NK1 antagonist | CINV (delayed phase)

| Ondansetron | 5-HT3 antagonist | Acute vomiting

| Metoclopramide | D2 antagonist | General antiemetic

| Domperidone | Peripheral D2 blocker | GI motility
